questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 28-year-old woman visits the clinic for a routine check-up. She has a history of epilepsy and has been taking anti-epileptic medication for the past five years. Which of the following statements about folic acid supplementation in patients on anti-epileptic drugs is most accurate?
options: The daily requirement of folic acid is .
The daily requirement of folic acid is .
The daily requirement of folic acid is .
The daily requirement of folic acid is .
questions.explanation: Women on anti-epileptic drugs (AEDs), such as valproate or carbamazepine, are at a significantly increased risk of having a baby with neural tube defects (NTDs). This is because many AEDs interfere with folate metabolism. Therefore, for these high-risk patients, the recommended dose of folic acid is (or depending on the local guideline), which is ten times the standard dose of (Option A) given to low-risk women. Options C and D are also insufficient for this high-risk population. Ideally, this high-dose supplementation should begin at least one to three months before conception and continue through the first trimester. Clinicians must also review and optimize the epilepsy treatment, aiming for the lowest effective dose of the safest possible AED (e.g., lamotrigine or levetiracetam) before the patient becomes pregnant. This targeted nutritional intervention is vital for preventing life-altering congenital malformations
questions.learning: Women on anti-epileptic drugs (AEDs), such as valproate or carbamazepine, are at a significantly increased risk of having a baby with neural tube defects (NTDs).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the condition characterized by painless vision loss among the options provided?
questions.explanation: The image shows a classic “blood and thunder” appearance of the retina, characterized by diffuse retinal hemorrhages, dilated and tortuous veins, and optic disc edema. This is typical of central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO). CRVO occurs due to thrombosis of the central retinal vein, leading to impaired venous drainage, retinal ischemia, and widespread hemorrhages. Clinically, CRVO presents with sudden, painless loss of vision, which is a key feature highlighted in the question. The involvement is diffuse, affecting the entire retina, which helps distinguish it from branch occlusions. Why other options are wrong: (B) Branch retinal vein occlusion (BRVO) → hemorrhages limited to one quadrant, not diffuse (C) Central retinal arterial occlusion (CRAO) → pale retina with cherry-red spot, not hemorrhagic (D) Branch retinal arterial occlusion (BRAO) → localized retinal whitening
questions.learning: The image shows a classic “blood and thunder” appearance of the retina, characterized by diffuse retinal hemorrhages, dilated and tortuous veins, and optic disc edema.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents with sudden onset of chest pain shooting to the neck and interscapular region. X-ray shows widened mediastinum. BP is 110/90 mmHg in the right upper limb and 160/100 mmHg in the left upper limb. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Acute aortic dissection

Sudden-onset severe chest pain, with a wide discrepancy in blood pressure between the two limbs, and a widened mediastinum on x-ray point towards a diagnosis of aortic dissection.

It is initiated by an intimal tear, which allows blood to penetrate into the medial layer, producing a cleavage plane (false lumen) between the inner two-thirds and outer one-third of the media. The true lumen is separated from the false lumen by an intimomedial flap.

Classification of aortic dissection:

Acute aortic dissection can be classified by the original DeBakey system, which is based on the location of the proximal tear and distal extent of the dissection flap, or the Stanford system, which is based only on the location of the proximal tear.

DeBakey
Stanford

Site of dissection

Both ascending and descending aorta
Type I
Type A

Only ascending aorta and arch of the aorta
Type II
Type A

Descending the aorta distal to the subclavian artery

Type IIIa

Limited to the thoracic aorta

Type B

Type IIIb

Extends to the abdominal aorta

Clinically, patients present with tearing chest/back pain associated with diaphoresis, syncope, weakness, and dyspnea or neurological manifestations.

On examination, unequal pulses or blood pressure in the extremities may be seen due to changes of flow in the true and false lumens. There can be hypertension or hypotension, loss of pulses, findings of aortic regurgitation, and pulmonary edema.

Imaging:

Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) is the investigation of choice in a hemodynamically unstable patient. In hemodynamically stable patients, the diagnosis is established with a contrast-enhanced CT scan. The characteristic diagnostic finding is a double-lumen aorta. The image below shows aortic dissection in the thoracic aorta with the true lumen, as well as the false lumen. The true lumen is often the smaller of the two because of being compressed by the false lumen.

Acute coronary syndrome and acute pulmonary embolism may both present with sudden onset chest pain but widened mediastinum and blood pressure discrepancy make aortic dissection more likely. (Options A and B)

Both sudden onset chest pain and widened mediastinum may be seen in esophageal rupture but blood pressure discrepancy between the upper limbs makes aortic dissection more likely. (Option D)

Chest x-ray showing widened mediastinum in a patient with aortic dissection

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: All of the following can activate Hormone- sensitive lipase. Except?
questions.explanation: Hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL) is a key enzyme in adipocytes responsible for the breakdown of stored triacylglycerols into free fatty acids and glycerol (lipolysis). It is activated by phosphorylation in response to hormones that signal a need for energy. Glucagon (Option A), Epinephrine (Option B), and ACTH (Option C) all bind to G-protein coupled receptors that increase intracellular cAMP, thereby activating HSL. Insulin, conversely, is the primary inhibitor of HSL. When blood glucose is high, insulin is secreted to promote fat storage (lipogenesis) and inhibit the breakdown of fat. It acts by activating a phosphatase that dephosphorylates and inactivates HSL, effectively shutting down lipolysis. This regulatory mechanism ensures that fat stores are mobilized only when other energy sources are low. Therefore, insulin is the exception among the hormones listed, as its role is to suppress rather than activate this enzyme
questions.learning: Hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL) is a key enzyme in adipocytes responsible for the breakdown of stored triacylglycerols into free fatty acids and glycerol (lipolysis).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is not considered a contraindication to BCT?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Tumour limited to one quadrant

Breast-conserving therapy (BCT) = lumpectomy + radiotherapy.

Pre requisites for BCT: Tumor must be localised, preferably-  within a single quadrant.

Because:

• Clear tumor margins are obtained  →  lower risk of local recurrence
• Normal breast tissue preserved → better cosmetic appearance.
• Remaining microscopic disease —> treated with radiotherapy.**

Hence,results of BCT become comparable to mastectomy with better cosmetic result —>

✅ Option D. Tumour limited to one quadrant

Prior chest radiation — ❌

• BCT requires postoperative radiotherapy.
• If the patient already received radiation to the chest, additional RT can cause severe tissue damage→ hence, BCT is contraindicated.

Involved margins after resection — ❌

• Positive margins mean residual tumour.
• BCT requires clear margins; otherwise re-excision or mastectomy is needed→ hence, BCT is contraindicated.

Scleroderma — ❌

• It is a collagen vascular disease.
• Such patients have severe radiation toxicity, fibrosis, and poor healing after RT—> hence, BCT is contraindicated.

Key contraindications to BCT

Absolute

• Prior chest RT
• Pregnancy (when RT required)
• Multicentric disease
• Persistent positive margins
• Collagen vascular diseases

Relative

• Large tumour relative to breast size
• Locally advanced breast cancer (LABC)
questions.learning: Tumour limited to one quadrant Breast-conserving therapy (BCT) = lumpectomy + radiotherapy. Pre requisites for BCT: Tumor must be localised, preferably- within a single quadrant.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Insect in ear can be killed by:
questions.explanation: When a live insect enters the external auditory canal, it can cause severe pain and distress due to its movements against the tympanic membrane. The immediate management priority is to kill or immobilize the insect before attempting removal. Instilling a few drops of oil (such as olive oil, mineral oil, or even baby oil) is the safest and most effective method. The oil suffocates the insect quickly by blocking its respiratory spiracles. Once dead, it can be easily removed by irrigation or forceps. Hydrogen peroxide (Option B) can cause bubbling and irritation that may provoke the insect to sting or bite. Water (Option C) may cause some insects to swell, making removal more difficult. Petrol (Option D) is highly toxic and corrosive to the delicate skin of the ear canal and should never be used. Therefore, oil is the standard clinical recommendation for safely killing an insect in the ear
questions.learning: When a live insect enters the external auditory canal, it can cause severe pain and distress due to its movements against the tympanic membrane. The immediate management priority is to kill or immobilize the insect before attempting removal.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In the case of a 7-year-old school-going child, which would be the most appropriate indicator to measure the current nutritional status?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Weight for height

In school-aged children (5–19 years), weight-for-height is the most appropriate indicator for assessing current nutritional status, as it reflects acute malnutrition (wasting) and is independent of age. Indicators such as birth weight, head circumference, and mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) have limited utility in a 7-year-old child.

High-Yield Pearls

• Weight-for-height: Best indicator of current nutritional status (wasting/acute malnutrition).
• Height-for-age: Indicates chronic malnutrition (stunting).
• Weight-for-age: Reflects underweight but cannot differentiate between acute and chronic malnutrition.
• Birth weight: Assesses intrauterine growth, not current nutritional status.
• Head circumference: Useful only up to 2 years of age for monitoring brain growth.
• MUAC: Primarily used to screen acute malnutrition in children 6–59 months, not school-aged children.
questions.learning: Weight for height — In school-aged children (5–19 years), weight-for-height is the most appropriate indicator for assessing current nutritional status, as it reflects acute malnutrition (wasting) and is independent of age.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 32-year-old woman, G2P1L1, comes for a quadruple test at 16 weeks. Which of the following is not included in the quadruple test?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Dimeric inhibin B

Dimeric inhibin B is not included in the quadruple test.

The quadruple test, performed during the second trimester (15–22 weeks, ideally around 16–18 weeks), includes the following markers:

1. Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP)
2. Unconjugated estriol (uE3)
3. Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG)
4. Inhibin A

The quadruple test is primarily used for screening chromosomal abnormalities such as Down syndrome (trisomy 21), Edward syndrome (trisomy 18), and neural tube defects.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text:
Identify the chart given in the picture below.

ETDRS- Early treatment diabetic retinopathy study
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hess chart

The chart given in the picture is Hess's chart.

Hess chart is used to diagnose and monitor patients with incomitant strabismus by assessing the field of a binocular single vision. In its interpretation, a smaller chart indicates the eye with the paretic muscle and a larger chart indicates the eye with an overacting muscle.

Incomitant strabismus is one where squint generally results from the limitation of eye movement associated with paralytic or mechanical etiologies like extraocular muscle palsy, thyroid ophthalmopathy, blow-out fracture, myasthenia gravis, etc. The field of binocular single vision is the area where bifoveal fusion of an object of interest occurs.

Other options:

Option B: The Snellen chart is used to test visual acuity. Visual acuity is the eye's ability to discriminate between two points.

A picture of the Snellen chart is given below.

Option C: The Pelli-Robson contrast sensitivity letter chart consists of letters of constant size but decreasing contrast. It is viewed by the patient from a distance of 1 meter until the lowest resolvable group of three letters on the chart is reached. It is used to measure contrast sensitivity, a measure of the ability to distinguish an object against its background.

An image of the Pelli-Robson chart used in the middle east is given below.

Option D: The early treatment diabetic retinopathy study or ETDRS chart presents a series of 5 letters of equal difficulty on each row, with standardized spacing between letters and rows. It consists of a total of 14 lines having 70 letters. It is also used to test visual acuity. An image of the ETDRS chart is given below.
questions.learning: Hess chart — The chart given in the picture is Hess's chart. Hess chart is used to diagnose and monitor patients with incomitant strabismus by assessing the field of a binocular single vision.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The most commonly involved artery in pseudoaneurysm formation:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Femoral artery

The most commonly involved artery in pseudoaneurysm is the femoral artery.

A true aneurysm involves all three vessel wall layers, while a pseudoaneurysm involves only the intimal and medial layers. Pseudoaneurysms are most commonly iatrogenic due to repeated arterial puncture for blood sampling or catheterization procedures which injure the arterial wall. The most commonly used artery in endovascular surgeries is the femoral artery, and hence, also the most commonly involved in the formation of pseudo aneurysms.

Aneurysms are usually pulsatile on palpation and a systolic bruit can be heard on auscultation.

Doppler ultrasound reveals a bidirectional, 'to-and-fro' flow of blood which is known as the yin-yang sign.

Treatment options include endovascular stent insertion, ultrasound-guided thrombin injection, and surgical repair.

Other options:

Option A: Aortic aneurysm can be types - thoracic or abdominal. They are usually seen in heritable conditions like Marfan syndrome or vascular-type Ehlers-Danlos.

Option C: The most common peripheral aneurysm is the popliteal aneurysm (80% of the cases) followed by the femoral aneurysm.
questions.learning: Femoral artery — The most commonly involved artery in pseudoaneurysm is the femoral artery. A true aneurysm involves all three vessel wall layers, while a pseudoaneurysm involves only the intimal and medial layers.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient involved in a road traffic accident presents with subcutaneous emphysema, absent air entry on the right side, and unstable vital signs. What is the immediate management in this situation?
options: Insertion of wide bore needle in the 5th intercostal space
Wide bore needle decompression and IV fluids
questions.explanation: The patient’s presentation—history of trauma, subcutaneous emphysema, absent air entry on one side, and hemodynamic instability—is highly suggestive of tension pneumothorax, a life-threatening emergency. In this condition, air accumulates under pressure in the pleural space, leading to lung collapse, mediastinal shift, and reduced venous return, which can rapidly cause shock and death if not treated immediately. The first and most crucial step in management is emergency needle decompression using a wide bore needle. The currently preferred site is the 5th intercostal space in the anterior or mid-axillary line, as it is safer and more accessible in trauma patients. This procedure rapidly relieves intrathoracic pressure and stabilizes the patient. Why other options are incorrect: (B) Needle decompression with IV fluids: Fluids are supportive but do not address the primary problem immediately. (C) Intubation and PPV: May worsen tension pneumothorax if done before decompression. (D) e-FAST: Diagnostic tool; treatment should not be delayed in unstable patients
questions.learning: The patient’s presentation—history of trauma, subcutaneous emphysema, absent air entry on one side, and hemodynamic instability—is highly suggestive of tension pneumothorax, a life-threatening emergency.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Considering the structural organization of the esophageal wall, which consists of several distinct layers, which of the following is NOT a recognized layer of the esophagus?
questions.explanation: The esophagus is unique among the organs of the gastrointestinal tract because it lacks a true serosa. Most other abdominal digestive organs are covered by a serous membrane (visceral peritoneum). Instead, the outermost layer of the esophagus is the adventitia, which consists of loose connective tissue that anchors the esophagus to surrounding structures in the mediastinum. The other listed layers are standard components of the esophageal wall: the mucosa (Option A), which is the innermost lining; the submucosa (Option B), which contains glands and blood vessels; and the muscularis externa (Option D), which consists of both skeletal and smooth muscle layers to facilitate peristalsis. The absence of a serosa is clinically important because it allows esophageal infections and tumors to spread more easily into the surrounding mediastinal space, often leading to more rapid complications compared to organs with a protective serous layer
questions.learning: The esophagus is unique among the organs of the gastrointestinal tract because it lacks a true serosa. Most other abdominal digestive organs are covered by a serous membrane (visceral peritoneum).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis in a cricket player who sustained a head injury, appeared normal initially, but was later found unconscious?
questions.explanation: (EDH). The clinical history of a head injury followed by a "lucid interval"—where the patient is temporarily conscious and appears fine before rapidly deteriorating—is the classic textbook presentation of an Extradural Hemorrhage (Option A). This typically results from a traumatic rupture of the middle meningeal artery. The provided CT scan provides the definitive diagnosis, showing the pathognomonic biconvex (lentiform), hyperdense lesion that does not cross suture lines. A subdural hemorrhage (Option C) would appear as a crescent-shaped lesion on CT and usually lacks a clear lucid interval. Subarachnoid hemorrhage (Option D) would show hyperdensity within the brain's cisterns and sulci . EDH is a neurosurgical emergency; as the arterial bleed expands, it increases intracranial pressure, leading to the sudden collapse. Immediate surgical evacuation via craniotomy is often life-saving and leads to a full recovery if performed early
questions.learning: The clinical history of a head injury followed by a "lucid interval"—where the patient is temporarily conscious and appears fine before rapidly deteriorating—is the classic textbook presentation of an Extradural Hemorrhage (Option A).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the structure marked in the image given below.
questions.explanation: The provided image is a horizontal (axial) section of the human brain at the level of the basal ganglia. The marked structure is a V-shaped band of white matter situated between the thalamus and caudate nucleus medially and the lentiform nucleus laterally. This is the internal capsule, a major highway for motor and sensory fibers connecting the cerebral cortex with the brainstem and spinal cord. The external capsule (Option A) is a thinner band of white matter located lateral to the putamen. The putamen (Option C) is the large, lateral portion of the lentiform nucleus. The caudate nucleus (Option D) is the C-shaped gray matter structure located in the wall of the lateral ventricle, medial to the internal capsule's anterior limb. Strokes involving the posterior limb of the internal capsule are common and result in significant contralateral hemiparesis. Precise identification of these deep brain structures is fundamental for neurologists to localize lesions based on a patient's clinical deficits
questions.learning: The provided image is a horizontal (axial) section of the human brain at the level of the basal ganglia. The marked structure is a V-shaped band of white matter situated between the thalamus and caudate nucleus medially and the lentiform nucleus laterally.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is the correct definition of postpartum pyrexia?
questions.explanation: Postpartum pyrexia, or puerperal pyrexia, is traditionally defined as a temperature rise to ≥ 100.4°F (38°C) or higher, occurring on any two of the first ten days following delivery, excluding the initial 24 hours. The first 24 hours are typically excluded because a mild temperature elevation during this period is often due to dehydration or the physiological stress of labor. Option B, C, and D are incorrect because they specify timeframes within the first 24 hours, which do not meet the standard diagnostic criteria for morbid pyrexia. The most common cause of pyrexia during the puerperium is genital tract infection (puerperal sepsis), but clinicians must also consider urinary tract infections, mastitis, and deep vein thrombosis. Accurate diagnosis requires a thorough physical examination and relevant cultures. Prompt treatment with broad-spectrum antibiotics is vital to prevent severe maternal morbidity or mortality associated with sepsis
questions.learning: Postpartum pyrexia, or puerperal pyrexia, is traditionally defined as a temperature rise to ≥ 100.4°F (38°C) or higher, occurring on any two of the first ten days following delivery, excluding the initial 24 hours.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient came to the hospital with complaint of abdominal pain. Routine investigations were unremarkable. On observation, the urine turned black on standing. Which of the following enzymes is likely to be defective in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Homogentisate oxidase

Urine turning black on exposure to air is suggestive of alkaptonuria which occurs due to the defect in homogentisate oxidase enzyme.

Alkaptonuria is a disorder of tyrosine metabolism, that develops due to the defect in homogentisate oxidase, which oxidizes homogentisate to maleylacetoacetate. The defect in this enzyme leads to the accumulation of homogentisate, which is then excreted in the urine. The excreted homogentisate gets oxidized when exposed to the air and causes the urine to turn black.

In some cases, the excessive homogentisate may get oxidized to benzoquinone acetate, which binds to the connective tissue. This leads to arthritis and pigmentation of the connective tissue, a condition called ochronosis.

Other options:

Option B: Xanthine oxidase deficiency results in hypouricemia, xanthinuria, and xanthine lithiasis.

Option C: Defects in phenylalanine hydroxylase can lead to phenylketonuria characterised by hyperreflexia, seizures, hypopigmentation, low IQ, hyperactivity, and tremors.

Option D: Defects in dihydroorotate dehydrogenase are rarely seen in clinical practice. Miller syndrome is associated with this defect.
questions.learning: Homogentisate oxidase Urine turning black on exposure to air is suggestive of alkaptonuria which occurs due to the defect in homogentisate oxidase enzyme.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient is confused, opens his eyes on painful stimuli, flexes one limb on painful stimuli, and can localize the stimulus with the other limb. His Glasgow Coma Score is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 11

The Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) is a standardized tool used to assess the level of consciousness by evaluating eye opening, verbal response, and motor response. The total score ranges from 3 to 15, with lower scores indicating more severe neurologic impairment.

In this patient:

• Eye opening to pain = E2
• Confused verbal response = V4
• Localizes painful stimulus with one limb = M5

Although the other limb demonstrates abnormal flexion, the best motor response is used when calculating the GCS.

Total GCS = E2 + V4 + M5 = 11
questions.learning: 11 The Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) is a standardized tool used to assess the level of consciousness by evaluating eye opening, verbal response, and motor response.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 33-year-old male met with a road traffic accident. There is persistent watery discharge mixed with blood from his nose for 3 days which cannot be sniffed back. Which of the following should not be done in this condition?
options: Plan surgical treatment with functional endoscopic sinus surgery
Bed rest and avoiding strenuous activity
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Plan surgical treatment with functional endoscopic sinus surgery

In the given scenario of a male presenting with watery nasal discharge mixed with blood that cannot be sniffed back following a road traffic accident is suggestive of CSF rhinorrhea. Surgical treatment with functional endoscopic sinus surgery should not be done in this patient.

CSF rhinorrhea refers to the leakage of cerebrospinal fluid into the nose. It can occur as clear fluid or be mixed with blood, particularly in cases of acute head injuries. Fracture of the cribriform plate of the ethmoid is the most common cause of this. Other causes include accidental or surgical trauma, infection and inflammation of the sinuses, neoplasms, and congenital lesions associated with skull base defects or may occur spontaneously.

When CSF rhinorrhea occurs after head trauma, it often contains a mixture of blood, leading to a characteristic appearance known as the double-target sign when collected on a piece of filter paper. This sign presents as a central red spot (indicating blood) surrounded by a lighter peripheral halo.

CSF fluid gushes down on straining and bending forward. It cannot be sniffed back. CSF doesn’t stiffen a handkerchief, but nasal secretions do because of their mucus content.

High-resolution computerized tomography (HRCT) is the investigation of choice for localizing the site of the leak.(Option A)

Beta-2 transferrin protein detection by electrophoresis is a sensitive and specific test for detecting CSF rhinorrhea. Beta trace protein is another protein that is secreted by meninges and choroid plexus and is specific to CSF.

Treatment of CSF rhinorrhea:

* Bed rest with head elevation.

* Avoid blowing the nose, sneezing, and straining. (Option C)

* Prophylactic antibiotics can be administered to prevent meningitis. (Option D)

* Early cases of post-traumatic CSF rhinorrhea are managed conservatively by placing the patient in a semi-sitting position.

* Persistent cases may be treated surgically by intracranial or nasal endoscopic approach.(option B)

Feature
CSF fluid
Nasal secretion

History

Nasal or sinus surgery, Sneezing, nasal stuffiness, head injury, or intracranial tumor

Sneezing, nasal stuffiness, head injury, or itching in the nose, or lacrimation

Flow of discharge

A few drops or a stream of fluid gushes down when bending forward or straining and cannot be sniffed back

Continuous. No effect on bending forward or straining. Can be sniffed back

Character of discharge

Thin, watery, and clear

Slimy (mucous) or clear (tears)

Sugar content

More than 30 mg/dl

Less than 10 mg/dl

The presence of beta-2 transferrin and beta-trace proteins

Always present. It is specific to CSF

Always absent

Pearl PF1951: Features of CSF rhinorrhea

* Reservoir sign - In CSF rhinorrhea, the fluid which had collected in the sinuses, particularly sphenoid, empties into the nose.

* Double ring sign or halo sign or target sign - CSF is mixed with blood and collected on a piece of filter paper. It shows a central red spot (blood) and a peripheral lighter halo.

The image below shows the double ring sign in CSF rhinorrhoea:

* CSF can’t be sniffed back.

* CSF doesn’t stiffen the handkerchief.

Note: The repeated reappearance of pus immediately after cleaning, in the external auditory canal of patients with acute mastoiditis/coalescent mastoiditis is also referred to as Reservoir sign.
questions.learning: Plan surgical treatment with functional endoscopic sinus surgery In the given scenario of a male presenting with watery nasal discharge mixed with blood that cannot be sniffed back following a road traffic accident is suggestive of CSF rhinorrhea.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: What nerve fibers are responsible for the transmission of proprioception?
questions.explanation: The Erlanger-Gasser classification categorizes nerve fibers based on their diameter and conduction velocity. Proprioception—the sense of self-movement and body position—is transmitted by the largest and fastest myelinated fibers, categorized as A alpha fibers (or Group Ia/Ib). These fibers carry signals from muscle spindles and Golgi tendon organs to the central nervous system with speeds up to 120 m/s. A beta fibers (Option B) are slightly smaller and slower, primarily responsible for carrying sensations of touch, pressure, and vibration. A gamma fibers (Option C) are motor fibers that innervate the contractile ends of muscle spindles to regulate their sensitivity. A delta fibers (Option D) are thin, myelinated fibers that transmit "fast" pain and cold temperature. C fibers (not listed) are unmyelinated and carry "slow" burning pain and warmth. High-speed proprioceptive feedback is essential for maintaining balance, coordinating complex motor tasks, and protecting joints from overextension during movement
questions.learning: The Erlanger-Gasser classification categorizes nerve fibers based on their diameter and conduction velocity. Proprioception—the sense of self-movement and body position—is transmitted by the largest and fastest myelinated fibers, categorized as A alpha…

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: An 8-year-old boy is brought to the dermatology clinic because of severe sun sensitivity since infancy. His parents report that even brief exposure to sunlight causes blistering and persistent freckles over his face. Examination reveals multiple hyperpigmented macules on sun-exposed areas and a non-healing ulcer over the nose. Skin biopsy confirms basal cell carcinoma. The underlying genetic defect most likely involves failure of which of the following DNA repair mechanisms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Nucleotide excision repair

This child has xeroderma pigmentosum (XP), an autosomal recessive disorder caused by defective nucleotide excision repair (NER).

• NER normally removes UV-induced pyrimidine (thymine) dimers.
• Failure to repair these lesions leads to accumulation of DNA mutations, causing:

• Extreme photosensitivity
• Early freckling of sun-exposed skin
• Premature skin aging
• Early-onset basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and melanoma

Why the other options are incorrect?

• A. Base excision repair: Repairs small, non-helix-distorting DNA lesions (eg, oxidized, alkylated, or deaminated bases and uracil incorporation).
• B. Mismatch repair: Corrects replication errors such as base mismatches and insertion-deletion loops; defects cause Lynch syndrome (HNPCC) with microsatellite instability.
• D. Non-homologous end joining: Repairs double-stranded DNA breaks; defects impair V(D)J recombination, leading to immunodeficiency.
questions.learning: Nucleotide excision repair — This child has xeroderma pigmentosum (XP), an autosomal recessive disorder caused by defective nucleotide excision repair (NER). • NER normally removes UV-induced pyrimidine (thymine) dimers. • Failure to repair these lesions…

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In a patient with an inguinal hernia, the surgeon reduces the entire hernial sac into the abdominal cavity without reducing the contents. What is this known as?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Reduction en masse

The surgeon reducing the entire hernial sac into the abdominal cavity without reducing the contents is referred to as reduction en masse of the hernia.

Reduction en-masse of inguinal hernia refers to the reduction or migration of the hernial sac along with the incarcerated bowel into the properitoneal space. The properitoneal space lies between the parietal peritoneum and the anterior abdominal wall. This is likely to occur following forcible attempts to reduce the hernia but may occur spontaneously. Though the hernial sac no longer lies in the inguinal or femoral canal, it contains an obstructed bowel loop that causes small bowel obstruction. This is a rare condition as forcible reduction of hernias is not done and early repair is carried out.

The patient may give a history of difficult reduction and the symptoms of bowel obstruction persist even after the hernia is reduced. On a CT scan, a hernial sac in properitoneal space with a fibrous constriction at the neck may be visualized. This hernial sac will contain the bowel loop with wall enhancement and fluid that suggest strangulation. Early surgical intervention is required.

Other options:

Option A: Maydl's hernias are defined as the presence of two small bowel loops within a single hernial sac, that is, there are two efferent and two afferent loops of the bowel, forming a "W" shape.

Option B: Sliding hernia occurs when an internal organ composes a portion of the wall of the hernia sac. The most common viscus involved is the sigmoid colon and its mesentery on the left side and the caecum on the right side. It is more common on the left side. They are usually variants of indirect inguinal hernias. The failure to recognize the visceral component of the hernia sac resulting in injury to the bowel or bladder is the major concern in sliding hernia.

Option D: Hernias which cannot be reduced are referred to as incarcerated hernias while hernias with compromised blood supply to its contents are known as strangulated hernias.
questions.learning: Reduction en masse — The surgeon reducing the entire hernial sac into the abdominal cavity without reducing the contents is referred to as reduction en masse of the hernia.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following biologic agents used in the treatment of inflammatory bowel disease acts by inhibiting the enzyme 'Janus Kinase'?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Tofacitinib

Tofacitinib is an oral targeted synthetic disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (tsDMARD) that acts by inhibiting Janus kinase (JAK) enzymes, primarily JAK1 and JAK3. This blocks the JAK-STAT signaling pathway, thereby reducing the production of multiple pro-inflammatory cytokines involved in immune-mediated diseases.

In inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), tofacitinib is approved for the treatment of moderate to severe ulcerative colitis in patients who have had an inadequate response or intolerance to conventional therapy or anti-TNF agents.

Why not the other options?

• A. Infliximab: A chimeric monoclonal antibody against TNF-α; used in Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis.
• B. Adalimumab: A fully human monoclonal antibody against TNF-α.
• C. Vedolizumab: A monoclonal antibody against α4β7 integrin, preventing lymphocyte migration specifically into the gastrointestinal tract.
questions.learning: Tofacitinib Tofacitinib is an oral targeted synthetic disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (tsDMARD) that acts by inhibiting Janus kinase (JAK) enzymes, primarily JAK1 and JAK3.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman presents with hearing loss and pulsatile tinnitus. Examination reveals conductive hearing loss with a negative Rinne test (bone conduction better than air conduction), and a reddish mass is seen behind the tympanic membrane. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical combination of hearing loss, pulsatile tinnitus (hearing a heartbeat in the ear), and a reddish-blue mass visible behind an intact tympanic membrane is pathognomonic for a Glomus tumour (paraganglioma). Specifically, this could be a Glomus tympanicum or a Glomus jugulare. The reddish mass is often described as the "Rising Sun" sign. Acute otitis media (Option A) presents with severe pain and a bulging, opaque eardrum. Chronic otitis media (Option B) typically involves a perforation and discharge. Serous otitis media (Option D) involves fluid but appears amber or yellowish with bubbles, and lacks pulsatile tinnitus. Glomus tumors are highly vascular, benign growths arising from the chemoreceptor cells. Conductive hearing loss occurs because the mass restricts ossicular movement. Diagnosis is confirmed through imaging like CT (showing "moth-eaten" bone) and MRI. Management typically involves surgical excision or radiotherapy for large or inoperable cases. Recognizing pulsatile tinnitus and a vascular mass is the key to identifying this rare middle ear neoplasm
questions.learning: The clinical combination of hearing loss, pulsatile tinnitus (hearing a heartbeat in the ear), and a reddish-blue mass visible behind an intact tympanic membrane is pathognomonic for a Glomus tumour (paraganglioma).

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: The organism with following life cycle is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Strongyloides stercoralis

The given life cycle is of Strongyloides stercoralis.

The organism has a parasitic cycle and a free-living soil cycle. Humans are the natural host but morphologically indistinguishable strains may be seen in dogs and cats.

Filariform larvae are the infective form and there are two modes of infection:

1. Penetration of skin by 3rd stage filariform larva.
2. Autoinfection (external and internal).

The female worms present in the intestine lays eggs in the mucosa which hatches immediately, releasing the rhabditiform larva. The larva migrates into the lumen of the intestine and passes down to be released in the feces. The rhabditiform larva may change into filariform larva while passing through the bowel.

The filariform larvae in the bowel do not leave the host and become a source of autoinfection as they penetrate the colonic mucosa or perianal skin.

The rhabditiform larvae passed in the feces may undergo two types of development in the soil:

1. Direct development: The rhabditiform larva moults twice on reaching the soil to become the infective filariform larva. The filariform larva can penetrate the skin and enter the circulation.
2. Indirect development: The rhabditiform larvae develop into free-living males and females in the soil.

Other options:

Option B: Humans are the only natural host and the life-cycle of Ancylostoma duodenale is completed in a single host. The eggs laid by the female worms in the intestine are passed in feces. The embryo develops inside the egg and a rhabditiform larva hatches out in about 2 days.

The rhabditiform larva moults twice to form the filariform larva (infective stage). It penetrates the skin and enters the subcutaneous tissue.

Option C: Humans are the only natural host for Ascaris lumbricoides and have no intermediate host. The infection is acquired by ingestion of embryonated eggs (infective stage).

Option D: Enterobius vermicularis completes its entire life cycle in the human host and has no intermediate host. Embryonated eggs are the infective form. Infection is acquired by ingestion of the eggs. Autoinfection and retroinfection are seen.
questions.learning: Strongyloides stercoralis — The given life cycle is of Strongyloides stercoralis. The organism has a parasitic cycle and a free-living soil cycle.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: During a measles epidemic in the community, a 6-month-old child was vaccinated against the same. When should the second dose be administered to this child?
options: The child should be given a second dose as soon as she reaches 9 months of age
The child should be given a second dose after 2 weeks of last dose
The child should be given a second dose after 6 weeks of last dose
The child should be given the second dose of measles at 12 months of age
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. The child should be given a second dose as soon as she reaches 9 months of age

An infant immunized between 6-9 months should receive a second dose as soon as the child reaches 9 months of age.

While the scheduled age of receiving the 1st dose of measles vaccine is at 9 months, it can be lowered to 6 months during a measles epidemic in the community. For infants immunized between 6 months to 9 months of age, a second dose should be administered as soon as the child reaches the age of 9 months, provided that 4 weeks have elapsed since the last dose.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following is not included in the components of Child-Pugh scoring?
questions.explanation: The Child-Pugh score is used to assess the prognosis of chronic liver disease, primarily cirrhosis. It consists of exactly five clinical and laboratory variables: 1. Total Bilirubin (Option B) 2. Serum Albumin (Option A) 3. Prothrombin Time or INR (Option C) 4. Ascites (none, mild, or moderate) 5. Hepatic Encephalopathy (none, grade 1-2, or grade 3-4) "LFT" (Liver Function Test) is a broad term that encompasses many enzymes like ALT and AST. While bilirubin and albumin are part of a liver function panel, the general term "LFT" is NOT a specific component of the Child-Pugh score. Specifically, the levels of transaminases (ALT/AST) do not influence the Child-Pugh calculation. Therefore, LFT is the "except" choice. The score is used to categorize patients into Class A, B, or C, which correlates with 1-year and 2-year survival rates
questions.learning: The Child-Pugh score is used to assess the prognosis of chronic liver disease, primarily cirrhosis. It consists of exactly five clinical and laboratory variables: 1.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: All lung carcinomas for diagnosis requires CECT thorax but MRI is useful in which of the following:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Pancoast tumor

MRI is useful in Pancoast tumor because of the associated soft tissue infiltration, extent of which can be best visualised using an MRI

Pancoast syndrome/superior sulcus tumor results from a local extension of a tumor growing in the apex of the lung, with the involvement of C8, T1, and T2 nerve roots.

It presents with pain that radiates to the ulnar distribution of the arm, often with the destruction of the 1st and 2nd ribs. Patients with the central or endobronchial growth of the primary tumor may present with a cough, hemoptysis, wheeze, stridor, dyspnea, or post-obstructive pneumonitis.

Regional spread can cause

• Tracheal obstruction,
• Esophageal compression with dysphagia
• Recurrent laryngeal paralysis with hoarseness
• Phrenic nerve palsy with the elevation of the hemidiaphragm and dyspnea
• Sympathetic nerve paralysis with Horner’s syndrome (enophthalmos, ptosis, miosis, and anhydrosis).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which statement about Marjolin's ulcer is incorrect?
options: It is seen in sites of chronic wounds or scars.
It can progress to squamous cell carcinoma.
It is radioresistant due to avascularity.
questions.explanation: Marjolin's ulcer refers to a malignancy that arises in a chronic, non-healing wound, burn scar, or site of chronic osteomyelitis. Statement B is "incorrect" because the defining characteristic of a Marjolin's ulcer is that it typically takes a very long time to develop, often 20 to 30 years after the initial injury. It is not an acute transformation. Statement A is correct as chronic wounds are the primary site. Statement C is correct; while other cancers can occur, squamous cell carcinoma is by far the most common histological type. Statement D is also correct; these ulcers are notoriously "radioresistant" because the thick scar tissue (avascularity) creates a hypoxic environment where radiotherapy is less effective. Because these tumors are aggressive and have a higher rate of metastasis than standard skin cancers, wide surgical excision with skin grafting or flap reconstruction is the treatment of choice

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient in the ICU underwent a failed attempt at subclavian catheterization. Following the procedure, the patient developed respiratory distress and unilateral chest retraction. On examination, BP was low and pulse rate was elevated, with decreased breath sounds. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pneumothorax

The above clinical scenario of an ICU patient following a failed attempt of subclavian catheterization, developed respiratory distress and retraction, with low blood pressure, elevated pulse, and decreased breath sounds, is characteristic of one of the complications of the procedure, pneumothorax.

A tension pneumothorax develops when a ‘one-way valve’ air leak occurs either from the lung or through the chest wall. Air is sucked into the thoracic cavity without any means of escape, completely collapsing and then compressing the afected lung. Common causes of tension pneumothorax are penetrating chest trauma, blunt chest trauma with a parenchymal lung injury and air leak that did not spontaneously close, iatrogenic lung injury (e.g. due to central venepuncture) and mechanical positive-pressure ventilation.

Complications of central vein catheterization are:

* Pneumothorax is more common in subclavian vein catheterization as a result of injury to the underlying pleura.

* Arterial puncture is the most common mechanical complication.

* Cardiac tamponade is the most important life-threatening complication. It occurs as a result of the puncture of the intrapericardial superior vena cava, right atrium, or right ventricle.

* Chylothorax can occur particularly in left subclavian vein catheterization. But it is not the most common.

* Injury to the associated nerves, like brachial plexus, stellate ganglion, phrenic nerve, or vocal cords.

* Thromboembolism- can lead to venous thrombosis and pulmonary embolism. It is more common with femoral veins.

* Infections- the most common late complication.

A central venous catheter (CVC) is an indwelling device inserted into a large, central vein and advanced until the terminal lumen resides within the inferior vena cava, superior vena cava, or right atrium. It is indicated for the administration of vasopressors, medications, and total parenteral nutrition. It is also useful in procedures like dialysis, plasmapheresis, and interventions such as transvenous pacemaker placement.

Cannulation can be done at various sites, namely the internal jugular, common femoral, and subclavian veins.

The image below shows central venous catheterization:

Other options:

Option B: Displacement of the endotracheal tube typically presents with hypoxia and inadequate ventilation, not chest retraction and hypotension.

Option C: Air embolism occurs when air bubbles enter the pulmonary circulation and are absorbed in large quantities. Severe hypotension and hypoxemia are seen in this condition. The patient is then placed in Trendelenburg's left lateral decubitus position.

Option D: Dislodgement of the endotracheal tube would typically affect bilateral lungs, not just unilateral, leading to difficult ventilation and global hypoxia.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 10-year-old male child presents with a history of spontaneous excessive bruising and haemarthrosis. On investigation, he has a normal platelet count, prolonged PTT, and a normal PT. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hemophilia A

The most likely diagnosis is Haemophilia A. Bleeding into joints (hemarthrosis) following minor trauma is particularly characteristic of hemophilia.

* Hemophilia A, the most common hereditary disease associated with life-threatening bleeding, is caused by mutations in factor VIII, an essential cofactor for factor IX in the coagulation cascade.

* Hemophilia A is inherited as an X-linked recessive trait and thus affects mainly males and homozygous females.

* About 30% of patients have no family history; their disease is caused by new mutations.

* Hemophilia A -  clinical severity correlates well with the level of factor VIII activity.

* Those with less than 1% of normal levels have a severe disease; those with 2% to 5% of normal levels have moderately severe disease, and those with 6% to 50% of normal levels have mild disease.

* A tendency toward easy bruising and massive hemorrhage after trauma or operative procedures.

* Spontaneous hemorrhages frequently occur in regions of the body that are susceptible to trauma, particularly the joints, where they are known as hemarthroses.

* Recurrent bleeding into the joints leads to progressive deformities that can be crippling.

* Petechiae are characteristically absent.

* Patients with hemophilia A have a prolonged PTT and a normal PT results that point to an abnormality of the intrinsic coagulation pathway.

* Factor VIII-specific assays are required for diagnosis.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A young boy from a low socioeconomic background presents with hyperemia and yellowish nodules at the limbus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Phlyctenular conjunctivitis is an allergic hypersensitivity reaction of the conjunctiva and cornea to endogenous microbial proteins, most commonly those from Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It is frequently seen in children from poor socioeconomic backgrounds who may have underlying malnutrition or subclinical tuberculosis. The characteristic clinical finding is a small, yellowish-grey nodule at the limbus (the phlycten) surrounded by a localized area of hyperemia. Bitot's spots (Option A) are dry, foamy patches on the conjunctiva associated with Vitamin A deficiency and are not usually hyperemic. Pterygium (Option B) is a wing-shaped fibrovascular growth onto the cornea, typically seen in older adults with chronic sun exposure. Pinguecula (Option C) is a common, non-progressive yellowish thickening of the bulbar conjunctiva that does not involve the limbus in the same inflammatory manner. Management of phlyctenular conjunctivitis involves topical steroids and, crucially, investigating and treating the underlying cause, such as tuberculosis or staphylococcal blepharitis
questions.learning: Phlyctenular conjunctivitis is an allergic hypersensitivity reaction of the conjunctiva and cornea to endogenous microbial proteins, most commonly those from Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: What is Prosopagnosia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Difficulty in identifying known faces

Prosopagnosia is difficulty in identifying known faces.

In humans, storage and recognition of faces is more strongly represented in the right inferior temporal lobe in right-handed individuals, though the left lobe is also active. Damage to this area can cause prosopagnosia.

Patients with this abnormality can recognize forms and reproduce them. They can recognize people by their voices, and many of them show autonomic responses when they see familiar as opposed to unfamiliar faces. However, they cannot identify the familiar faces they see. The left hemisphere is also involved, but the role of the right hemisphere is primary.

The presence of autonomic response to a familiar face in the absence of recognition has been explained by postulating the existence of a separate dorsal pathway for processing information about faces that leads to recognition at only a subconscious level.

Note:

• Autotopagnosia - inability to recognize or to orient any part of one's own body
• Simultagnosia - inability to recognize multiple elements in a visual presentation, one object or some elements of a scene can be appreciated but not the display as a whole
• Somatagnosia - inability to identify any part of the body, either one’s own or another’s body
• Tactile agnosia (astereognosis) -  inability to recognize objects by touch, in the presence of intact cutaneous and proprioceptive hand sensation; caused by a lesion in the contralateral parietal lobe

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Regarding the parvocellular and magnocellular visual pathways, consider the following statements: 1. The parvocellular pathway is primarily involved in color vision and fine spatial resolution. 2. The magnocellular pathway is more sensitive to motion and temporal changes in visual stimuli. 3. Parvocellular fibers predominantly terminate in layers 3–6 of the lateral geniculate nucleus. 4. Magnocellular fibers project mainly to layers 1 and 2 of the lateral geniculate nucleus. 5. Lesions affecting the magnocellular pathway preferentially impair red–green color discrimination. 6. Parvocellular ganglion cells have smaller receptive fields and slower conduction velocity compared to magnocellular cells. Which of the above statements are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2, 3, 4 and 6

There are two major parallel visual pathways from retina → LGN → visual cortex:

• Parvocellular (P pathway) → detail & color
• Magnocellular (M pathway) → motion & luminance contrast

Both terminate in the Lateral geniculate nucleus.

| Feature | Parvocellular (P pathway) | Magnocellular (M pathway)

| ------- | ------------------------- | -------------------------

| Cell size | Small | Large

| Receptive field | Small | Large

| Conduction speed | Slower | Faster

| Function | Color & detail | Motion

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A diabetic patient enters the OPD and greets you with a namaste. As the doctor, you notice a deformity in his hand which is shown in the image below. Based on your observation, what is the likely cause of this deformity?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cheiroarthropathy

The image shows a positive namaste or prayer sign where the patient is unable to touch the palmar aspects of both hands and fingers together which is suggestive of diabetic cheiroarthropathy.

Diabetic cheiroarthropathy also known as diabetic stiff hand syndrome is a cutaneous condition characterized by waxy, thickened skin and limited joint mobility of the hands and fingers leading to flexion contractures (namaste or prayer sign). This occurs due to the non-enzymatic glycosylation of collagen. It is seen in both diabetes type 1 and type 2. Its prevalence increases with age and poor glycemic control.

Other options:

Option A: Flexor tenosynovitis refers to inflammation of the sheath surrounding the flexor tendons in the hand. Infectious flexor tenosynovitis is associated with the Kanavel’s signs which include:

• Fusiform swelling along the affected finger
• Tenderness with palpation along the tendon sheath
• Flexed posture of the affected finger
• Pain with passive extension

Option C: Dupuytren's contracture is a fibroproliferative disorder affecting the palmar aponeurosis of mainly the 4th and 5th fingers. Skin puckering proximal to the flexor crease is the earliest sign, followed by the development of nodules and cords in the palmar fascia, leading to flexion contractures at the MCP and PIP joints as the disease progresses.

Option D: Ankylosis refers to the fusion of a joint, resulting in limited or no movement. It can occur due to various causes such as rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, trauma, or infection.
questions.learning: Cheiroarthropathy — The image shows a positive namaste or prayer sign where the patient is unable to touch the palmar aspects of both hands and fingers together which is suggestive of diabetic cheiroarthropathy.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text:
A 10-year-old child weighing 30 kg presents with a history of loose stools for 2 days. On examination, there is severe dehydration. Laboratory investigations are as follows. What is the initial management as per ISPAD guidelines?

RBS
550 mg/dL

pH
7.01

Na+
158 mEq/L

Urine glucose
3+
options: Manage ABC, NS 20 mL/kg and start insulin after 1 hour
Manage ABC, NS 20 mL/kg along with insulin 0.1 IU/kg/hr
Manage ABC, NS 10 mL/kg along with insulin 0.1 IU/kg/hr
Manage ABC, NS 10 mL/kg and start insulin after 1 hour
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Manage ABC, NS 20 mL/kg and start insulin after 1 hour

The given clinical scenario with severe dehydration, hyperglycemia, glucosuria, and metabolic acidosis is suggestive of diabetic ketoacidosis. Based on the ISPAD guidelines, the initial management includes management of the airway, breathing, and circulation (ABC) and fluid replacement with an IV bolus of 20 mL/kg NS (Normal saline). This is followed by an IV insulin infusion of 0.05 - 0.1 U/kg/hr, at least 1 hour after starting fluid replacement therapy.

The International Society for Pediatric and Adolescent Diabetes (ISPAD) guidelines provide evidence-based recommendations for the management of DKA (diabetic ketoacidosis) in children and adolescents.

Diabetic ketoacidosis is the most serious complication of type 1 diabetes mellitus. Clinical manifestations of diabetic ketoacidosis include:

• Dehydration, tachypnea with deep, sighing respiration (Kussmaul breathing)
• Nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain that may mimic an acute abdominal condition
• Confusion, drowsiness, and coma in severe cases.

The diagnosis of DKA is based on the triad of hyperglycemia, ketosis, and metabolic acidosis. All three biochemical criteria are required to diagnose DKA

• Hyperglycemia (blood glucose >200 mg/dl)
• Venous pH < 7.3 or serum bicarbonate <18 mmol/L
• Ketonemia or ketonuria

Initial management includes management of the airway, breathing, and circulation (ABC) according to Pediatric Advanced Life Support (PALS) guidelines. Following that emergency assessment is done, which includes:

• Immediate measurement of blood glucose, blood or urine ketones, serum electrolytes and blood gases
• Assessment of level of consciousness.
• Two peripheral intravenous (IV) lines should be inserted.

The goal of therapy is to correct dehydration, correct acidosis, reverse ketosis, and gradually blood glucose concentration to near normal. Monitor for acute complications, and identify and treat any precipitating event.

Fluid replacement should always begin before starting insulin therapy. One or more boluses of 0.9% saline at 20 mL/kg are given to restore peripheral circulation. Insulin therapy with 0.05–0.1 U/kg/hr must begin at least 1 hour after starting fluid replacement therapy. Insulin of 0.05 U/kg/hr can be considered if pH is > 7.15.

Potassium replacement is given only when potassium is <5.5 mmol/L. In rare cases of hypokalemia with potassium <3.0 mmol/L, defer insulin treatment.

Bicarbonate administration is not recommended except for treatment of severe acidosis (pH < 6.9) or in cases of life-threatening hyperkalemia.
questions.learning: Manage ABC, NS 20 mL/kg and start insulin after 1 hour The given clinical scenario with severe dehydration, hyperglycemia, glucosuria, and metabolic acidosis is suggestive of diabetic ketoacidosis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · Pleural Effusion Pulmonary Embolism Pah
questions.text: Consider the following criteria: 1. Pleural fluid protein:Serum protein ratio > 0.5 2. Pleural fluid LDH:Serum LDH ratio > 0.6 3. Pleural fluid LDH > Two-thirds of the upper limit of normal serum LDH Which of the above criteria, if present in pleural fluid, will indicate an exudate?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2 and 3

The Light’s criteria are the most widely used criteria to differentiate exudative from transudative pleural effusions. A pleural effusion is classified as an exudate if any one of the following criteria is present:

1. Pleural fluid protein / Serum protein ratio > 0.5
2. Pleural fluid LDH / Serum LDH ratio > 0.6
3. Pleural fluid LDH > two-thirds of the upper limit of normal serum LDH

Common causes:

• Exudative effusions: Pneumonia (parapneumonic effusion), tuberculosis, malignancy, pulmonary embolism, pancreatitis, connective tissue diseases.
• Transudative effusions: Congestive heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, hypoalbuminemia.

Limitations:

• Light’s criteria are highly sensitive for detecting exudates but may misclassify some transudates (especially in patients with heart failure receiving diuretics) as exudates. In such cases, the serum–pleural fluid albumin gradient (>1.2 g/dL) or protein gradient (>3.1 g/dL) can help identify a true transudate.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 9-month-old infant is brought for a routine health check-up. Which developmental milestone is most commonly expected to be achieved at this age?
options: Creeps well on hands and knees
questions.explanation: By 9 months of age, most infants have achieved the gross motor milestone of creeping well on their hands and knees. They are also beginning to pull themselves up to stand and typically demonstrate an immature pincer grasp. A mature grasp (Option A), specifically the ability to pick up small objects with precision, is typically achieved closer to 12 months. Hopping on one foot (Option C) is a complex gross motor skill that does not develop until approximately 4 years of age. Running steadily (Option D) is a milestone reached around 18 to 24 months as the child gains better coordination. Therefore, at the 9-month check-up, creeping is the most developmentally appropriate skill to expect. Other typical findings at this age include "waving bye-bye" and expressing stranger anxiety
questions.learning: By 9 months of age, most infants have achieved the gross motor milestone of creeping well on their hands and knees. They are also beginning to pull themselves up to stand and typically demonstrate an immature pincer grasp.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A child on workup is found to be suffering from a rare form of pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency for which he has developed high anion gap metabolic acidosis. Which of the following is the best dietary advice for the patient?
options: High protein and low carbohydrate intake
High carbohydrate and low fat intake
High fat and low carbohydrate intake
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. High fat and low carbohydrate intake

Pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency(PDH) can be due to a defect in any one/more of the components of the PDH enzyme complex. Patients are advised to follow a high fat and low carbohydrate intake.

In pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency, there is a defect in the pyruvate dehydrogenase enzyme complex, leading to impaired conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA. This results in the accumulation of pyruvate and subsequent conversion to lactate, causing lactic acidosis and high anion gap metabolic acidosis.

To provide an alternative fuel source for the body, patients with pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency are often advised to follow a high-fat and low-carbohydrate diet. By reducing the intake of carbohydrates, which are metabolized to pyruvate, and increasing the intake of fats, which can be metabolized via alternative pathways, the reliance on the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex can be minimized.

Therefore, option C (High fat and low carbohydrate intake) is the most appropriate dietary advice for a patient with pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency and high anion gap metabolic acidosis.

Other options:

Option A: High protein and low carbohydrate intake - This option is incorrect because a high protein intake would still involve the metabolism of amino acids, which can contribute to the production of pyruvate and further exacerbate the metabolic acidosis in pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency.

Option B: High carbohydrate and low-fat intake - This option is incorrect because pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency impairs the conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA, resulting in the accumulation of pyruvate and subsequent lactic acidosis.

Option D: Only carbohydrate intake henceforth - This option is incorrect because pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency specifically affects the metabolism of carbohydrates, leading to the accumulation of pyruvate. Relying solely on carbohydrate intake would exacerbate the metabolic acidosis by increasing pyruvate levels.
questions.learning: High fat and low carbohydrate intake Pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency(PDH) can be due to a defect in any one/more of the components of the PDH enzyme complex.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 50-year-old male presents to the emergency with a BP of 160/100 mmHg and a heart rate of 120. CECT done reveals a Stanford A aortic dissection. What is the initial management of this given condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Beta blocker medication

The initial management of patients with all types of aortic dissection is beta blocker medication to control hypertension along with pain management. Patients with Stanford Type A (DeBakey Types I and II) will require surgical intervention once the patient's blood pressure is stabilized.

Aortic dissection occurs when a defect or flap occurs in the intima of the aorta.

Predisposing factors:

1. Age
2. Hypertension
3. Marfan syndrome
4. Pregnancy
5. Other connective tissue disorders, for example, Ehlers–Danlos syndrome, giant cell arteritis, systemic lupus erythematosus
6. Coarctation of the aorta
7. Turner or Noonan syndromes
8. Aortic cannulation site (iatrogenic).

The most typical presentation of aortic dissection is a tearing interscapular pain. The dissection may also result in aortic wall rupture into the pericardium (cardiac tamponade) or mediastinum (left haemothorax).

Contrast-enhanced CT is currently the most preferred imaging modality for aortic dissection. Double-lumen aorta is seen on CECT. Transesophageal echocardiography is preferred for patients who are unstable for transportation.

Acute aortic dissection can be classified by the original DeBakey system, based on the location of the proximal tear and distal extent of the dissection flap, or the Stanford system which uses the location of the proximal tear alone.

Site of dissection
DeBakey
Stanford

Type I
Type A

Only ascending aorta and arch of aorta
Type II
Type A

Descending the aorta distal to the subclavian artery

Type IIIa

Type B

Type IIIb

Extends to the abdominal aorta

Management of aortic dissection:

The initial management of patients with all types of aortic dissection is beta-blocker medication to control hypertension along with pain management. The preferred beta-blocker drug is esmolol. Hemodynamic stability is an important consideration.

• Stanford Type A (DeBakey Types I and II) requires surgical intervention once the patient's blood pressure is stabilized.
• Stanford Type B (DeBakey type III) is best managed by antihypertensive drugs. For patients with complicated type B dissection, percutaneously placed endovascular stents are currently preferred. Surgery is reserved for the rare patients not suitable for stenting.

Other options:

Options B and D: Low molecular weight heparin and vitamin K inhibitors are contraindicated in aortic dissection as they can worsen the risk of bleeding.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Identify the true statement regarding the given nerve action potential curve.
options: At point E, the nerve is more excitable
Point C to D is due to opening of Na+ and closure of K+ channels
Point B to D is refractory period
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Point B to D is refractory period

The correct statement regarding the given nerve action potential curve is point B to D is the refractory period.

The sequence of events occurring during an action potential is shown below

• Point A represents the resting state where both channels are closed.
• Na+ channels open in response to depolarizing stimulus and sodium enters the cell. The initiation of action potential occurs only after a certain potential is reached, which is called the threshold potential represented by point B. (Option A)
• After this, the sodium influx causes the opening of more Na+ channels through a positive feedback mechanism. Rapid depolarization occurs to reach point C.
• At point C, Na+ channels close and K+ channels open, causing repolarization due to K+ efflux. (Option C)
• Point D represents continued repolarization due to potassium efflux.
• At point E, Na+ channels are reset and are ready to respond to another depolarizing stimulus. During this phase, the K+ channels remain open and slowly return to the closed state, causing after-hyperpolarization. As a stronger stimulus is required to reach the threshold potential, the excitability of nerve fiber is reduced at point E. (Option B)
• As both channels close, the membrane returns to resting membrane potential back to point A.

Point B-D is a part of the refractory period. During this period, the application of even a stronger stimulus will not elicit an action potential.

The refractory period is divided into an absolute refractory period and a relative refractory period. During the absolute refractory period, the nerve will not be excited no matter how strong a stimulus is given. However, during the relative refractory period, stronger than normal stimuli can cause excitation.

questions.text: What is the diagnosis from the given abdominal X-ray?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Rectal foreign body

The image shows a foreign body in the rectum which is most likely a bottle.

A variety of foreign bodies are seen in the rectum many of which are hard to remove due to the difficulty in vacuum creation while removing it through the anus.

The object can be pushed from above into the assistant’s fingers in the rectum, or removed by means of a rectotomy in a proximal area of the rectum.

If there is difficulty in removing then laparotomy is advised.

If a considerable laceration is seen while removing then a temporary colostomy is necessary for healing as there is a high risk of associated necrotizing fascitis which needs broad-spectrum antibiotics. There can be associated bladder or urethral damage.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which type of ion channel is affected by mutations in the CFTR gene?
questions.explanation: The CFTR (Cystic Fibrosis Transmembrane Conductance Regulator) gene encodes a protein that functions as a chloride ion channel located in the membranes of epithelial cells. Mutations in this gene cause Cystic Fibrosis. This channel is vital for regulating the movement of salt and water in and out of cells. In the lungs, a defective CFTR channel prevents the normal secretion of chloride and water, leading to the production of abnormally thick, sticky mucus that traps bacteria and causes recurrent infections. In the sweat glands, it prevents the reabsorption of chloride, leading to "salty sweat," which is the basis for the diagnostic sweat chloride test. Sodium (Option B), Potassium (Option C), and Calcium (Option D) channels are not the primary proteins affected by CFTR mutations. The most common mutation is , which leads to misfolding of the protein. Modern treatments include CFTR modulators that help the defective channel function more normally, significantly improving the quality of life and lifespan for these patients
questions.learning: The CFTR (Cystic Fibrosis Transmembrane Conductance Regulator) gene encodes a protein that functions as a chloride ion channel located in the membranes of epithelial cells.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 30-year-old man initially develops paralysis in both legs, which later progresses to involve the upper limbs. Over time, he improves but is left with paralysis affecting only his lower trunk and both legs. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This patient's final neurological status is defined by paralysis of the lower trunk and both legs, which is the clinical definition of paraplegia. Paraplegia typically results from a lesion in the thoracic or lumbar spinal cord. Diplegia (Option A) refers to symmetrical paralysis of any two similar parts (usually both legs more than arms), often associated with cerebral palsy. Quadriplegia (Option B), also known as tetraplegia, involves paralysis of all four limbs and the trunk, typically resulting from a cervical spinal cord injury. Monoplegia (Option D) is the paralysis of a single limb. While the patient initially had symptoms suggesting quadriplegia (as the weakness progressed to the arms), the final outcome after improvement is paraplegia. This sequence of "ascending" and then "descending" recovery is sometimes seen in Guillain-Barré Syndrome or transverse myelitis as the inflammation resolves
questions.learning: This patient's final neurological status is defined by paralysis of the lower trunk and both legs, which is the clinical definition of paraplegia. Paraplegia typically results from a lesion in the thoracic or lumbar spinal cord.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient underwent abdominal surgery during which a surgical gauze was inadvertently left inside the abdomen. The patient subsequently developed septic shock and died. This incident is best classified as:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Never event

A never event is a serious, preventable patient safety incident that should never occur if appropriate safety systems are in place. Leaving a surgical gauze (retained surgical item/gossypiboma) inside a patient after surgery is a classic example of a never event.

• Retained surgical items (e.g., gauze, sponge, instrument) are completely preventable through proper surgical counts and safety checklists.
• In this case, the retained gauze led to sepsis, septic shock, and death, making it a classic never event.

Why not the other options?

• A. Sentinel event: Incorrect in this question. Although the patient’s death qualifies as a sentinel event, the emphasis is on the retained surgical gauze, which is specifically classified as a never event.
• C. Adverse event: Too broad; it includes any injury caused by medical management and may not be preventable.
• D. Active event: Not a recognized patient safety classification.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A young man presented with painful lesions as shown in the image below. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Herpes Zoster

The above image shows unilateral, red, closely grouped vesicles in a single dermatome associated with severe pain is suggestive of herpes zoster or shingles.

It is a segmental eruption due to the reactivation of latent varicella-zoster virus from dorsal root ganglia. An earlier infection with varicella is essential before zoster can occur.

The first symptom of zoster is usually pain and it may be accompanied by fever, headache, malaise, and tenderness localized to areas of one or more dorsal roots. The mucous membranes within the affected dermatomes are involved. The lymph nodes draining the affected area are enlarged and tender.

The patients are infectious, both from the virus in the lesions and nasopharynx. The most commonly involved dermatomes in decreasing order of frequency are thoracic > cervical > trigeminal > lumbosacral. The posterior nerve roots and ganglia show inflammatory changes.

Zoster is a self‐limiting infection but it is painful and carries a risk of secondary infection and post‐herpetic neuralgia. Analgesia and treatment of secondary infections are sufficient for mild infections.

Indications for antivirals in VZV (Acyclovir 800 mg):

• Painful zoster infections in adults
• Facial zoster at any age
• Immunocompromised

Other options:

Option B: The lesions of the molluscum contagiosum are shiny, white, and hemispherical. It is umbilicated with a central pore. It is caused by poxvirus.

The below image shows the lesions seen in Molluscum contagiosum

Option C: Herpes simplex virus are classified into two major antigenic types,

• Type 1 (HSV-1) which is classically associated with facial infections;
• Type 2 (HSV-2) which is typically genital.

Below image shows small, closely grouped vesicles on an inflamed base and is characteristic of Herpes Labialis or Cold sore.

Option D: Lymphangiomas are dilated dermal lymphatics that blister onto the skin surface. The fluid is usually clear, but occasionally maybe blood-stained. Lymphangiomas may thrombose and get fibrosed, to form hard nodules in the long term. This may raise concerns about malignancy.

If lymphangiomas are <5 cm across, they are called lymphangioma circumscriptum (shown below), and they are called lymphangioma diffusum if they are more widespread.
