questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which one of the following is not a risk factor for pre-eclampsia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Placenta previa

Pre-eclampsia is associated with abnormal placentation and maternal vascular dysfunction. Several maternal factors increase the risk, but placenta previa is not a risk factor.

Why not the other options?

• A. Primigravida: Risk factor for pre-eclampsia.
• B. Obesity: Risk factor due to increased metabolic and inflammatory changes.
• C. Pre-existing vascular disease: Risk factor (e.g., chronic hypertension, diabetes with vasculopathy, chronic kidney disease).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents since birth with ptosis and a right eye positioned in a “down and out” posture. Which cranial nerve palsy is most likely responsible for this finding?
questions.explanation: The "down and out" eye position is the classic sign of an oculomotor nerve (CN III) palsy. CN III supplies the superior, inferior, and medial recti, as well as the inferior oblique. When these are paralyzed, the lateral rectus (CN VI) and superior oblique (CN IV) act unopposed, pulling the eye outward and downward. The accompanying ptosis results from paralysis of the levator palpebrae superioris, also supplied by CN III. 4th nerve palsy (Option A) causes vertical diplopia and an "up and in" eye position. 6th nerve palsy (Option C) results in an "inward" deviation (esotropia) due to medial rectus action. 7th nerve palsy (Option D) affects facial expression and eye closure but not eye position. Thus, the "down and out" triad with ptosis confirms CN III involvement
questions.learning: The "down and out" eye position is the classic sign of an oculomotor nerve (CN III) palsy. CN III supplies the superior, inferior, and medial recti, as well as the inferior oblique.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: As an index of thermal comfort, the ‘Corrected Effective Temperature’ is considered to be an improvement over ‘Effective Temperature’. It deals with which of the following factors? I. Air velocity II. Humidity III. Mean radiant heat IV. Sweat rate Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. I, II and III

Corrected Effective Temperature (CET) is an improved index of thermal comfort that assesses the combined effect of air temperature, humidity, air velocity, and mean radiant temperature on human comfort. It is more accurate than Effective Temperature (ET) because it also incorporates the effect of radiant heat.

• Effective Temperature (ET): Based on air temperature, humidity, and air velocity.
• Corrected Effective Temperature (CET): ET + Mean Radiant Temperature (Radiant heat).
• Sweat rate is not a component of CET.
• CET is widely used to evaluate thermal comfort in homes, workplaces, hospitals, and industrial settings.
questions.learning: I, II and III Corrected Effective Temperature (CET) is an improved index of thermal comfort that assesses the combined effect of air temperature, humidity, air velocity, and mean radiant temperature on human comfort.

questions.text: The following image shows
questions.explanation: The image shows craniorachischisis, the most severe form of an open neural tube defect (NTD). It is characterized by the failure of the neural tube to close along its entire length, resulting in both anencephaly (absence of the brain vault) and rachischisis (completely exposed spinal cord). Regarding the distractors, a meningocele (Option B) is a much less severe, skin-covered defect containing only meninges. Spina bifida (Option C) is a broad umbrella term that includes both open and closed types, but "Open NTD" is more descriptive of this fatal malformation. A myelomeningocele (Option D) is a localized open defect, typically in the lumbosacral region, rather than the total neural exposure seen in the image. Therefore, craniorachischisis is the specific diagnosis represented by this open NTD

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 60-year-old man with metastatic testicular cancer is planned for chemotherapy. Among the chemotherapeutic agents used in this setting, which drug is most commonly associated with renal tubular toxicity?
questions.explanation: Cisplatin is a foundational platinum-based chemotherapy drug used for many solid tumors, including testicular cancer. Its primary and dose-limiting toxicity is nephrotoxicity, specifically causing renal tubular damage. This can lead to acute kidney injury or chronic renal insufficiency if not carefully managed. Streptozocin (Option B) is an alkylating agent used for pancreatic islet cell tumors and is also nephrotoxic, but it is not the standard treatment for metastatic testicular cancer. Methysergide (Option C) is a serotonin antagonist used for migraines, not a chemotherapeutic agent. Cyclophosphamide (Option D) is notoriously associated with hemorrhagic cystitis (bladder damage) rather than primary renal tubular necrosis. To prevent cisplatin-induced kidney damage, patients receive aggressive intravenous hydration with normal saline before and after the infusion, often supplemented with mannitol to maintain high urine output. Regular monitoring of serum creatinine and electrolytes is mandatory for all patients on cisplatin therapy to ensure safe treatment delivery
questions.learning: Cisplatin is a foundational platinum-based chemotherapy drug used for many solid tumors, including testicular cancer. Its primary and dose-limiting toxicity is nephrotoxicity, specifically causing renal tubular damage.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A person presents with complaints of numbness, tingling and paresthesias of the thumb, index finger and middle finger. There is numbness at the dorsum of the base of the thumb as well. What structure is most likely to be damaged?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Median nerve

Patient presents with pain and paresthesia over the lateral 3 and a half digits and numbness at the dorsum of the base of the thumb, both of which are indicative of a median nerve injury.

There may be weakness of thumb opposition. In chronic cases, the thenar eminence is wasted. Carpal tunnel syndrome is a common cause and can be associated with rheumatoid arthritis, pregnancy, chronic renal failure, acromegaly, hypothyroidism and gout. The diagnosis is usually made on clinical grounds but nerve conduction studies can confirm the diagnosis.

Median nerve injuries:

Distal injury: Thus an injury to the distal median nerve affects the 1st and 2nd lumbricals sparing the flexor digitorum profundus. This causes hyperextension at the metacarpophalangeal joints and flexion at the interphalangeal joints, involving the index and middle fingers. This attitude of the hand known as the median claw hand may be seen at rest and is more pronounced on attempting to extend the fingers (attitude is similar to proximal ulnar injury).

Proximal injury: Since the opposing flexor digitorum profundus of the 2nd and 3rd digit that causes the clawing is also affected, the clawing of the hand is less pronounced in distal injuries of the ulnar nerve. The deficits present during voluntary flexion of the digits. Thus, on attempting to make a fist, the flexion of the 2nd and 3rd digits is affected while the 4th and 5th digits are normal giving the Benediction hand sign.

In both cases of median nerve palsy, there is loss of sensations on lateral 3½ digits including the nail beds and distal phalanges on the dorsum of the hand.

Tinel's sign is positive where percussing over the median nerve reproduces symptoms. Phalen's test is positive where the symptoms are reproduced by holding the wrists in full flexion with the dorsum of the hands pressed together.

Other Options:

Option A: Injury to the anterior interosseous nerve, a branch of the median nerve. It results in the loss of function of both flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) and flexor digitorum superficialis (FDS). Hence, the index finger sticks out when the patient is asked to clasp their hand.

Option B: In ulnar nerve palsy, only the medial two fingers develop clawing, while in a combined median and ulnar nerve palsy, all four fingers develop clawing.

Option C:  In radial nerve palsy, the patient presents with 'wrist drop' in case of paralyzed wrist extensors, and 'finger drop' when extensor digitorum is paralyzed. When there is compression in the axilla, radial nerve palsy is called Saturday night palsy. There is paralysis of the triceps, and weakness of the wrist and hand. In high lesions, there is sensory loss on the dorsum of the hand over the anatomical stuff box.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 55-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes attends a routine follow-up visit. Investigations show normal serum creatinine and potassium levels, but microalbuminuria is present, and her HbA1c is 8%. Her blood pressure and pulse are within normal limits, and she is currently being treated with metformin. What should be the next step in her management?
options: Stop Metformin and start a different OHA
questions.explanation: The patient exhibits microalbuminuria, which is the earliest clinical sign of diabetic nephropathy. Starting an ACE inhibitor (or ARB) is the critical next step, even if blood pressure is normal, because these drugs provide renoprotection by lowering intraglomerular pressure and reducing the progression of albuminuria. Thiazide diuretics (Option A) may be used for edema but do not offer the same kidney-protective benefits. Insulin (Option B) is considered if HbA1c remains despite oral agents, which is not the case here. Metformin should only be stopped (Option C) if the eGFR falls below 30 ml/min, whereas this patient has normal creatinine. Early intervention with RAAS blockade significantly reduces the long-term risk of end-stage renal disease and major cardiovascular events in diabetics

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: On finding a congenital heart block in a fetus, which of the following conditions would you evaluate for in the mother?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. SLE

On finding a congenital heart block in the fetus, the mother should be evaluated for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).

Fetal and neonatal heart blocks occur due to myocarditis and fibrosis in the region between the AV node and the bundle of His. Congenital heart block primarily develops in fetuses of women with antibodies to the SS-A or SS-B antigens, and up to 50 percent of women with SLE test positive for these antibodies. So in pregnancies with either of these antibodies, fetal cardiac monitoring is performed between 18 and 26 weeks of gestation.

The cardiac lesion is permanent, and in most cases, a pacemaker is required. Maternal hydroxychloroquine therapy is associated with a reduced incidence of fetal heart block, particularly in women who have previously had an affected child.

Neonatal lupus erythematosus is thought to be caused by the transplacental passage of maternal antibodies. It is characterized by skin lesions known as lupus dermatitis in newborns, as well as various hematological and systemic abnormalities. In some cases, congenital heart block may also occur. Thrombocytopenia and hepatic involvement are also seen.

The most common cutaneous finding in neonatal lupus erythematosus is an erythematous, slightly scaly eruption on the face and periorbital skin (raccoon sign/owl eye/eye mask). The eruption can be exacerbated by UV exposure. The rash improves over the first few months of life and usually resolves without scarring by 12 months of age.

Avoidance of sunlight should be advised and low‐potency topical steroids may be of benefit.

The pregnancy outcomes are best in women with:

•  Dormant lupus activity for at least 6 months before conception
•  No lupus nephritis manifestation in the form of proteinuria or renal dysfunction
•  Absent anti-phospholipid syndrome or lupus anticoagulant
•  Superimposed preeclampsia does not develop
questions.learning: SLE On finding a congenital heart block in the fetus, the mother should be evaluated for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). Fetal and neonatal heart blocks occur due to myocarditis and fibrosis in the region between the AV node and the bundle of His.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: While performing surgery on a patient who presented with clinical features suggestive of peritonitis, a diverticular perforation is seen along with fecal peritonitis. What is the Hinchey's stage?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Stage 4

Fecal peritonitis belongs to grade 4 in the Hinchey classification.

Diverticulitis refers to the inflammation and infection associated with the diverticula. Hinchey classification is the most commonly used classification for the severity and complication of acute diverticulitis. It is used additionally to guide the overall management of acute diverticulitis.

Hinchey classification:

Stage 1

Mesenteric or pericolic abscess

Stage 2

Pelvic abscess

Stage 3

Purulent peritonitis

Stage 4

Fecal peritonitis
questions.learning: Stage 4 Fecal peritonitis belongs to grade 4 in the Hinchey classification. Diverticulitis refers to the inflammation and infection associated with the diverticula.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A G2P1L1 lady underwent LSCS in previous pregnancy for fetal distress.This time she had an uneventful vaginal birth after caesarean section (VBAC) but the placenta could not be removed completely.The cord snapped on traction but the placenta did not deliver.She also started to bleed more profusely now.What is the likely reason for this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Placenta percreta

The above clinical scenario with a h/o caesarean section with adherent placenta is placenta percreta.

Placenta accreta syndromes (PAS) include any placental implantation with abnormally firm adherence to myometrium because of the partial or total absence of the decidua basalis and imperfect development of the fibrinoid.

* The increased risk conveyed by previous uterine trauma(Ex, cesarean delivery) may be partially explained by increased vulnerability of the decidua to trophoblast invasion following incision into the decidua.

* Microscopically, placental villi are anchored to muscle fibers rather than to decidual cells. Decidual deficiency then prevents normal placental separation after delivery.

* In cases of first- and second-trimester accrete syndromes, there is usually hemorrhage that is the consequence of coexisting placenta previa.

* MR imaging can be used as an adjunct to sonography to define anatomy, degree of invasion, and possible ureteral or bladder involvement.

* Complications: Variable degree of hemorrhage

* Treatment: C-section followed by Hysterectomy

Variants of placenta accreta syndromes are classified by the depth of trophoblastic growth:

* Placenta accreta: Villi are attached to the myometrium.

* Placenta increta: Villi invade the myometrium.

* Placenta percreta: Villi penetrate through the myometrium and to or through the serosa.

The Nitabuch layer (also known as the fibrinoid layer) is a layer of fibrinoid degeneration where the invading trophoblasts meet the decidua basalis. The absence of the Nitabuch layer in the uterine decidua leads to the placenta accreta spectrum.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 30-year-old man with a history of using contact lenses, presented with pain, redness and purulent discharge from his right eye. A greyish-white serpiginous ulcer was noted over the lower third of the cornea. The anterior chamber showed a 4 mm hypopyon and a moderate flare reaction. What is the most likely diagnosis ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bacterial corneal ulcer

Hypopyon corneal ulcer with a characteristic serpiginous description (ulcus serpens) is typically caused by Pneumococcus. The bacterial hypopyon is sterile.

Ulcus serpens is a greyish-white or yellowish disc-shaped ulcer occurring near the centre of the cornea. The ulcer has a tendency to creep over the cornea in a serpiginous fashion.

Risk factors include both surgical and non-surgical ocular trauma, dry eye, chronic corneal disease, immune alterations and contact lenses.

An examination may reveal the following signs:

* Swelling of lids and blepharospasm

* Conjunctival hyperemia

* Ciliary congestion, hypopyon and anterior chamber flare reaction

* Iridocyclitis

Image given below shows ulcus serpens.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: All the following cause widening of confidence interval except?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Increase in sample size

All the given options cause a widening of confidence interval except for an increase in sample size. An increase in sample size leads to a narrower confidence interval.

Research is usually done with samples drawn from a population, rather than by using the entire population. In order to get a fair idea of the population parameters, sample statistics and estimates of error in the sample are used to get a range of values. This range is the confidence interval (CI). It is estimated based on a desirable confidence level.

The confidence interval is calculated as the difference between upper and lower confidence limits.

The width of the CI is an indication of the utility of our population parameter estimation. Factors affecting the width of the confidence interval include:

• Desired confidence level- width of CI is directly proportionate to the confidence level
• Variability in the sample- width of CI is directly proportionate to the variability in the data
• Sample size- width of the CI is inversely related to the sample size

Therefore, increases in variability and confidence levels and decreases in sample size lead to wider confidence intervals.
questions.learning: Increase in sample size All the given options cause a widening of confidence interval except for an increase in sample size. An increase in sample size leads to a narrower confidence interval.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 46-year-old male presented with chronic back pain and neck stiffness. X-ray cervical spine is given below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis

The given clinical scenario and the radiograph showing ossification of the anterior longitudinal ligament, in front of the C2 to C7 cervical vertebral bodies, point towards a diagnosis of Diffuse Idiopathic Skeletal Hyperostosis (DISH). It is also referred to as Forestier disease.

DISH is a common disorder characterized by bone and calcium formation at the sites of ligamentous insertions. It occurs in the middle-aged or elderly. The radiograph shows calcification of anterior and sometimes posterior longitudinal ligaments appearing as flowing or dripping-like candle wax. It is usually asymptomatic but the calcification might cause compression of the spinal cord and can be better visualized on CT and MRI. In contrast to ankylosing spondylitis, the sacroiliac joints are usually spared.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A patient is diagnosed with cancer and is undergoing chemotherapy. What type of prevention is this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Tertiary prevention

The clinical scenario of a patient diagnosed with cancer and undergoing chemotherapy points towards tertiary prevention, as it is already diagnosed and treatment aimed at reducing the number and impact of complications.

The tertiary level of prevention signifies intervention in the late pathogenesis phase. Tertiary prevention can be defined as "all measures available to reduce or limit impairments and disabilities, minimize suffering caused by existing departures from good health, and promote the patient's adjustment to irremediable conditions". Examples include occupational and physical therapy in burns patients and cardiac rehabilitation in post-myocardial infarction patients.

Other options:

Option A: Secondary prevention includes early disease detection and targets healthy-looking individuals with subclinical forms of the disease. Secondary prevention is defined by an intervention that halts the progress of the disease at its incipient stage and prevents complications. A Papanicolaou (Pap) smear is an example of secondary prevention aimed at diagnosing cervical cancer in its subclinical state before progression.

Option C: Primordial prevention prevents the emergence or development of risk factors in population groups or countries where they have not appeared yet through individual and mass education. For example lifestyle modifications such as eating patterns and physical exercise to prevent obesity in later years.

Option D: Primary prevention is the action taken before the onset of the disease to prevent the possibility that a disease will ever occur. Here, intervention is initiated in the pre-pathogenesis phase of a disease. It is accomplished by population strategy and high-risk strategy. Examples of primary prevention are immunization and sanitising hands.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A 25-year-old male patient presents to the emergency department after a car crash. On examination, his BP was 80/40mmHg and pulses were feeble, neck veins distended, and heart sounds were muffled. Which of the following changes will you expect in the jvp of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Absent Y descent

The given clinical scenario with hypotension, muffled heart sounds, and distended neck vein suggests a diagnosis of cardiac tamponade. The JVP finding most likely to be seen is absent y descent.

Cardiac tamponade is the accumulation of fluid in the pericardial space. It results in the obstruction of the blood flow into the ventricles.

This manifests as Beck's triad which consists of the following:

* Distended neck veins (due to decreased venous return)

* Muffled heart sounds (fluid accumulation in the pericardial space)

* Hypotension

The physical examination findings in a patient with cardiac tamponade are:

* Tachycardia

* Hypotension

* Elevated JVP

* Pulsus paradoxus

Jugular venous pulse (JVP) findings include:

* Prominent 'x' descent (early systolic) but

* Lacks 'y' descent (early diastolic) due to reduced or absent early diastolic ventricular filling.

An eFAST is reliable and will show fluid in the pericardial space. A chest X-ray will show an enlarged heart shadow.

Cardiac tamponade can also be treated with open surgery procedures like sternotomy or left thoracotomy. This also allows for the heart to be repaired during the procedure.

Pearl PF0262: JVP waveform and the abnormalities

1) The a-wave corresponds to atrial contraction.

Abnormality
Conditions

Prominent a-waves
Pulmonary hypertension, right atrial thrombus/ mass, and tricuspid stenosis

Cannon a-waves

Complete AV block, ventricular tachycardia, and premature atrial/ junctional/ ventricular beats

Absent a-waves
Atrial fibrillation

2) The c-wave corresponds to the bulging of tricuspid valve into right atrium during ventricular contraction.

3) The x-descent corresponds to atrial relaxation during atrial diastole.

Abnormality
Conditions

Absent x-descent
Severe tricuspid regurgitation

Rapid x-descent
Cardiac tamponade

4) The v-wave corresponds to the venous filling of right atrium.

Abnormality
Conditions

Dominant v-waves
Tricuspid regurgitation

5) The y-descent corresponds to the passive emptying of the right atrium into right ventricle.

Abnormality
Conditions

Prolonged y-descent
Tricuspid stenosis

Rapid y-descent

Constrictive pericarditis and isolated severe tricuspid regurgitation

Absent y-descent
Cardiac tamponade
questions.learning: Absent Y descent — The given clinical scenario with hypotension, muffled heart sounds, and distended neck vein suggests a diagnosis of cardiac tamponade.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 28-year-old woman presents with a one- week history of creamy white vaginal discharge accompanied by a fishy odor, particularly noticeable after intercourse. Microscopic examination of a vaginal swab is provided. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with creamy white vaginal discharge and a fishy odor, especially after intercourse—classic features of bacterial vaginosis (BV). The odor is due to amine release (positive whiff test with KOH). The microscopy image shows clue cells, which are vaginal epithelial cells coated with bacteria, giving a granular, indistinct border appearance. This is a key diagnostic feature of BV and forms part of Amsel’s criteria. Why other options are incorrect: (A) Trichomoniasis: Characterized by greenish-yellow, frothy discharge and motile organisms on microscopy, not clue cells. (B) Candidiasis: Presents with thick, curdy discharge and itching; microscopy shows budding yeast/pseudohyphae, not clue cells. (D) Gonorrhoea: Produces purulent discharge with intracellular diplococci; no fishy odor or clue cells are seen
questions.learning: The patient presents with creamy white vaginal discharge and a fishy odor, especially after intercourse—classic features of bacterial vaginosis (BV). The odor is due to amine release (positive whiff test with KOH).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A primigravida at 32 weeks of gestation presents to the emergency department with severe abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding. On examination, the uterus is tense and tender, and fetal parts are not easily palpable through the abdominal wall. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical triad of significant abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, and a tender, board-like uterus in the third trimester is highly diagnostic for Abruptio placenta. This condition involve the premature separation of a normally implanted placenta from the uterine wall. The difficulty in palpating fetal parts occurs due to the extreme uterine hypertonicity and tenderness associated with retroplacental hemorrhage. In contrast, placenta previa (Option B) is characteristically associated with painless vaginal bleeding and a soft, non-tender uterus. Uterine rupture (Option C) is rare in a primigravida and usually presents with the recession of the presenting part and easily palpable fetal parts under the maternal skin. Polyhydramnios (Option D) involves excessive amniotic fluid and would present with an oversized but non-tender uterus without acute bleeding. Abruptio placenta is an obstetric emergency that carries high risks of disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) and fetal distress, necessitating immediate stabilization and often urgent delivery to ensure both maternal and fetal safety
questions.learning: The clinical triad of significant abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, and a tender, board-like uterus in the third trimester is highly diagnostic for Abruptio placenta.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 28-year-old man reports arm and hand weakness and numbness after sleeping with his arm over a chair post heavy drinking. What is the correct order of susceptibility of different nerve Fibers to pressure?
options: A Fiber is less susceptible than B Fibers
B Fiber is more susceptible than A Fibers
C Fiber is less susceptible than B Fibers
C Fiber is more susceptible than A Fibers
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. C Fiber is less susceptible than B Fibers

Pressure neuropathy preferentially affects larger, myelinated Fibers.

B Fibers (preganglionic autonomic, myelinated) are more susceptible to pressure than C Fibers (unmyelinated).

C Fibers are relatively resistant to compression and hypoxia.

| Fiber | Myelination | Size | Function

| ----- | ----------- | ---- | --------

| A Fibers | Heavy | Large | Motor, proprioception

| B Fibers | Light | Small | Autonomic

| C Fibers | None | Very small | Pain, temperature
questions.learning: C Fiber is less susceptible than B Fibers Pressure neuropathy preferentially affects larger, myelinated Fibers. B Fibers (preganglionic autonomic, myelinated) are more susceptible to pressure than C Fibers (unmyelinated).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The nerve of the second branchial arch is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Facial nerve

The facial nerve is the nerve of the 2nd pharyngeal arch.

Each pharyngeal arch is characterized by its own muscular components. The muscular components of each arch have their own cranial nerve. Wherever the muscle cells migrate, they carry their nerve component with them.

The neurons of the 5th, 7th, 9th, and 10th cranial sensory ganglia that supply the pharyngeal arch structures are derived from ectodermal placodes (epipharyngeal placodes) and from the neural crest cells.
questions.learning: Facial nerve — The facial nerve is the nerve of the 2nd pharyngeal arch. Each pharyngeal arch is characterized by its own muscular components.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Transcutaneous electric nerve stimulation is used to reduce pain. What is the mechanism behind this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Gate control theory

Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) used for pain relief is based on the gate theory of pain. This method uses electrodes to activate Aα and Aβ fibers near the injury to relieve pain.

Gate control theory is based on the inhibition of pain pathway in the spinal cord. Various sensory inputs from a particular dermatome reach the dorsal horn of the spinal cord. The pain is transmitted via A-delta and C fibers, whereas, A-beta fibers carry tactile sensations (touch, pressure) and A-alpha fibers carry proprioception.

When these large-diameter A-beta/A-alpha fibers are stimulated, they inhibit the pain pathway in the spinal cord. This inhibition is thought to result from the local lateral inhibition of interneurons in the spinal cord.

Gate control theory operates at the substantia gelatinosa of the dorsal horn of the spinal cord.

questions.learning: Gate control theory Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) used for pain relief is based on the gate theory of pain. This method uses electrodes to activate Aα and Aβ fibers near the injury to relieve pain.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: During a routine health assessment using the STEP approach, a physician collects key information from the patient. If a patient reports fatigue and dizziness, which of the following parameters would not usually be evaluated as part of the STEP approach?
questions.explanation: The "STEP" approach in clinical medicine or screening is often utilized to monitor metabolic parameters that contribute to chronic lifestyle diseases. Typical components include checking Blood Pressure (Option B), Blood Sugar (Option C), and Blood Lipids (Option D). These are modifiable risk factors that can explain symptoms like fatigue and dizziness. In contrast, a patient's Blood Group (Option A) is a fixed genetic characteristic that is not routinely assessed as part of a general diagnostic "STEP" screening for symptoms of fatigue or metabolic health. Blood grouping is generally reserved for pre-operative planning, blood transfusion, or obstetric care. When a patient presents with dizziness, assessing for hypertension or diabetes (via pressure and sugar checks) is high-yield, whereas knowing the blood type does not provide immediate diagnostic value for the underlying clinical complaint
questions.learning: The "STEP" approach in clinical medicine or screening is often utilized to monitor metabolic parameters that contribute to chronic lifestyle diseases.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 35-year-old patient is scheduled for laparoscopic surgery, and the surgical team plans to create a pneumoperitoneum to facilitate the procedure. Which gas is most commonly used to establish pneumoperitoneum in laparoscopic surgeries?
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide (CO2) is the gold standard and most commonly used gas for creating pneumoperitoneum during laparoscopic procedures. Its widespread use is attributed to several critical physiological and safety advantages. is highly soluble in blood, which significantly reduces the risk of a fatal gas embolism compared to other gases. Furthermore, is non-combustible, ensuring safety during the use of electrosurgical instruments like cautery or lasers within the abdominal cavity. While helium (Option A) is also non-combustible, its low solubility increases the risk of embolism. Oxygen (Option B) is strictly avoided as it supports combustion and poses a fire hazard. Nitrogen (Option D) is insoluble in blood, making any potential embolism extremely dangerous. Consequently, due to its high margin of safety regarding embolism and its non-flammable properties, carbon dioxide remains the preferred medium for maintaining the necessary workspace and visibility required for successful laparoscopic interventions
questions.learning: Carbon dioxide (CO2) is the gold standard and most commonly used gas for creating pneumoperitoneum during laparoscopic procedures. Its widespread use is attributed to several critical physiological and safety advantages. is highly soluble in blood, which…

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which hormone levels increase during stress, starvation, and deep sleep?
questions.explanation: Growth Hormone (GH) secretion is pulsatile and is significantly stimulated by various physiological factors, including stress, starvation (hypoglycemia), and deep sleep (Stage 3 and 4). During starvation, GH helps mobilize fatty acids for energy while sparing glucose. Its secretion peaks during the early hours of deep sleep, which is vital for tissue repair and growth in children. Glucocorticoids/Cortisol (Options B and C) definitely increase during stress and starvation but typically decrease during sleep. Prolactin (Option D) levels do rise during sleep and stress, but its primary stimulus is not starvation; rather, it's related to lactation and reproductive triggers. Understanding these hormonal triggers is crucial for diagnosing endocrine disorders. For example, the "insulin tolerance test" uses insulin-induced hypoglycemia (a form of starvation stress) to test if the pituitary gland can normally secrete GH. If GH levels fail to rise during this test, it indicates a deficiency
questions.learning: Growth Hormone (GH) secretion is pulsatile and is significantly stimulated by various physiological factors, including stress, starvation (hypoglycemia), and deep sleep (Stage 3 and 4).

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient receiving chemotherapy develops pneumonia with skin lesions. Microscopy of specimen from skin lesions showed broad based budding with a thick capsule. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Blastomycosis

In this case of an immunocompromised patient with pneumonia and skin lesions, the microscopy of specimens from skin lesions showing broad-based budding with a thick capsule suggests the diagnosis of Blastomycosis caused by Blastomyces dermitidis.

Blastomycosis is a chronic infection, characterized by the formation of suppurative and granulomatous lesions, especially, in the lungs and skin.

Blastomycosis predominantly affects individuals in regions where the fungus Blastomyces is endemic, such as the Midwest and southeastern United States. It is most common in North America and so is also called North American Blastomycosis.

The disease has a broad demographic impact, occurring in both immunocompetent and immunocompromised individuals. However, those with impaired immune systems—such as patients with AIDS, those on glucocorticoid therapy, or those receiving TNF-α inhibitors—are at higher risk for severe or disseminated disease involving the skin, bone, or central nervous system. Healthy individuals may experience a range of symptoms from mild pulmonary illness to more severe forms of pneumonia. It is more commonly observed in males aged 30-50 years, possibly due to occupational or recreational exposures.

Blastomycosis can present in three forms:

1. Pulmonary disease:

• Presents with cough, sputum production, chest pain, and fever
• Hilar lymphadenopathy may be present
• Focal or diffuse consolidation, miliary lesions, or abscess formation may occur.
• Resembles TB and Histoplasmosis

2. Cutaneous disease:

• Involvement of face and exposed parts of the skin
• Skin lesion: ulcerated verrucous granulomas with an advancing border and central scarring. The border is filled with microabscesses and has a sharp, sloping edge.

3. Disseminated disease:

• Multiple skin lesions are the most common presentation
• Highly fatal
• The genitourinary tract (especially the prostate) is frequently involved
• Bone involvement resembles chronic osteomyelitis.

It can be diagnosed based on culture findings. Characteristic findings include the presence of thick-walled round yeast cells with a single broad-based bud when cultured at 37°C. (figure of 8 appearance)

Treatment of localised mild/moderate disease includes Itraconazole (6 months) and for disseminated/ severe disease- amphotericin B.

The image given below shows the skin lesions and microscopy of broad-based budding by Blastomyces dermitidis.

Other options

Option B: Histoplasmosis is caused by Histoplasma capsulatum. It has tiny oval yeast cells with narrow-based budding within the macrophages with an underlying granulomatous response. This is a dimorphic fungus that exists in the yeast form in body tissues and cultures maintained at 37°C, and in the filamentous mould form in cultures at room temperature (25°C).

Option C: Coccidiomycosis is caused by Coccidioides immitis which is a thermally dimorphic fungus. It occurs as a spherule in tissues and culture at 37°C and as the mycelial form in soil and culture at room temperature. They are endemic to the arid desert regions of the southwestern USA and California. Infection is acquired by inhaling dust containing arthrospores of the fungus.

Option D: Candidiasis is caused by candida species which are yeast-like fungi. They exist as yeast and pseudohyphae. It appears as budding gram-positive cells on wet films and smears. Mycelial forms suggest colonization. Candida albicans form chlamydospores on corn meal agar.
questions.learning: Blastomycosis — In this case of an immunocompromised patient with pneumonia and skin lesions, the microscopy of specimens from skin lesions showing broad-based budding with a thick capsule suggests the diagnosis of Blastomycosis caused by Blastomyces…

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 17-year-old girl was brought by her mother to the outpatient department with primary amenorrhea. She had normal breast development and pubic hair. On examination, the vagina was blind-ending and the uterus was not palpable. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Mullerian agenesis

The given clinical scenario of a girl with primary amenorrhea, normal breasts, and pubic hair, with a blind-ending vagina and uterus not palpable, is suggestive of Mullerian agenesis.

Absent uterus and vagina in a person with female genotype and phenotype are features of Mullerian agenesis, also known as Mayer-Rokitansky-Kuster-Hauser syndrome.

Ovaries are normal and secondary sexual characters are well developed with normal external genitalia. This condition is associated with anomalies of the spine/skeleton and the kidneys along with the urinary tract.

Diagnosis is made with the help of pelvic sonography, MRI, and laparoscopy. Patients may have rudimentary Mullerian bulbs without an endometrial cavity. These should be surgically excised if they are symptomatic.

Other options:

Option B: Gonadal dysgenesis patients present with primary amenorrhoea, absence of secondary sex characters (poorly developed breasts), and female external genitalia.

Option C: In Turner syndrome, short stature with poor development of secondary sexual characters and short stature will be seen. It has a karyotype of 45 XO. Barr body will be absent. Female genital organs (vagina, uterus, fallopian tubes, ovaries) are present. The ovaries, though present, are atrophic.

Option D: Testicular feminization syndrome also known as androgen insensitivity syndrome has a karyotype of 46XY. Secondary sexual characters like the development of axillary hair and pubic hair are absent in these females. However, breast development is adequate due to the conversion of androgen into estrogen during puberty.
questions.learning: Mullerian agenesis — The given clinical scenario of a girl with primary amenorrhea, normal breasts, and pubic hair, with a blind-ending vagina and uterus not palpable, is suggestive of Mullerian agenesis.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which drug acts by inhibiting calcineurin and thereby decreasing IL-2 synthesis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cyclosporine

Cyclosporine binds the intracellular immunophilin cyclophilin; the drug–cyclophilin complex inhibits the phosphatase calcineurin. Calcineurin normally dephosphorylates NFAT (nuclear factor of activated T cells), allowing it to enter the nucleus and transcribe IL-2. Blocking calcineurin therefore prevents IL-2 gene transcription → failure of T-helper cell activation and clonal proliferation. Tacrolimus works identically but binds FKBP-12 instead.

Other options:

• A. Sirolimus: Also binds FKBP-12, but the complex inhibits mTOR, blocking the signal from the IL-2 receptor — i.e., it blocks IL-2 response, not IL-2 synthesis.
• C. Glucocorticoids: Inhibit NF-κB → broadly ↓ cytokines (IL-1, IL-2, IL-6, TNF-α); not a calcineurin action.
• D. Azathioprine → converted to 6-MP → inhibits purine synthesis → antiproliferative (S-phase).

Toxicity pearl:

• Cyclosporine → nephrotoxicity, hypertension, gum hyperplasia, hirsutism.
• Tacrolimus → more neurotoxicity and diabetogenicity, but no gum hyperplasia or hirsutism.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A neurologist evaluates a patient with rapidly progressive dementia, myoclonus, and periodic sharp-wave complexes on EEG. MRI shows hyperintensity in the caudate nucleus and putamen, raising suspicion for Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease (CJD). Which of the following best describes the causative agent?
options: An infectious protein lacking nucleic acid
A hybrid infectious particle composed of bacterial and viral components
An infectious agent containing abundant DNA responsible for replication
An organism that can be propagated on routine cell-free culture media
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. An infectious protein lacking nucleic acid

Prions are proteinaceous infectious particles composed of an abnormal isoform (PrPS) of the normal cellular prion protein (PrPC).

Key characteristics:

• No DNA or RNA
• Infectious despite lacking nucleic acid
• Propagate by inducing misfolding of normal prion proteins
• Resistant to heat, proteases, formalin, UV radiation, and standard sterilization methods
• Cause transmissible spongiform encephalopathies (TSEs)

Major Prion Diseases:

• Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease (CJD)
• Variant CJD
• Kuru
• Gerstmann–Sträussler–Scheinker syndrome
• Fatal familial insomnia
• Bovine spongiform encephalopathy ("Mad cow disease")
questions.learning: An infectious protein lacking nucleic acid Prions are proteinaceous infectious particles composed of an abnormal isoform (PrPS) of the normal cellular prion protein (PrPC).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Disappearance of loud S1 in mitral stenosis occurs in all except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Mild MS

Loud S1 is heard in mild mitral stenosis (MS).

The intensity of S1 depends on the distance over which the anterior leaflet of the mitral valve moves, leaflet mobility, LV contractility, and PR interval. It is independent of the severity of MS.

Loud S1 is seen in early rheumatic MS, short PR interval, and hyperdynamic circulatory states.

S1 becomes soft in case of calcified leaflets, long PR interval, associated aortic regurgitation and LV dysfunction.
questions.learning: Mild MS Loud S1 is heard in mild mitral stenosis (MS). The intensity of S1 depends on the distance over which the anterior leaflet of the mitral valve moves, leaflet mobility, LV contractility, and PR interval.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with sarcoidosis and multi-organ involvement is being evaluated for treatment options. Which of the following drugs is not commonly used in the management of sarcoidosis?
questions.explanation: Sarcoidosis is a systemic granulomatous disease. Prednisone (Option D) is the gold-standard first-line therapy to control inflammation. In cases where steroids are insufficient or not tolerated, steroid-sparing agents such as Methotrexate (Option C) or antimalarials like Hydroxychloroquine (Option B, particularly for skin or hypercalcemia) are typically used . Fludrocortisone (Option A) is a mineralocorticoid used primarily for the management of adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease) or orthostatic hypotension; it has no therapeutic role in treating the granulomatous inflammatory process of sarcoidosis. Because the other listed drugs are standard components of the sarcoidosis treatment ladder, Fludrocortisone is the correct "except" choice. Management of multi-organ sarcoidosis focuses on suppressing the immune-mediated formation of non-caseating granulomas to prevent permanent organ damage. Clinicians must balance the benefits of these immunosuppressants with their long-term side-effect profiles. Therefore, Fludrocortisone is the outlier in this list of sarcoidosis medications
questions.learning: Sarcoidosis is a systemic granulomatous disease. Prednisone (Option D) is the gold-standard first-line therapy to control inflammation.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient undergoes parotid gland surgery and subsequently develops loss of cutaneous sensation over the angle of the mandible and the lower part of the external ear. Which of the following nerves is most likely to have been injured during the procedure?
options: Temporofacial branch of the facial nerve
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Great auricular nerve

The great auricular nerve (C2–C3), a cutaneous branch of the cervical plexus, ascends superficially across the sternocleidomastoid muscle to supply cutaneous sensation over the angle of the mandible, parotid region, mastoid process, and the lower part of the auricle (external ear). Because it runs superficially over the parotid gland, it is commonly injured during parotidectomy, resulting in postoperative numbness over these areas.

Why not the other options?

• A. Marginal mandibular nerve: A motor branch of the facial nerve (CN VII) supplying muscles of the lower lip (depressor anguli oris, depressor labii inferioris, mentalis). Injury causes asymmetry of the lower lip, not sensory loss.
• B. Temporofacial branch of the facial nerve: A motor branch supplying muscles of facial expression in the upper face (frontalis, orbicularis oculi, etc.). Injury causes facial weakness, not cutaneous sensory loss.
• C. Auriculotemporal nerve: A sensory branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (V3) supplying the anterior auricle, external acoustic meatus, temporal region, and TMJ. It does not supply the angle of the mandible or lower ear. It also carries postganglionic parasympathetic fibers to the parotid gland and is involved in Frey syndrome after parotid surgery.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A young lady presented to the ENT OPD with a history of sudden onset unilateral hearing loss, tinnitus, and dizziness following an episode of acute otitis media two weeks back. Rinne test and fistula test were positive. She had refused treatment then and currently came with complaints of worsened hearing loss in the affected ear. On examination, the fistula test was negative. What would be the most likely finding on the Rinne test in this scenario?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. False negative

The given clinical scenario indicates severe sensorineural hearing loss as a consequence of untreated suppurative labyrinthitis and Rinne's test is a false negative in this case.

Initially, the patient had a positive fistula test, which implies that the labyrinth is still functioning. Rinne's test is positive which could be due to normal hearing or sensorineural hearing loss.

Currently, the patient has a negative fistula test which implies that the labyrinth is dead. This is an example of severe sensorineural hearing loss and here, Rinne test is a false negative.

If intermittent pressure applied to the external ear produces vertigo and nystagmus, it is a positive fistula test. The pressure changes in the external ear are transmitted to the labyrinth. This is suggestive of abnormal communication between the middle ear and the inner ear.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A 62-year-old man with diabetes, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia comes to the emergency department of an academic medical center with chest pain, nausea, vomiting, and diaphoresis. Investigators are designing a randomized control trial to test the hypothesis that drug B will decrease the mortality associated with acute ST-elevation myocardial infarction compared to standard of care. To ensure that investigators will not miss a difference between drug B and standard of care (if a difference truly exists), which of the following would they want to maximize?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1- beta

To avoid missing a real difference between treatments (i.e., reducing Type II error), investigators aim to maximize statistical power, which equals 1 − β. Higher power increases the likelihood of detecting a true effect if it exists. Alpha (α) relates to Type I error, not this concern.
questions.learning: 1- beta To avoid missing a real difference between treatments (i.e., reducing Type II error), investigators aim to maximize statistical power, which equals 1 − β.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Nitric oxide is synthesized from:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. L - arginine

Nitric oxide is synthesized from arginine by a calcium-dependent reaction catalyzed by NO synthase.

The co-enzymes of NO synthase include FMN, FAD, Heme, and Tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4).

Pearl PF0661: Amino Acid Derivatives
questions.learning: L - arginine Nitric oxide is synthesized from arginine by a calcium-dependent reaction catalyzed by NO synthase. The co-enzymes of NO synthase include FMN, FAD, Heme, and Tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Identify the visual field defect in the given image:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Homonymous hemianopia

The visual field defect in the given image is the right homonymous hemianopia.

Right homonymous hemianopia, marked by loss of vision in the right half of the visual field of both eyes, indicates a lesion in the left optic tract. This occurs because the optic tract transmits visual information from the left nasal retina and right temporal retina, and disruption leads to right-sided visual field loss.

This condition highlights a post-chiasmal visual pathway issue, primarily affecting the optic tract, which processes contralateral visual fields. Common causes of lesions include pituitary adenomas, craniopharyngiomas, optic thalamus tumours, and aneurysms of the superior cerebellar or posterior cerebral arteries, as well as demyelinating diseases and infarctions.

Complete homonymous hemianopia affects the complete visual hemifields of both eyes due to large lesions posterior to the optic chiasma. In contrast, smaller lesions can cause incomplete homonymous hemianopia, categorized as congruous or incongruous based on the similarity of defects in each half field. Lesions in the immediate post-chiasmal region often produce incongruent defects, while more posterior lesions in the occipital cortex result in congruous homonymous hemianopia.

Altitudinal hemianopia is defined as hemianopia affecting the upper or lower half of the visual field. It is most commonly seen in anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (AION). Also seen in suprasellar tumors and occipital lobe lesions.
questions.learning: Homonymous hemianopia — The visual field defect in the given image is the right homonymous hemianopia. Right homonymous hemianopia, marked by loss of vision in the right half of the visual field of both eyes, indicates a lesion in the left optic tract.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following tissues are dependent on insulin for glucose uptake?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Adipose tissue

Adipose tissue is dependent on insulin for glucose uptake.

The uptake of glucose in skeletal muscles is also dependent on insulin but may be mediated via non-insulin-dependent mechanisms as well (such as muscle contractions). Therefore the best answer out of the given options is adipose tissue.

Glucose uptake by skeletal muscle, cardiac muscle, and adipose tissues is via GLUT-4 which is insulin-dependent. In the presence of insulin, GLUT-4 receptors translocate to the cell membrane and hence, glucose uptake by the cell occurs.

Most of the other GLUT transporters are not insulin sensitive and are constitutively expressed in the cell membrane. Ex: GLUT-1 in RBCs, brain and kidneys. (GLUT-3 is also present in the brain and kidneys)
questions.learning: Adipose tissue Adipose tissue is dependent on insulin for glucose uptake. The uptake of glucose in skeletal muscles is also dependent on insulin but may be mediated via non-insulin-dependent mechanisms as well (such as muscle contractions).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Match the following organs with their embryological origin:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1-c, 2-d, 3-b

Knowledge of the embryological origin of organs is essential for understanding congenital anomalies and developmental disorders.

Correct Match:

• 1. Thyroid → Endoderm
• 2. Adrenal medulla → Neural crest cells
• 3. Kidney → Intermediate mesoderm

Why are these correct?

• 1. Thyroid (follicular cells) develops from the endoderm of the primitive pharyngeal floor. (Parafollicular/C cells are derived from neural crest via the ultimobranchial body.)
• 2. Adrenal medulla is derived from neural crest cells, which differentiate into chromaffin cells.
• 3. Kidneys develop from the intermediate mesoderm (metanephric mesenchyme and ureteric bud).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The following drain is placed after mastectomy. Identify the type of drain.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Closed

The Romo Vac drain, depicted in the image, is a closed type of drain commonly used after mastectomy.

Drains are placed at surgical sites to freely collect the air or fluids that may accumulate. This enhances wound healing by preventing the formation of unnecessary cavities. Drains are prophylactic in elective surgeries and therapeutic in emergency surgeries. Drains can be -

• Open - They are based on the principle of gravity
• Semi-open - Their action is based on capillary effect
• Closed - They carry out their actions through suction

Suction drains are commonly used in chest, breast, abdominal, thyroid, and plastic surgeries. They remove intraperitoneal secretions, anastomotic leaks, and blood from hemorrhage at the surgical site. Romo Vac drain is a negative suction drain closed drain kept in the subcutaneous tissue. Romo Vac drain is indicated in modified radical mastectomy, subcutaneous swelling excision, and amputations.

Special types of drains:

• Chest drains are connected to an underwater seal to aid the exit of air from the pleural cavity. They are used in pneumothorax, pleural effusion, and hemothorax.
• After surgical exploration of the bile duct, the sphincter of Oddi goes into spasm. To facilitate drainage of bile, a T tube may be used.

Drain insertion site care: The site of insertion of the drain is kept clean by drying and patting the drain insertion site with a clean towel after bath. The dressing is changed daily with folded gauze pieces placed below and above the drain site.

Removal of drains: The catheter at the site is milked for residual collections. It is then clamped and the suture holding the catheter is cut. The tube is then gently pulled out and any clots at the perforation end are removed. The time of removal of drains for various conditions is as given below.

• Drains used in surgeries like thyroidectomy are usually removed within 24 hours. Their main purpose is to cover postoperative bleeding.
• In a mastectomy, a drain is placed for 5 days to collect serous collections.
• Drains used to cover the colorectal anastomoses are placed for 5-7 days.
• Common bile duct T-tube drains are usually placed for 10 days.
• Drains for infections are removed when the infection subsides or when the content of the drain is minimal.

After the drain is removed, a folded gauze is placed over the drain insertion area. The dressing can be removed after 24 hours. The patient may be given an antibiotic ointment to apply over the area for a week.
questions.learning: Closed — The Romo Vac drain, depicted in the image, is a closed type of drain commonly used after mastectomy. Drains are placed at surgical sites to freely collect the air or fluids that may accumulate.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: An individual is in an environment of a temperature of 47°C. What is the mechanism of heat loss?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Sweating

The mechanism of heat loss in the given case where the surrounding temperatures are higher than the body temperature is sweating.

Different methods of heat loss:

• Radiation is heat loss in the form of infrared rays.
• Conduction is heat loss that occurs by direct contact with an object.
• Convection is heat loss resulting from air movement.

When the temperature of the surroundings is more than that of the skin, the body gains heat by both radiation and conduction. Under these conditions, the heat can be lost from the body only by evaporation or sweating.

When the body temperature is greater than the temperature of the surroundings, heat can be lost by radiation and conduction.
questions.learning: Sweating — The mechanism of heat loss in the given case where the surrounding temperatures are higher than the body temperature is sweating. Different methods of heat loss: • Radiation is heat loss in the form of infrared rays. • Conduction is heat loss…

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A child came for DPT vaccination at 10 weeks. He has a history of fever of more than 40°C and an inconsolable cry at 6 weeks of age following vaccination. What should be done next?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Give DPT vaccine

The next step for this patient should be to administer DPT vaccine.

Events such as persistent inconsolable crying (more than 3 hours in duration), hyperpyrexia (fever > 40°C), hypotonic-hyporesponsive episodes within 48 hours of DTwP administration, and seizures, with or without fever, within 72 hours DTwP administration are considered precautions but not contraindications to future doses of DTwP. These events don't recur with the next dose and have been shown to have no permanent sequelae.

Absolute contraindications to any pertussis vaccination are a history of anaphylaxis or development of encephalopathy within 7 days following previous DTwP vaccination. In case of anaphylaxis, further immunization with diphtheria, tetanus, and pertussis vaccines are contraindicated as it cannot be said with certainty which component caused anaphylaxis. For patients with a history of encephalopathy following vaccination, any pertussis vaccine is contraindicated, and only diphtheria and tetanus vaccines may be used.

Note: This answer might be controversial. The above answer is as per the IAP Guidebook on Immunization.
questions.learning: Give DPT vaccine — The next step for this patient should be to administer DPT vaccine. Events such as persistent inconsolable crying (more than 3 hours in duration), hyperpyrexia (fever > 40°C), hypotonic-hyporesponsive episodes within 48 hours of DTwP…

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following radioisotopes is used in a PET-CT scan?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 18F-FDG

18F-FDG is the radioisotope used in a PET-CT scan.

Positron emission tomography - CT (PET-CT):

* PET imaging is based on the detection of an injected positron-emitting radioactive tracer.

* It relies on the coincidence detection of the annihilation photons (γ), which are released when a positron combines with an electron.

* A glucose analogue called FDG (fluorodeoxyglucose) is used in PET imaging. FDG is taken up by metabolically active cells, where it undergoes phosphorylation to form FDG-6-phosphate. Unlike glucose, FDG-6-phosphate cannot undergo further metabolism and becomes trapped within the cell. (So, the patient must be fasted for 4-6 hrs prior to imaging).

* The trapped FDG-6-phosphate is detected by the PET scanner.

* Before injecting FDG, the blood glucose level should be measured. It should be < 150 mg/dL. Good blood glucose control is essential as FDG uptake is competitively inhibited by glucose.

* Imaging is started 60 minutes following FDG injection.

Indications of PET-CT:

* PET-CT is used in oncology imaging to detect malignant cells as they demonstrate increased glucose metabolism relative to normal tissues.

* It is indicated for the differentiation of a malignant from a benign lesion.

* It is indicated in tumour staging and evaluation of tumour recurrence.

Areas of normal physiological uptake in PET CT:

* Brain tissue

* Skeletal muscle, especially after strenuous activity, and laryngeal muscles following speech

* Myocardium

* Gastrointestinal tract, e.g. intestinal wall

* Genitourinary tract (FDG is excreted via the renal system and passes into the collecting systems)

* Brown fat (FDG accumulates here as glucose and ATP are required for heat production)

* Thymus

* Bone marrow

Other options:

Option A: 16F-FDG (Fluorodeoxyglucose) is a radiolabeled glucose analogue used in Positron Emission Tomography (PET) to assess metabolic activity in tissues. It is particularly useful for detecting cancer, and infections, and monitoring neurological disorders due to its ability to highlight areas with high glucose consumption.

Option C: Carbon-11 (C-11) is used for certain types of PET imaging, particularly in neurology and oncology.

Option D: Gallium-68 (Ga-68) is used for imaging certain types of neuroendocrine tumours and somatostatin receptor imaging.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following statements is true about vitamin K?
options: Deficiency of vitamin K leads to hypercoagulability.
It is a water soluble vitamin.
Prolonged use of antibiotics leads to vitamin K deficiency.
Menaquinone is the dietary source of vitamin K found in green vegetables.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Prolonged use of antibiotics leads to vitamin K deficiency.

Prolonged use of antibiotics leads to vitamin K deficiency. This is due to the loss of normal bowel flora that synthesizes menaquinones (vitamin K2).

Vitamin K is a fat-soluble vitamin. The following are the vitamers of vitamin K:

• Phylloquinone (Vitamin K1) is the normal dietary source of Vitamin K that is found in green vegetables.
• Menaquinones (Vitamin K2) are synthesized by intestinal bacteria.
• Menadione (Vitamin K3) is a synthetic compound that is metabolized to phylloquinone.
questions.learning: Prolonged use of antibiotics leads to vitamin K deficiency. Prolonged use of antibiotics leads to vitamin K deficiency.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: All the following can be treated with supportive psychotherapy except
options: Person with cognitive decline and physical symptoms
Person who has good motivation and control over frustration
Patient with acute psychiatric illness along with crisis
Patient with severe chronic disease and ego dysfunctioning
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Person who has good motivation and control over frustration

Supportive psychotherapy is not indicated in a person who has good motivation and control over frustration. Such individuals are better treated by expressive psychotherapy.

Supportive psychotherapy places major etiological emphasis on external rather than intrapsychic events, particularly on stressful environmental and interpersonal influences on a severely damaged self. The general aim of supportive treatment is the amelioration or relief of symptoms through behavioral or environmental restructuring within the existing psychic framework. This often means helping the patient to adapt better to problems and to live more comfortably with his or her psychopathology.

Supportive therapy uses several methods, either singly or in combination, including warm, friendly, strong leadership; help in developing pleasurable activities (e.g., hobbies); removal of excessive strain, when possible; medication to alleviate symptoms; and guidance and advice in dealing with current issues. This therapy uses techniques to help patients feel secure, accepted, encouraged, and not anxious.

Supportive psychotherapy is generally indicated for those patients for whom classic psychoanalysis or insight-oriented psychoanalytic psychotherapy is typically contraindicated- those who have poor ego strength and whose potential for decompensation is high.

Amenable patients fall into the following major areas:

• Individuals in acute crisis or a temporary state of disorganization and inability to cope, whose intolerable life circumstances have produced extreme anxiety or sudden turmoil (e.g., individuals going through grief reactions, illness, divorce, job loss, or who were victims of crime, abuse, natural disaster, or accident);
• Patients with chronic severe pathology with fragile or deficient ego functioning (e.g., those with latent psychosis, impulse disorder, or severe character disturbance);
• Patients whose cognitive deficits and physical symptoms make them particularly vulnerable and, thus, unsuitable for an insight-oriented approach (e.g., certain psychosomatic or medically ill persons);
• Individuals who are psychologically unmotivated (e.g., patients who come to treatment in response to family or agency pressure and are interested only in immediate relief or those who need assistance in very specific problem areas of social adjustment as a possible prelude to more exploratory work).

Because support forms a tacit part of every therapeutic modality, it is rarely contraindicated as such. The typical attitude regards better-functioning patients as unsuitable not because they will be harmed by a supportive approach, but because they will not be sufficiently benefited by it.
questions.learning: Person who has good motivation and control over frustration Supportive psychotherapy is not indicated in a person who has good motivation and control over frustration.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Extra mammary Paget's disease is commonly seen in the:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Vulva

Extramammary Paget's disease arises most frequently on the vulva. Other sites include the perineum, scrotum, perianal skin, and penis.

Extramammary Paget's disease (EMPD) can be primary or secondary.

• Primary EMPD is more common and occurs in the absence of an underlying malignancy, thought to arise from intraepidermal parts of apocrine glands or from pluripotent cells from the epidermis.
• Secondary EMPD arises from an underlying adnexal carcinoma or internal malignancy due to the epidermotropic spread of malignant cells from the underlying tumor.

Visceral malignancies associated with EMPD are carcinomas of the colon, rectum, bladder, urethra, cervix, and prostate. The patient presents with well-defined, moist, erythematous scaly plaques and severe pruritis. Lichenification and excoriations may also be seen.

Diagnosis is confirmed by punch, wedge, or excisional skin biopsy. A systemic workup should also be done to identify any underlying malignancy and they include colonoscopy, cystoscopy, colposcopy, and pelvic examination with pap smear in females.

Treatment:

• Mohs microscopic surgery with 5 cm margin clearance
• Radiotherapy
• Topical 5-fluorouracil and imiquimod
• Chemotherapy
• Photodynamic therapy

The given image below shows extramammary Paget's disease of the vulva.
questions.learning: Vulva Extramammary Paget's disease arises most frequently on the vulva. Other sites include the perineum, scrotum, perianal skin, and penis.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A person dies suddenly while their family is abroad, and the viscera is preserved during autopsy. Which substances can still be detected in the visceral organs even if the person did not consume them immediately before death?
questions.explanation: Alcohol (ethanol) is unique because it can be detected in viscera even if not consumed before death. This is due to postmortem production of alcohol by bacterial fermentation. After death, microorganisms such as Clostridium and Candida act on carbohydrates present in body tissues, leading to the formation of ethanol. This process is more common in decomposed bodies and can result in detectable alcohol levels despite no premortem intake. Therefore, the presence of alcohol in viscera must be interpreted carefully in forensic analysis, distinguishing between ante-mortem ingestion and post-mortem formation. Why other options are incorrect: (A) Morphine: Rapidly metabolized and can only be detected if taken before death. (B) Aconite: Unstable and decomposes quickly postmortem, making detection difficult unless recently ingested. (C) Arsenic: A cumulative poison but not produced postmortem; it is detectable only if consumed during life. Thus, only alcohol can appear in viscera without prior ingestion, making option (D) correct
questions.learning: Alcohol (ethanol) is unique because it can be detected in viscera even if not consumed before death. This is due to postmortem production of alcohol by bacterial fermentation.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 5-month-old infant is brought with a history of rhythmic elevation and depression of the left upper eyelid occurring during breastfeeding or thumb sucking, which disappears when feeding stops. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Marcus Gunn Jaw-Winking Syndrome is a congenital condition characterized by an abnormal synkinetic connection between the mandibular branch of the trigeminal nerve (CN V3) and the oculomotor nerve (CN III). Specifically, the branch of the trigeminal nerve that supplies the lateral pterygoid muscle (used for sucking and chewing) is misdirected to the levator palpebrae superioris (LPS) muscle of the eyelid. This results in the upper eyelid moving up and down in rhythm with jaw movements, such as during breastfeeding. Lagophthalmos (Option B) is the inability to close the eye completely. Myasthenia Gravis (Option C) presents with fatigable ptosis that worsens throughout the day, not jaw-related movement. A 3rd cranial nerve palsy (Option D) causes ptosis and limited eye motility but lacks the specific jaw-winking synchronization. This syndrome is typically unilateral and is most noticeable during infancy when the child is feeding
questions.learning: Marcus Gunn Jaw-Winking Syndrome is a congenital condition characterized by an abnormal synkinetic connection between the mandibular branch of the trigeminal nerve (CN V3) and the oculomotor nerve (CN III).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following vitamin deficiency is most likely to cause lactic acidosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Thiamine

Among the given options, thiamine is the most likely to cause lactic acidosis.

Thiamine is an essential cofactor for the enzyme pyruvate dehydrogenase, a key component of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex that converts pyruvate to acetyl-CoA. This conversion is critical for linking glycolysis to the citric acid cycle, thereby facilitating energy production in the body.

Without sufficient thiamine, the activity of pyruvate dehydrogenase is severely impaired, leading to an accumulation of pyruvate and lactate in the blood, causing lactic acidosis. This biochemical disturbance contributes to the neurological symptoms observed. Immediate administration of thiamine is crucial in treating Wernicke's encephalopathy. If left untreated, the condition can progress to Korsakoff syndrome, a chronic and debilitating memory disorder. Thus, recognising the signs and symptoms early and providing thiamine supplementation can lead to rapid improvement and prevent long-term complications.

Gingelly (sesame) seeds have the highest content of thiamine. Thiamine is lost from rice during the process of milling. As it is a water-soluble vitamin, washing and cooking rice cause further losses. Hence, it is advisable to avoid highly polished rice and eat parboiled or under-milled rice.

Thiamine's active form, thiamine diphosphate, acts as a coenzyme for three critical enzyme complexes: pyruvate dehydrogenase, α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and branched-chain keto acid dehydrogenase. This coenzyme facilitates oxidative decarboxylation by forming a reactive carbanion that attaches to carbonyl groups like those in pyruvate, leading to the release of CO₂. Thiamine diphosphate is also vital for transketolase in the pentose phosphate pathway.

Thiamine triphosphate, another form of thiamin, helps regulate nerve function by activating chloride channels in nerve membranes.

A thiamine deficiency can cause several conditions such as beriberi, characterised by peripheral neuritis, which can also involve heart failure and oedema. Additionally, thiamine deficiency can lead to Wernicke's encephalopathy and Korsakoff's psychosis, commonly associated with alcohol or drug abuse. The lack of thiamine impairs the conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA, leading to increased levels of lactate and pyruvate in the blood, which can result in dangerous lactic acidosis, especially in those consuming high-carbohydrate diets.
questions.learning: Thiamine Among the given options, thiamine is the most likely to cause lactic acidosis. Thiamine is an essential cofactor for the enzyme pyruvate dehydrogenase, a key component of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex that converts pyruvate to acetyl-CoA.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 5-year-old child presents with a history of approximately 18 episodes of watery diarrhea and two episodes of vomiting in a single day. The child appears irritable but is still able to take fluids orally. Based on this clinical presentation and hydration status, which treatment option would be the most appropriate for management?
options: Intravenous fluid initially for 4 hours followed by oral fluids
questions.explanation: Based on the WHO Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI) guidelines, this child is classified as having "some dehydration" because they are irritable and still able to drink. For children in this category, the first-line treatment is Oral Rehydration Therapy (ORT) using Oral Rehydration Salts (ORS) solution (Plan B). Intravenous fluids (Options A and C) are reserved for children with "severe dehydration" (Plan C), characterized by lethargy, unconsciousness, or inability to drink. Plain water with lithium (Option D) is medically incorrect and potentially toxic. ORS is highly effective because the glucose-sodium co-transport system in the gut remains intact even during most diarrheal illnesses, allowing for efficient fluid absorption. The child should be monitored for four hours while being given ORS, and then reassessed. Continued feeding and breastfeeding are also essential components of the diarrheal management protocol to prevent malnutrition and promote mucosal recovery
questions.learning: Based on the WHO Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI) guidelines, this child is classified as having "some dehydration" because they are irritable and still able to drink.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 27-year-old woman who is on oral contraceptive pills for contraception has forgotten to take her pills on 4 different days in the last 2 weeks. She presents to the primary health center, asking for advice. What would you suggest to her?
options: Take 4 pills now, continue the schedule, use barrier method of contraception
Take 1 pill now, continue the schedule, and use barrier method of contraception
Take 1 pill now, use barrier method, and consider emergency contraception in case of recent intercourse
Discard the pack, start a new pack with alternate method of contraception
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Discard the pack, start a new pack with alternate method of contraception

A woman who has missed 4 oral contraceptive pills in the last two weeks should take one hormonal pill as soon as possible and finish all hormonal pills in the pack as scheduled, throw away the 7 non-hormonal pills in a 28-pill pack and start a new pack the next day.

Missed pills
Management

Missed 1 or 2 pills/ started new pack 1 or 2 days late?

You have two options: take one hormonal pill right away, or take two pills at your usual scheduled time.

The risk of pregnancy is minimal to none.

Missed 3 or more pills in the first or second week/started new pack 3 or more days late?

Take one hormonal pill immediately and then continue taking your pills as scheduled.

Make sure to use a backup method of contraception for the next seven days.

Additionally, if you've had sexual intercourse within the last 72 hours, consider taking emergency contraceptive pills.

Missed 3 or more pills in the third week?

Take one hormonal pill as soon as you can and complete the entire pack of hormonal pills according to the schedule.

Discard the seven non-hormonal pills in a 28-pill pack.

Begin a new pack the following day.

Missed any nonhormonal pills? (last 7 pills in 28-pill pack)

Dispose of any missed non-hormonal pills.

Continue taking your combination oral contraceptives (COCs), one pill each day.

Begin the new pack as you normally would.

If any non-hormonal pills were missed, she can discard the remaining pills. Start the new pack of oral contraceptives and continue taking as usual.

If she vomits within 2 hours of taking a pill, another pill from the pack should be taken as soon as possible. After that, continue taking the pills as scheduled. If the vomiting or diarrhea persists for >2 days, follow the instructions for 1 or 2 missed pills as mentioned above.

The contraceptive method should be discontinued and changed in the following situations:

• Unexplained or prolonged heavy vaginal bleeding that suggests an underlying condition not related to the method
• Starting anticonvulsant medication or treatment with rifampicin
• Migraines
• Non-ambulatory conditions lasting for >1 week like major surgery, leg in a cast, etc. Combined oral contraceptives can be restarted 2 weeks after ambulation.
• Suspected heart or liver disease, hypertension, deep vein thrombosis, stroke, breast cancer, diabetes, or gall bladder disease
