questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Identify the area marked in the given image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Rectovesical pouch

The arrow in the image points to the rectovesical pouch.

The peritoneum covering the anterior surface of the rectum is reflected anteriorly to cover the posterosuperior surface of the bladder in males, forming a rectovesical pouch. This is the lowest part of the peritoneal cavity in males and an important site for pelvic fluid collection.

Other options:

Option B: Rectouterine pouch- The peritoneum which covers the anterior surface of the rectum is reflected anteriorly to cover the posterior surface of the posterior fornix of the vagina and the uterus, forming a rectouterine pouch.

Option C: Vesicouterine pouch- The peritoneum covering the fundus and body of the uterus, is reflected anteriorly to cover the posterosuperior surface of the bladder forming a vesico uterine pouch

Option D: Pouch of Morrison (hepatorenal recess) - The peritoneum covering the posterior surface of the right lobe of the liver is reflected posteriorly to cover the anterior surface of the right kidney and right suprarenal gland, forming a deep, vertical groove. This is the deepest peritoneal recess in the supine position and an important site for fluid collection.
questions.learning: Rectovesical pouch — The arrow in the image points to the rectovesical pouch. The peritoneum covering the anterior surface of the rectum is reflected anteriorly to cover the posterosuperior surface of the bladder in males, forming a rectovesical pouch.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following statements regarding Peutz-Jeghers syndrome are true? 1. Presents as multiple hamartomatous polyps in the GIT 2. Histology shows arborising smooth muscle bundles 3. It is an autosomal recessive condition 4. Extra-intestinal manifestations of Peutz-Jeghers syndrome include hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2

Peutz–Jeghers syndrome is an autosomal dominant hamartomatous polyposis syndrome caused by a mutation of the STK11/LKB1 tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 19p13.3.

1. Presents as multiple hamartomatous polyps in the GIT — TRUE

Peutz–Jeghers syndrome is characterized by:

• Multiple hamartomatous polyps
• Mainly in the small intestine (especially jejunum), but can occur throughout GIT.

2. Histology shows arborising smooth muscle bundles — TRUE

This is the classic histological hallmark of Peutz-Jeghers polyps.

Histology:

• Tree-like (“arborizing”) branching smooth muscle extending into the polyp.

3. It is an autosomal recessive condition — FALSE

Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is:

• Autosomal dominant
• Usually due to mutation in STK11/LKB1 tumor suppressor gene.

4. Extra-intestinal manifestations include hypertrophy of retinal pigment epithelium — FALSE

Congenital hypertrophy of retinal pigment epithelium (CHRPE) is associated with:

Familial adenomatous polyposis

—not Peutz-Jeghers syndrome.

Important Differential Diagnosis

| Syndrome | Polyp Type | Gene | Key Feature

| -------- | ---------- | ---- | -----------

| PJS | Hamartomatous | STK11 | Mucocutaneous pigmentation

| Juvenile polyposis | Hamartomatous | SMAD4/BMPR1A | Juvenile retention polyps

| FAP | Adenomatous | APC | CHRPE, colon cancer

| Cowden syndrome | Hamartomatous | PTEN | Trichilemmomas, breast/thyroid cancer
questions.learning: 1, 2 Peutz–Jeghers syndrome is an autosomal dominant hamartomatous polyposis syndrome caused by a mutation of the STK11/LKB1 tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 19p13.3.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following are indications of endometrial sampling? I. Endometrial tuberculosis II. Endometrial polyp III. Postmenopausal bleeding IV. Abnormal uterine bleeding Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. I, III and IV

Endometrial sampling (endometrial biopsy) is a minimally invasive procedure used to obtain endometrial tissue for histopathological examination. It is primarily indicated to evaluate abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB), exclude endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma, and diagnose specific endometrial diseases such as tuberculosis. The following are indications for endometrial sampling:

• I. Endometrial tuberculosis: Endometrial biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosing genital tuberculosis, demonstrating granulomatous inflammation and allowing microbiological testing (AFB stain, culture, PCR). ⭐
• III. Postmenopausal bleeding: Any postmenopausal bleeding requires evaluation for endometrial carcinoma, and endometrial sampling is indicated, especially when endometrial thickness is >4 mm or bleeding is recurrent. ⭐
• IV. Abnormal uterine bleeding: Endometrial biopsy is recommended in:

• Women ≥45 years with AUB
• Women <45 years with persistent AUB, failed medical treatment, or risk factors for endometrial carcinoma.

Why is II incorrect?

• II. Endometrial polyp: The preferred investigations are transvaginal ultrasound, saline infusion sonography, or hysteroscopy. Although a removed polyp is sent for histopathology, endometrial sampling alone is not the investigation of choice for diagnosing an endometrial polyp.
questions.learning: I, III and IV Endometrial sampling (endometrial biopsy) is a minimally invasive procedure used to obtain endometrial tissue for histopathological examination.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 33-year-old patient presented with chest pain, shortness of breath, and edema. On examination, his pulse was irregularly irregular, his JVP was elevated and showed a prominent ‘Y’ descent. On auscultation, he had a high-pitched diastolic sound. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Constrictive Pericarditis

Constrictive pericarditis presents with elevated JVP and a prominent ‘Y’ descent due to rapid early diastolic filling.

The high-pitched early diastolic sound (pericardial knock) is characteristic.

Systemic congestion with edema and dyspnea reflects impaired ventricular filling.

Cardiac tamponade has an absent Y descent, and valvular lesions do not produce a pericardial knock.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 24-year-old woman presented with severe pain and swelling in her right hand which is increasing in size and severity. She had a prick injury while in the garden 5 days back. On examination, she cries out in pain when you try to extend the hand and palpate the palmar aspect passively. Which of the following statements is true about this condition?
options: It is more common on the dorsal aspect of the hand
X ray imaging will aid in location of the foreign body in all patients.
Oral analgesics are the mainstay of treatment
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. It requires incision and drainage.

The above clinical scenario is suggestive of a deep palmar abscess secondary to a foreign body and it requires incision and drainage.

Foreign body intrusions into the hand are among the most common injuries to the upper extremity seen in the Emergency Department. They can present with pain and swelling initially. The patient also presents with partial foreign bodies after the partial removal of the object. The delayed presentation can lead to the development of deep palmar abscesses with severe pain and systemic signs (fever, tachycardia)

Diagnosis: History is useful. If a metal object is suspected, an X-ray can be used to locate the object. In patients with non-metallic objects, high-frequency ultrasound can be used.

Treatment requires exploration under anesthesia to remove the foreign body along with incision and drainage of the abscess.

Other options:

Option A: It is more common in the palmar space.

Option B: X-ray imaging can detect metallic objects. In the above case of splinters/thorns- high frequency musculoskeletal ultrasound probe can be used.

Option D: Analgesics are necessary but not the mainstay of treatment.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following features is not characteristic of the El Tor biotype of Vibrio cholerae, the organism responsible for epidemic diarrhea?
options: Resistant to El Tor phage V
Not susceptible to group IV phage
questions.explanation: Vibrio cholerae is divided into two main biotypes: Classical and El Tor. The El Tor biotype is actually "susceptible" to El Tor phage V; therefore, statement A is "not" a characteristic. The Classical biotype is resistant to phage V. The other statements are accurate descriptions of the El Tor biotype: it has "intrinsic resistance to Polymyxin B" (Option B, unlike Classical) , it is "Voges-Proskauer (VP) positive" (Option C, unlike Classical) , and it is "not susceptible to Group IV phage" (Option D, unlike Classical). Additionally, El Tor vibrios are generally more robust in the environment and are responsible for the current (seventh) cholera pandemic. These laboratory tests are used in epidemiological surveillance to track the spread of different cholera strains during outbreaks. Understanding biotype differences helps in predicting the severity and duration of diarrhea epidemics in a population
questions.learning: Vibrio cholerae is divided into two main biotypes: Classical and El Tor. The El Tor biotype is actually "susceptible" to El Tor phage V; therefore, statement A is "not" a characteristic.

Pulmonary artery hypertrophy with increased resistance

DAD is characterized by hyaline membranes, formed by fibrin-rich exudate lining the alveoli.

questions.text: A chronic smoker presents with cough and weight loss. Chest X-ray reveals a lung mass, and biopsy demonstrates chromogranin and synaptophysin positivity. Which of the following paraneoplastic syndromes is most likely associated with this condition?

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 34-year-old female presented with a painless mass in the right inguinal region. On examination, there is a cough impulse on the index finger and the swelling reduced completely on pressing it through the deep inguinal ring with a gurgling sound. What is the likely diagnosis in this lady?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Indirect inguinal hernia

The presentation of a painless swelling with a cough impulse is suggestive of a hernia. A hernia that reduces when pressing on the deep inguinal ring suggests a case of indirect inguinal hernia while a direct inguinal hernia emerges through the Hesselbach's triangle.

A femoral hernia passes through the femoral triangle whereas an umbilical hernia protrudes through the umbilicus.

The boundaries of Hesselbach’s triangle are:

* Lateral - inferior epigastric artery

* Medial - lateral border of rectus abdominis

* Inferior - inguinal ligament

Indirect inguinal hernias are by far the most common type of hernia in women. It is the most common hernia regardless of gender.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A comatose patient after sustaining severe head injury has been admitted in neurosurgical ICU. Which of the following parameters should ideally be maintained in this patient? 1. pCO₂ = 4.5–5.0 kPa (33–38 mmHg) 2. MAP = 80–90 mmHg 3. pO₂ > 11 kPa (>80 mmHg) 4. Na⁺ <130 mEq/L Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2 and 3

In severe traumatic brain injury (TBI), the goal is to prevent secondary brain injury by maintaining adequate oxygenation, cerebral perfusion, and normocapnia.

Why are the statements correct/incorrect?

• 1. pCO₂ = 4.5–5.0 kPa (33–38 mmHg): Correct. Normocapnia is maintained; prolonged hyperventilation is avoided.
• 2. MAP = 80–90 mmHg: Correct. Adequate MAP is required to maintain cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP).
• 3. pO₂ >11 kPa (>80 mmHg): Correct. Hypoxia must be avoided.
• 4. Na⁺ <130 mEq/L: Incorrect. Hyponatremia worsens cerebral edema. Serum sodium should be maintained in the normal or slightly high range.
questions.learning: 1, 2 and 3 In severe traumatic brain injury (TBI), the goal is to prevent secondary brain injury by maintaining adequate oxygenation, cerebral perfusion, and normocapnia.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which gene is not involved in SCID?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. BTK

BTK mutation causes X-linked agammaglobulinemia and not SCID (severe combined immunodeficiency).

Severe combined immunodeficiency is a defect in both humoral and cell-mediated immune responses. In this condition, the following genes are involved:

• JAK3
• RAG1
• IL-7R

Persons with SCID are extremely susceptible to recurrent, severe infections by a wide range of pathogens, including:

• Candida albicans
• Pneumocystis jiroveci
• Pseudomonas
• Cytomegalovirus
• Varicella
questions.learning: BTK BTK mutation causes X-linked agammaglobulinemia and not SCID (severe combined immunodeficiency). Severe combined immunodeficiency is a defect in both humoral and cell-mediated immune responses.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which of the following does not exhibit the Koebner's phenomenon?
questions.explanation: Koebner’s phenomenon, also known as the "isomorphic response," refers to the development of new skin lesions typical of a pre-existing dermatosis at sites of local trauma or injury. Classic examples of skin diseases that exhibit this phenomenon include Vitiligo (Option A), Psoriasis (Option B), and Lichen planus (Option C). Herpes (Option D) is a viral infection; while trauma can reactivate a latent virus (triggering a cold sore), it does not follow the definitive clinical definition of Koebner’s phenomenon, which specifically describes the linear induction of chronic dermatoses by trauma. Other conditions showing Koebner’s include warts and molluscum contagiosum (due to autoinoculation). Because Herpes is an acute, localized viral process rather than a trauma-induced distribution of a chronic dermatosis, it is the correct "not" choice. Recognizing this phenomenon is useful for clinicians when assessing the distribution of lesions
questions.learning: Koebner’s phenomenon, also known as the "isomorphic response," refers to the development of new skin lesions typical of a pre-existing dermatosis at sites of local trauma or injury.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text:
A pregnant lady with 34 weeks of amenorrhea has the following findings: LDH - 700 IU/L, platelets - 75,000/mm3, serum bilirubin - 1.5 mg/dL, SGOT - 200 U/L, SGPT - 150 U/L, and BP - 140/96 mm Hg. Her coagulation profile and renal function tests are normal. What is the diagnosis?

LDH - Lactate dehydrogenase
SGOT - Serum glutamic-oxaloacetic transaminase/AST - Aspartate transaminase
SGPT - Serum glutamic pyruvic transaminase/ALT - Alanine transaminase
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. HELLP syndrome

The given clinical scenario with elevated liver enzymes and bilirubin, low platelet count, and hypertension indicates the diagnosis of HELLP syndrome.

HELLP is an acronym for hemolysis (H), elevated liver enzymes (EL), and low platelet count (LP). It usually occurs in patients with severe preeclampsia. The patients typically present with right upper quadrant pain, nausea, and vomiting. Hypertension and proteinuria are seen but may be absent in some cases.

In this condition, there is periportal necrosis of the liver causing an elevation in liver enzymes (AST, ALT, and LDH) and bilirubin. Tennessee criteria used to diagnose HELLP syndrome include:

• Platelet count - <1 lakh/mm3
• AST - >70 IU/L
• LDH - >600 IU/L
• Hemolysis

Prompt delivery is indicated for ≥34 weeks gestational age. Vaginal delivery is the preferred route of delivery if cervix is favorable. Platelet transfusion is required if counts are less than 50,000/mm3. Magnesium sulfate is given as antiseizure prophylaxis, and anti-hypertensives are given for severe hypertension.

Complications of HELLP include eclampsia, placental abruption, hepatic subcapsular hematoma, coagulopathy, stroke, and pulmonary edema.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: GI Hepatobiliary System · Ascites Chronic Diarrhoea
questions.text: The most common causative agent for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Escherichia coli

Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) is an infection of ascitic fluid without an intra-abdominal surgically treatable source, occurring most commonly in patients with cirrhosis and ascites. The most common causative organism is Escherichia coli due to translocation of gut bacteria.

Why not the other options?

• B. Enterococcus spp: Less common; usually associated with healthcare-associated infections.
• C. Staphylococcus aureus: Uncommon cause of classic SBP.
• D. Streptococcus viridans: Can occur but is much less common than E. coli.
questions.learning: Escherichia coli Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) is an infection of ascitic fluid without an intra-abdominal surgically treatable source, occurring most commonly in patients with cirrhosis and ascites.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A patient presents with an endometrial thickness of 14mm with an adnexal mass. She has a history of complex endometrial hyperplasia with the presence of atypical cells. Which of the following is likely the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Metastasis endometrial cancer to ovary

This patient with endometrial hyperplasia and an adnexal mass likely has endometrial cancer with metastasis to the ovaries.

For those who undergo TVUS (transvaginal USG) and have an EEC (endometrial echo complex) >4 mm, localized thickening, or an indistinct or nonvisible EEC, endometrial sampling is a reasonable next step.

Investigations for endometrial carcinoma include:

* Endometrial aspiration biopsy is the first investigation for abnormal uterine bleeding, especially in females >35 years.

* Dilatation and fractional curettage was the best diagnosis method, but now it is not used.

* Hysteroscopy and biopsy: The investigation of choice for endometrial cancer.

* Transvaginal USG is used as an adjunct to endometrial biopsy.

* A Pap smear is not reliable to diagnose endometrial carcinoma. It is more useful as a screening tool rather than a diagnostic tool.

If symptoms of postmenopausal bleeding persist, imaging of the endometrial cavity should be performed with one or a combination of the following: TVUS, contrast sonography, or hysteroscopy.

Note: Surgical staging is the gold standard investigation for staging endometrial carcinoma.

Other options:

Option A: Struma ovarii is a type of highly specialized teratoma that contains only thyroid tissue. If it is functioning, it may lead to hyperthyroidism.

Option C: Polycystic ovarian disease is a disease characterized by menstrual abnormalities and hyperandrogenism in women of reproductive age. This condition has been linked to risk factors such as obesity and insulin resistance. Clinically these patients present with infertility and features of hyperandrogenism such as hirsutism and acne. On ultrasound, these patients have larger ovaries with an increased number of follicles. Multiple follicles that are peripherally located in the ovary can be seen on ultrasound. This is also called the string of pearls sign.

Option D: Immature teratomas such as solid teratomas of the ovary are solid and trabeculated. They also contain cartilage, bone, hair, and sebaceous material. There is no structural order. They are generally malignant. Grossly, they have a smooth external surface and are solid on sectioning. There may be areas of necrosis or hemorrhage.
questions.learning: Metastasis endometrial cancer to ovary — This patient with endometrial hyperplasia and an adnexal mass likely has endometrial cancer with metastasis to the ovaries.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following statements is false about thoracolumbar fascia?
options: In the lumbar region it is in 4 layers
In the thoraic region it is attatched medially to the vertebrae
The posterior and middle layers join with the anterior layer to form the aponeurotic origin of transversus abdominis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. In the lumbar region it is in 4 layers

In the lumbar region, the fascia consists of 3 layers - anterior, middle and posterior.

The thoracolumbar fascia is a complex arrangement of multiple fascial layers in the thoracolumbar region. This fascia encloses the paraspinal, quadratus lumborum, and lattismus dorsi muscles.

a) Thoraic region: The thoracolumbar fascia provides a thin fibrous covering for the extensor muscles of the vertebral column.

Relations:

* Medially attached to the spines of the thoracic vertebrae

* Laterally to the angles of the ribs

b)Lumbar region: It is in three layers:

* Anterior

* Medially - anterior surface of the lumbar transverse processes.

* Laterally - blends with the middle layer at the lateral border of the quadratus lumborum.

* Superiorly - lateral arcuate ligament and tip of Transverse process L1 to 12th rib.

* Inferiorly - inner lip of iliac crest and the ilio-lumbar ligament.

* Middle

* Medially - tips of the lumbar transverse processes and inter-transverse ligaments.

* Laterally - blends with the anterior layer at the lateral border of the quadratus lumborum.

* Superiorly - lower border of the 12th rib and lumbocostal ligament.

* Inferiorly - intermediate area of the iliac crest.

* Posterior

* Medially - lumbar and sacral spines and interspinous ligaments.

* Laterally - blends with the middle layer at the lateral border of the erector spinae.

* Superiorly - back of thorax - lumbar vertebral spines.

* Inferiorly - outer lip of the iliac crest

The posterior and middle layers unite to form a tough raphe at the lateral margin of erector spinae, and at the lateral border of quadratus lumborum they are joined by the anterior layer to form the aponeurotic origin of transversus abdominis.

Function:

* The attachments have a role in lifting and load transfer ,although controversial.

* They contain nociceptive nerve endings that may be responsible for back pain due to injury to the area and also impaired proprioceptive signalling.
questions.learning: In the lumbar region it is in 4 layers — In the lumbar region, the fascia consists of 3 layers - anterior, middle and posterior. The thoracolumbar fascia is a complex arrangement of multiple fascial layers in the thoracolumbar region.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which is not a product of heme catabolism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Aminolaevulinic acid

During heme catabolism, heme is degraded by the enzyme heme oxygenase to produce biliverdin, ferrous iron (Fe²⁺), and carbon monoxide (CO). Biliverdin is subsequently reduced to bilirubin by biliverdin reductase.

Aminolevulinic acid (ALA) is not a product of heme breakdown; instead, it is an intermediate in heme synthesis, formed from glycine and succinyl-CoA by ALA synthase in mitochondria.

Therefore, aminolevulinic acid belongs to the heme biosynthesis pathway, not the catabolic pathway, making it the correct answer.
questions.learning: Aminolaevulinic acid During heme catabolism, heme is degraded by the enzyme heme oxygenase to produce biliverdin, ferrous iron (Fe²⁺), and carbon monoxide (CO).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 42-year-old patient presents to the emergency department after a road traffic accident and is diagnosed with an extradural (epidural) hematoma caused by injury to the middle meningeal artery. At which site of the skull is the impact of collision most likely to have occurred?
questions.explanation: In cases of extradural hematoma (EDH) resulting from a road traffic accident, the site of impact is characteristically the Pterion. The Pterion is an H-shaped junction where the frontal, parietal, temporal, and greater wing of the sphenoid bones meet. This anatomical region is clinically significant because the bone is notably thin here and lies directly over the anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery. Trauma to this area often results in a fracture that ruptures the artery, causing blood to collect between the skull and the dura mater. The angle of the mandible (Option A) is located much lower and is not associated with the middle meningeal artery. The lambdoid suture (Option B) is at the posterior of the skull, while the nasion (Option C) is the midline depression at the bridge of the nose. Neither site typically underlies the specific arterial branches involved in the classic presentation of a temporal-region EDH
questions.learning: In cases of extradural hematoma (EDH) resulting from a road traffic accident, the site of impact is characteristically the Pterion. The Pterion is an H-shaped junction where the frontal, parietal, temporal, and greater wing of the sphenoid bones meet.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which among the following drugs does not require any renal dose modification in those with chronic kidney disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Linagliptin

Linagliptin is a competitive dipeptidyl peptidase - 4 inhibitor does not require any renal dose modification.

Linagliptin binds extensively to plasma proteins and is cleared primarily by the hepatobiliary system, with very little renal clearance.

It is used in type 2 diabetes as monotherapy or as combination therapy with other drugs when metformin is not tolerated or contraindicated.

Other options:

Saxagliptin and other DPP - 4 inhibitors circulate primarily in unbound form and are excreted largely unchanged in the urine. Renal dose modification is required in patients with reduced renal function.

Repaglinide is a non-sulfonylurea insulin secretagogue. A proportion of the drug is eliminated by the kidney and dose modification is required.

Glyburide is a sulfonylurea insulin secretagogue which is metabolised in the liver and the metabolites are excreted in the urine. Thus it requires dose modification in both renal and hepatic insufficiency.

The mechanism of action of DPP-4 inhibitors are:
questions.learning: Linagliptin Linagliptin is a competitive dipeptidyl peptidase - 4 inhibitor does not require any renal dose modification. Linagliptin binds extensively to plasma proteins and is cleared primarily by the hepatobiliary system, with very little renal clearance.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A person is diagnosed to have diabetes on his 45th birthday. When will you recommend a dilated fundus examination for him?
options: When he complains of decrease in vision
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Immediately

A 45 year old diagnosed with diabetes mellitus is likely to have type 2 diabetes and thus, he should undergo screening for diabetic retinopathy immediately.

Duration of diabetes is the most important risk factor for developing diabetic retinopathy, especially proliferative diabetic retinopathy. The recommendations for first fundus examination in diabetic retinopathy is:

• Within 3-5 years of diagnosis in type 1 diabetes
• Immediately in type 2 diabetes.

Later, the screening is continued once every year in both Type 1 and Type 2 diabetes. In the event proliferative diabetic retinopathy develops, screening is done more frequently - once every 2 months.
questions.learning: Immediately — A 45 year old diagnosed with diabetes mellitus is likely to have type 2 diabetes and thus, he should undergo screening for diabetic retinopathy immediately.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A neonate is found to have increased irritability, poor feeding, and 2 episodes of seizures. Lumbar puncture was done and the findings were suggestive of meningitis. What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Escherichia coli

The given clinical scenario describes neonatal meningitis. E. coli > Streptococcus agalactiae, part of group B streptococci, are the most likely causative organism of neonatal meningitis.

Early features of meningitis include temperature instability (hypo or hyperthermia), lethargy, bradycardia, and feed intolerance. Late features include seizures, bulging fontanelle, and nuchal rigidity.

The most common cause of bacterial meningitis in a 0 to 2-month baby is group B streptococci (Option B) worldwide and gram-ve bacteria like E.coli and Klebsiella (option A) in India. In babies aged 2 to 24 months, pneumococci are the primary causative pathogens, followed by H. influenzae. For children older than 2 years, pneumococci remain a prominent cause of meningitis, with Neisseria meningitidis being the second most common pathogen.

The most common etiological agents of neonatal meningitis and sepsis are listed in the table below:

India
Worldwide

Neonatal meningitis
E. coli, Klebsiella
Group B Streptococci

Neonatal sepsis
Klebsiella, S. aures, E. coli
Group B Streptococci

Neonates have immature cellular and humoral immunity. This makes them prone to meningitis and sepsis. Thus, an infant with a fever who is 28 days or younger, should be evaluated for sepsis.

Option C: Meningococcal infections are usually asymptomatic. If invasive disease occurs, then the clinical spectrum varies widely from meningococcal meningitis (highest proportion) to bacteremia without sepsis, meningococcal septicemia with or without meningitis, pneumonia, chronic meningococcemia, and occult bacteremia.

Option D: Meningitis caused by Listeria monocytogenes is rare but clinically significant. Infants can acquire the infection in utero or through an infected birth canal. Neonatal listeriosis can manifest as early-onset disease, typically within 1-2 days of birth, primarily as a septicemic form. Alternatively, it can present as a late-onset disease in infants older than 5 days, predominantly as a meningitic form.
questions.learning: Escherichia coli — The given clinical scenario describes neonatal meningitis. E. coli > Streptococcus agalactiae, part of group B streptococci, are the most likely causative organism of neonatal meningitis.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is an absolute contraindication for the device shown in the image below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vaginal bleeding of unknown etiology

The device shown in the image is of a CuT 380 A(IUD) and vaginal bleeding of unknown etiology is an absolute contraindication.

Absolute contraindications

Relative contraindications

• Suspected pregnancy
• PID

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The blood pressure of a population was tracked from childhood to adulthood. It was observed that those who had lower BP in childhood had low BP in adulthood, while those who had higher BP in childhood had high BP in adulthood. This can be best described as____
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Tracking of blood pressure

The above phenomenon is best described as the "tracking" of blood pressure.

In this phenomenon, the blood pressure of individuals is followed up from early childhood into adulthood. The BP in individuals with low BP levels tend to remain low, and in those with high BP levels, they tend to remain high. This phenomenon of persistence of rank order of blood pressure has been described as "tracking".

Other options:

Option A: The rule of halves depicts the disease burden of hypertension in the community. It states that only about half of the hypertensive subjects in the general population are aware of the condition. Only half of those aware are being treated and only half of those being treated are considered to be adequately treated.

A pictorial representation of the rule of halves in hypertension is shown below:

Option B: The WHO STEPwise approach to non-communicable disease (NCD) risk factor surveillance (STEPS) is a simple, standardized method for collecting, analyzing, and disseminating data on key NCD risk factors such as tobacco use, alcohol use, physical inactivity, unhealthy diet, overweight and obesity, raised blood pressure, raised blood glucose, and abnormal blood lipids.
questions.learning: Tracking of blood pressure — The above phenomenon is best described as the "tracking" of blood pressure. In this phenomenon, the blood pressure of individuals is followed up from early childhood into adulthood.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is not an indication of splenectomy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Bone marrow failure

Among the given options, bone marrow failure is not an indication of splenectomy.

Overall, the most common indication for splenectomy is trauma to the spleen, whether external (blunt or penetrating) or iatrogenic (e.g., during operative procedures for other reasons).

The most common indication for:

* Elective splenectomy - Haematological disorders such as hereditary spherocytosis, Idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP), thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP), etc.

* Emergency splenectomy - Trauma

* Splenectomy (overall) - Trauma.

Oncological

* Part of en bloc resection

* Diagnostic

* Therapeutic

Haematological

* Purpura (idiopathic/immune thrombocytopenic purpura)

* Hypersplenism

Portal hypertension

* Variceal surgery

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient is found on a railway track with hot dry skin, raised temperature, dilated pupils, slurred speech, and a staggering gait. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Dhatura poisoning

Dhatura (Datura stramonium)

A plant packed with anticholinergic alkaloids:

• Atropine
• Scopolamine
• Hyoscyamine

Hot dry skin, hyperthermia, mydriasis, slurred speech, and ataxia indicate an anticholinergic toxidrome. Dhatura contains atropine-like alkaloids causing central and peripheral antimuscarinic effects. Classic features are “hot as a hare, dry as a bone, blind as a bat.”

Opioids cause miosis and respiratory depression, not dryness or hyperthermia.

| Feature | Anticholinergic | Opioid | Cocaine

| ------- | --------------- | ------ | -------

| Skin | Dry | Normal | Sweaty

| Pupils | Dilated | Pinpoint | Dilated

| Temp | ↑ | ↓/normal | ↑

| CNS | Delirium | Depressed | Agitated
questions.learning: Dhatura poisoning Dhatura (Datura stramonium) — A plant packed with anticholinergic alkaloids: • Atropine • Scopolamine • Hyoscyamine Hot dry skin, hyperthermia, mydriasis, slurred speech, and ataxia indicate an anticholinergic toxidrome.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient with rectal prolapse underwent surgery. The postoperative image is given below. Identify the procedure.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Thiersch wiring

The postoperative image shows a purse-string suture which is suggestive of Thiersch wiring for rectal prolapse.

In Thiersch's wiring, a steel wire or a silastic/nylon tape is placed around the anal canal. It is rarely done now due to post-operative problems like chronic perineal sepsis, anal stenosis, and obstructed defecation.

Rectal prolapse is of two types:

1. Partial rectal prolapse - only the mucosal layer of the rectum is prolapsed. It is seen in children and is managed by digital repositioning. If there is a recurrence, then Theirsch's wiring or sclerotherapy is performed.
2. Complete rectal prolapse - all the layers of the rectum are involved. It is seen in adults due to the weakening of the pelvic floor. It is managed by using the following approaches:

1. The perineal approach - easy to perform, and has fewer complications but a high recurrence rate. It is preferred in elderly patients with comorbidities. The surgeries done include:

1. Thiersch's wiring
2. Delorme's mucosectomy - In this procedure, the rectal mucosa is stripped circumferentially from the rectum over the length of the prolapse. The underlying muscle is plicated with a series of sutures. The excess rectal mucosa is excised and a mucosal anastomosis is performed.
3. Altemeier's recto sigmoidectomy (option D) - In this procedure, full-thickness resection of the prolapsed rectum is performed, incorporating any associated colonic prolapse. Restoration of colorectal continuity can be performed by hand-sewn/stapled anastomosis. This is the procedure of choice in patients presenting with incarcerated and strangulated prolapse.

2. The abdominal approach - It is difficult to perform and has more complications, but a lower recurrence rate. The surgeries done include:

1. Ripstein's procedure - It involves the placement of a prosthetic mesh around the mobilized rectum, with the attachment of the mesh to the presacral fascia below the sacral promontory.
2. Well's procedure (option B) - It involves posterior rectopexy.

Other options:

Option A: Stapled hemorroidopexy is used in the treatment of internal hemorrhoids, where a circular stapling device is used to excise a cylinder of mucosa and submucosa and simultaneously staple the mucosal ends together.
questions.learning: Thiersch wiring — The postoperative image shows a purse-string suture which is suggestive of Thiersch wiring for rectal prolapse. In Thiersch's wiring, a steel wire or a silastic/nylon tape is placed around the anal canal.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: All the following can result in non-immune hydrops except
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. ABO incompatibility

ABO incompatibility is not a cause of nonimmune hydrops.

Hydrops is diagnosed by identifying two or more fetal effusions—pleural, pericardial, or ascites—or one effusion plus anasarca. Hydrops can be seen in association with red cell auto immunization, which is termed immune hydrops. Otherwise, it is nonimmune. Pathogenesis of hydrops includes decreased colloid oncotic pressure, increased hydrostatic or central venous pressure, and enhanced vascular permeability.

Etiology of hydrops fetalis

Cardiovascular

• Structural defects: Ebstein anomaly, tetralogy of Fallot with absent pulmonary valve, hypoplastic left or right heart, premature closure of ductus arteriosus, arteriovenous malformation (vein of Galen aneurysm)
• Cardiomyopathies
• Tachyarrhythmias
• Bradycardia, as may occur in heterotaxy syndrome with endocardial cushion defect or with anti-Ro/La antibodies

Chromosomal

• Turner syndrome (45,X), triploidy, trisomies 21, 18, and 13

Hematological

• Hemoglobinopathies, such as α4 thalassemia
• Erythrocyte enzyme and membrane disorders
• Erythrocyte aplasia/dyserythropoiesis
• Decreased erythrocyte production (myeloproliferative disorders)
• Fetomaternal hemorrhage

Lymphatic Abnormalities

• Cystic hygroma, systemic lymphangiectasis, pulmonary lymphangiectasis

Infections

• Parvovirus B19, syphilis, cytomegalovirus, toxoplasmosis, rubella, enterovirus, varicella, herpes simplex, coxsackievirus, listeriosis, leptospirosis, Chagas disease, Lyme disease

Syndromic

• Arthrogryposis multiplex congenita, lethal multiple pterygium, congenital lymphedema, myotonic dystrophy type I, Neu-Laxova, Noonan, and Pena-Shokeir syndromes

Thoracic Abnormalities

• Cystic adenomatoid malformation
• Pulmonary sequestration
• Diaphragmatic hernia
• Hydro/chylothorax
• Congenital high airway obstruction sequence (CHAOS)
• Mediastinal tumors
• Skeletal dysplasia with very small thorax

Gastrointestinal

• Meconium peritonitis, gastrointestinal tract obstruction

Kidney and Urinary Tract

• Kidney malformations
• Bladder outlet obstructions
• Congenital (Finnish) nephrosis, Bartter syndrome, mesoblastic nephroma

Placental, Twin, and Cord Abnormalities

• Placental chorioangioma, twin-twin transfusion syndrome, twin reversed arterial perfusion sequence, twin anemia polycythemia sequence, cord vessel thrombosis

Other Rare Disorders

• Inborn errors of metabolism: Gaucher disease, galactosialidosis, GM1 gangliosidosis, sialidosis, mucopolysaccharidoses, mucolipidoses
• Tumors: sacrococcygeal teratoma, hemangioendothelioma with Kasabach-Merritt syndrome

Idiopathic

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Beta 2 receptor action leading to hyperglycemia/ hypoglycemia is mediated by which of the following enzymes?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Adenylyl cyclase

Beta 2 receptor action leading to hypoglycemia/ hyperglycemia is mediated by adenylyl cyclase. Catecholamines act through beta 2 receptors and they use adenylyl cyclase - cAMP second messenger system to stimulate the target tissues.

Other hormones that use adenylyl cyclase - cAMP second messenger system are :

• Adrenocorticotropic hormone
• Angiotensin II
• Corticotropin-releasing hormone
• Calcitonin
• Follicle-stimulating hormone
• Glucagon
• Growth hormone-releasing hormone
• Human chorionic gonadotropin
• Luteinizing hormone
• Parathyroid hormone
• Secretin
• Somatostatin
• Thyroid-stimulating hormone
• Vasopressin

Hormones exert their actions by stimulating cAMP production within the cells. When the hormone binds to the membrane receptor, the receptor is coupled to the G protein. This G protein can either stimulate (Gs protein) or inhibit (Gi protein) adenylyl cyclase that controls the conversion of cytoplasmic adenosine triphosphate to adenosine monophosphate (cAMP). The protein kinases dependent on cAMP are thus activated. This leads to a series of biochemical reactions enabling the hormone to exert its actions.

Guanylyl cyclase is the enzyme that catalyzes the formation of cGMP.
questions.learning: Adenylyl cyclase Beta 2 receptor action leading to hypoglycemia/ hyperglycemia is mediated by adenylyl cyclase. Catecholamines act through beta 2 receptors and they use adenylyl cyclase - cAMP second messenger system to stimulate the target tissues.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient's Hepatitis B virus serology panel shows HBsAg +ve, Anti-HBc IgM +ve, HBeAg –ve, Anti-HBs –ve. Choose the correct diagnosis.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Acute hepatitis

• The single most decisive marker here is Anti-HBc IgM, which is the specific serological marker of recent/acute HBV infection (appears within weeks of HBsAg and persists \~6 months). Its presence, together with HBsAg positivity (active viral surface antigen) and absent anti-HBs (no recovery/immunity), confirms acute hepatitis B.
• The HBeAg-negative status does not exclude acute infection — it may reflect the late/resolving phase of acute illness (HBeAg is transient, appearing early and disappearing before HBsAg) or infection with a precore mutant strain, which cannot produce HBeAg despite active replication.

Other options:

• B. Chronic hepatitis → requires HBsAg persisting >6 months with Anti-HBc IgG (not IgM) positive.
• C. Window period → HBsAg negative and anti-HBs negative, with Anti-HBc IgM the ONLY positive marker — here HBsAg is positive, so it is excluded.
• D. Vaccination → isolated Anti-HBs positive; all core markers and HBsAg negative (vaccine contains only surface antigen).

Pearl:

• Anti-HBc IgM = acute infection / window period
• Anti-HBc IgG + Anti-HBs = past natural infection with recovery
• Anti-HBs alone = vaccination
• HBsAg > 6 months = chronic carrier
questions.learning: Acute hepatitis • — The single most decisive marker here is Anti-HBc IgM, which is the specific serological marker of recent/acute HBV infection (appears within weeks of HBsAg and persists \~6 months).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which is the least commonly used graft for coronary artery bypass graft (CABG)?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Intercostal artery

The intercostal artery is the least likely to be used as a graft in CABG.

The left internal mammary artery (LIMA) provides long-lasting results in a coronary artery bypass graft (CABG). The conduit with the highest patency rate is the left internal mammary artery or internal thoracic artery. Long patency rates of >98 percent have been reported.

Venous grafts:

* The long saphenous vein is the most common vein used as a conduit as it is straightforward to harvest, provides good length, and is easy to handle.

* The ten-year patency rate for long saphenous vein grafts is reported to be 50–60 percent.

Arterial grafts:

* The Left internal mammary artery (LIMA) or internal thoracic artery has become the conduit of choice for the left anterior descending (LAD) coronary artery. The radial artery can be used as a second or alternative arterial bypass graft. Other arterial bypass grafts include the gastroepiploic artery and the inferior epigastric artery.

Pearl PF1920: Indications for Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting (CABG)

Class I indications for CABG from the American College of Cardiology(ACC) and American Heart Association(AHA).

* Left main disease

* Three-vessel disease with or without proximal LAD disease

* Two vessel disease with proximal LAD disease

* Survivors of sudden cardiac death with presumed ischemia-mediated VT

Other indications for CABG include the following:

* Disabling angina

* Ongoing ischemia in the setting of a non–ST-segment elevation (MI) that is unresponsive to medical therapy

* Poor LV function but with viable, nonfunctioning myocardium above the anatomic defect that can be revascularized
questions.learning: Intercostal artery — The intercostal artery is the least likely to be used as a graft in CABG. The left internal mammary artery (LIMA) provides long-lasting results in a coronary artery bypass graft (CABG).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 70-year-old patient presents with absolute constipation and abdominal distension, and an abdominal X-ray is provided. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The X-ray reveals a characteristic "coffee bean sign" or "omega loop," which is a massively dilated loop of the sigmoid colon with an inverted U-shape. This finding, combined with the clinical symptoms of absolute constipation and abdominal distension in an elderly patient, is highly diagnostic of sigmoid volvulus. Sigmoid volvulus occurs when the colon twists on its mesentery. Caecal Volvulus (Option A) typically shows a kidney-shaped distended caecum displaced toward the upper abdomen or midline. Intestinal Obstruction (Option C) is a generalized term that does not describe the specific loop seen here. Small Bowel Volvulus (Option D) presents with centrally located dilated loops of small intestine with multiple air-fluid levels rather than a single large colonic loop. Management for sigmoid volvulus often begins with endoscopic detorsion, while surgery is reserved for gangrenous or recurrent cases
questions.learning: The X-ray reveals a characteristic "coffee bean sign" or "omega loop," which is a massively dilated loop of the sigmoid colon with an inverted U-shape.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A patient presents with hypertension,palpitations and sweating. His catecholamine and aldosterone levels were found to be elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pheochromocytoma

The clinical vignette of hypertension, sweating and palpitation with elevated catecholamine levels point towards pheochromocytoma.

Pearl PF0334: Clinical features of Pheochromocytoma (By frequency of occurrence)

* Clinical triad:

* Headaches – M/C symptom

* Profuse sweating

* Palpitations and tachycardia

* Hypertension, sustained or paroxysmal – M/C Sign

* Anxiety and panic attacks

* Weight loss

* Polyuria and polydipsia

* Constipation

* Orthostatic hypotension

* Dilated cardiomyopathy

* Erythrocytosis

* Elevated blood sugar

* Hypercalcemia

Pearl PF1539: Pheochromocytoma

Features:

* When pheochromocytoma is associated with the MEN syndrome it is rarely malignant.

* Phaeochromocytomas are greyish-pink on the cut surface and are usually highly vascularised.

* Zellbalen cells and nuclei with salt and pepper chromatin are seen.

Factors indicating more chances of malignancy:

* An increased PASS (phaeochromocytoma of the adrenal gland scale score)

* High number of Ki-67-positive cells

* Vascular invasion or a breached capsule

Diagnosis:

* Urinary catecholamine and VMA level assay are most sensitive screening test.

* MRI is the IOC.

* Biopsy and CT Contrast scan are contraindicated in order to avoid Hypertensive crisis.

Treatment:

* Adrenalectomy is preferred TOC.

* Size<5 cm -  Laparoscopic adrenalectomy

* Preop Alpha blockers should be given

* Mitotane should be started as adjuvant or palliative treatment

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A pregnant female with bipolar disorder came to the clinic in the third trimester. She has had 4 episodes in the past and is stable on lithium 750 mg/day since 1 year during which time she has not had any episodes. What is the next best step in management?
options: Stop lithium and let her be drug free
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Decrease lithium dosage

In this scenario of a pregnant woman in her third trimester with bipolar disorder with multiple past episodes and currently stable on lithium, the best next step in management is to decrease lithium dosage within therapeutic levels.
Lithium is a mood stabilizer with a very narrow therapeutic index and is the first line of management in bipolar disorder. Lithium therapy should be continued throughout the pregnancy in women who have severe, frequent episodes, and these patients should be counseled about the reproductive risks associated with therapy. Ideally, the next best step in this scenario would be to monitor lithium blood levels monthly until 34 weeks, and weekly monitoring thereafter until delivery. However, dose reduction can be considered closer to delivery as there may be an increased risk of lithium toxicity in the fetus. According to NICE guidelines, it is recommended to stop lithium during active labour, measure lithium levels 12 hours after the last dose and reestablish prophylactic levels after delivery.
First and second trimester are characterised by a significant decrease of lithium blood levels with a risk of subtherapeutic levels. In third trimester and the postpartum, lithium levels gradually return to their preconception level which implicates that in this period clinicians need to be aware of the risk of lithium intoxication (Option B).
Bipolar disorder has been associated with adverse perinatal outcomes such as preterm birth. Medication discontinuation in pregnancy (Option A) can pose an increased risk for relapse. Moreover, symptomatic women during pregnancy more likely have postpartum relapses that can be severe.
Typical therapy for bipolar disorder includes mood stabilizers such as lithium, valproic acid, and carbamazepine and antipsychotic medications. Bipolar disorder during pregnancy is a complicated condition that is best treated in tandem with psychiatric care. Risks and advantages of mood stabilizers, some of which are teratogenic, must be considered while making decisions.

For example, lithium use during the first trimester has been linked to Ebstein anomaly, although very rarely. Fetal echocardiography is recommended for lithium-exposed fetuses. Fetal lithium exposure is also associated with neonatal goiter, CNS depression, hypotonia (floppy baby syndrome), and cardiac murmur.

Maternal adverse effects of lithium can be acute such as tremors, ataxia, weakness, polyuria, polydipsia or chronic such as nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, thyroid dysfunction, and hyperparathyroidism.

Due to all these adverse effects, patients on lithium therapy should have routine monitoring of serum electrolytes, serum calcium, thyroid profile, renal function tests, ECG, and serum lithium levels.

Other options :
Option D : It is not necessary to switch to valproate in the third trimester as the patient is already stable on lithium. Use of valproate in the first trimester is associated with significant teratogenicity.
questions.learning: Decrease lithium dosage — In this scenario of a pregnant woman in her third trimester with bipolar disorder with multiple past episodes and currently stable on lithium, the best next step in management is to decrease lithium dosage within therapeutic levels.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Immunology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 52-year-old man undergoes a renal transplant. On post-operative day 6, he develops sudden rise in serum creatinine and oliguria. Doppler shows good graft perfusion. Renal biopsy demonstrates capillary endothelial swelling, neutrophilic infiltration, fibrinoid necrosis of vessels, and linear C4d deposition along peritubular capillaries. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism?
options: Formation of donor-specific anti-HLA antibodies with complement activation
Progressive intimal fibrosis due to smooth muscle proliferation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Formation of donor-specific anti-HLA antibodies with complement activation

This presentation is characteristic of acute antibody-mediated (humoral) rejection after renal transplantation.

• Recipient forms donor-specific antibodies (DSA) against donor HLA antigens on graft endothelial cells.
• These antibodies activate the complement cascade, leading to endothelial injury, neutrophilic infiltration, and vascular damage.
• C4d deposition in peritubular capillaries is a key diagnostic marker of complement activation in antibody-mediated rejection.

Typical biopsy findings:

• Endothelial swelling
• Neutrophils in capillaries
• Fibrinoid necrosis of vessels
• Linear C4d staining in peritubular capillaries
questions.learning: Formation of donor-specific anti-HLA antibodies with complement activation This presentation is characteristic of acute antibody-mediated (humoral) rejection after renal transplantation. • Recipient forms donor-specific antibodies (DSA) against donor HLA…

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A male patient who lost his job recently became irritable and had a sad mood for most of the time. Thinking about the future worried him and he felt irritation towards his family members. He occasionally went out to watch movies with his friends and was able to enjoy but on returning home he felt similar symptoms. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Adjustment disorder

The clinical features are suggestive of an adjustment disorder.

Adjustment disorder is an emotional response to a stressful event. Stressors may be single like loss of job or divorce; multiple like the death of a parent together with loss of a job; or recurrent like seasonal business difficulties.

Diagnosing criteria for adjustment disorder:

• Development of emotional or behavioural response within 3 months of the onset of the stressor.
• The symptoms or behaviour are clinically significant, where, any one of the following are met:

• The response is out of proportion to the severity or intensity of the stressor.
• Significant impairment in social, occupational, or other areas of functioning.

• The stress-related disturbance does not meet the criteria for another mental disorder or exacerbation of pre-existing mental disorder.
• Mostly depressive but can also have anxiety symptoms.
• The symptoms disappear within 6 months if the stressor is removed.

In the given case, it has been mentioned that the patient lost his job recently. Although a time period is not mentioned in the question, the term recently can be understood as well within the 3 months duration. The patient's behaviour such as sad and irritated affected his social functioning. As he was finding joy in watching movies, depression can be ruled out.
questions.learning: Adjustment disorder — The clinical features are suggestive of an adjustment disorder. Adjustment disorder is an emotional response to a stressful event.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is the afferent limb of the corneal reflex?
questions.explanation: The corneal reflex is an important protective reflex of the eye that involves both a sensory (afferent) and a motor (efferent) component. The afferent limb is carried by the trigeminal nerve (cranial nerve V), specifically its ophthalmic division (V₁). This division supplies sensory innervation to the cornea and detects tactile or noxious stimuli applied to it, transmitting the impulse to the brainstem. The efferent limb of the corneal reflex is mediated by the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII), which innervates the orbicularis oculi muscle, producing bilateral blinking in response to corneal stimulation. The optic nerve (Option A) is involved in visual pathways and serves as the afferent limb of the pupillary light reflex, not the corneal reflex. The trochlear nerve (Option D) innervates the superior oblique muscle and has no role in corneal sensation or blinking. Therefore, the trigeminal nerve is the correct answer, as it provides the sensory input necessary to initiate the corneal reflex
questions.learning: The corneal reflex is an important protective reflex of the eye that involves both a sensory (afferent) and a motor (efferent) component. The afferent limb is carried by the trigeminal nerve (cranial nerve V), specifically its ophthalmic division (V₁).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Identify the defect in the given image:
questions.explanation: The provided clinical image depicts a severe form of spina bifida known as rachischisis or myeloschisis, which is a type of open neural tube defect. This condition occurs due to the failure of the neural tube and covering ectoderm to close properly, leaving neural tissue exposed to the environment without any skin or meningeal covering. In contrast, occult spina bifida (Option C) is a closed defect where the vertebral arch fails to fuse, but the skin remains intact, often marked only by a tuft of hair or a dimple. A meningoencephalocele (Option B) involves a sac-like protrusion of both meninges and brain tissue through a skull defect. An encephalocele (Option D) specifically refers to a protrusion of brain tissue through a cranial opening. Because the image shows a contiguous spinal defect with exposed neural elements, it is definitively classified as an open neural tube defect

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A young patient started to take a weight loss medication that acts by inhibiting fat absorption from food. After a few weeks, she developed easy bruising and increased menstrual bleeding. Deficiency of which of the following vitamins is responsible for her condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vitamin K

The clinical scenario of easy bruising and increased menstrual bleeding following weight loss medication that inhibits fat absorption from food is suggestive of vitamin K deficiency.

Vitamin K is a fat-soluble vitamin. Hence, drugs that inhibit the absorption of fat (eg; ezetimibe) also inhibit the absorption of fat-soluble vitamin K. The following are the vitamers of vitamin K:

• Phylloquinone (Vitamin K1) is the normal dietary source of Vitamin K that is found in green vegetables.
• Menaquinone (Vitamin K2) is synthesized by intestinal bacteria.
• Menadione (Vitamin K3) is a synthetic compound that is metabolized to phylloquinone.

Vitamin K is required for γ-carboxylation of glutamate residues of clotting factors like prothrombin (factor II), factors VII, IX, and X. Warfarin inhibits γ-carboxylation by preventing the conversion of vitamin K to its active hydroquinone form.

Vitamin K deficiency in adults may be seen in patients with liver disease, obstructive jaundice, malabsorption, and prolonged antimicrobial therapy. Vitamin K deficiency is usually diagnosed on the basis of an elevated prothrombin time or reduced clotting factors.

Vitamin K deficiency is treated with a parenteral dose of 10 mg followed by 5mg (duration depends on the severity of vitamin K deficiency).

Other options:

Option A: Vitamin E is a fat-soluble vitamin. The levels of vitamin E also will get decreased following taking weight loss medication that inhibits fat absorption from food. But the symptoms of vitamin E deficiency include hemolytic anemia and neuromuscular manifestations.

Option C: Vitamin B6 is a water-soluble vitamin. Drugs that cause vitamin B6 deficiency are isoniazid, hydralazine, cycloserine, penicillamine, and oral contraceptives. Patients usually present with peripheral neuritis, anemia, seborrheic dermatitis, glossitis, lowered seizure threshold, or convulsions (due to fall in brain GABA levels).

Option D: Vitamin D is a fat-soluble vitamin. Vitamin D levels will also decrease following weight loss medication that inhibits fat absorption from food. Patients with vitamin D deficiency will typically develop rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults.
questions.learning: Vitamin K — The clinical scenario of easy bruising and increased menstrual bleeding following weight loss medication that inhibits fat absorption from food is suggestive of vitamin K deficiency.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient undergoes bronchoscopy, and a perforation occurs at 25 cm. Which anatomical structure is most likely damaged?
questions.explanation: During bronchoscopy, the distance measured from the upper incisors helps localize structures in relation to the trachea and esophagus. At approximately 25 cm from the incisors, the arch of the aorta lies in close relation to the trachea and left main bronchus. Therefore, a perforation occurring at this level is most likely to damage the aortic arch. Why other options are incorrect: (A) Diaphragm – Located much lower, around 40 cm from the incisors. (C) Pharyngoesophageal junction – Situated at about 15 cm from the incisors. (D) T10 – Corresponds to the esophageal hiatus of the diaphragm, again much lower than 25 cm. Hence, the structure most likely to be damaged at 25 cm during bronchoscopy is the arch of the aorta
questions.learning: During bronchoscopy, the distance measured from the upper incisors helps localize structures in relation to the trachea and esophagus. At approximately 25 cm from the incisors, the arch of the aorta lies in close relation to the trachea and left main bronchus.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient after severe traumatic brain injury opens eyes, is awake, recognizes family, but requires assistance for dressing, feeding, and daily activities. What is the GOS category?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Severe disability

• The Glasgow Outcome Scale (GOS) is used to assess functional outcome after traumatic brain injury (TBI) by categorizing recovery based on the patient’s level of consciousness, independence, and ability to resume normal life.
• It has 5 outcome categories: Death, Vegetative state, Severe disability, Moderate disability, and Good recovery.
• A patient who is awake, can open eyes, and recognizes family is clearly not vegetative (vegetative patients have wakefulness without awareness).
• However, if the patient requires assistance for dressing, feeding, and daily activities, they are dependent for activities of daily living (ADLs).
• This level of dependence corresponds to Severe Disability on GOS.

Analysing all options:

• A. Vegetative state: Awake but no awareness/interaction
• B. Severe disability: Conscious but dependent, needs help with ADLs
• C. Moderate disability: Independent but with deficits (cannot fully return to work/social activities)
• D. Good recovery: Returns to normal life with minimal deficits

Thus, an awake patient with awareness but dependence for daily care = GOS Severe disability (Option B).
