questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 35-year-old man presents with episodes of hematemesis following recent heavy alcohol consumption. He appears pale but is hemodynamically stable, with no ongoing bleeding at presentation. Liver function tests are within normal limits, and an upper gastrointestinal endoscopy is planned. Based on this clinical scenario, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A Mallory-Weiss tear is a longitudinal mucosal laceration at the gastroesophageal junction, typically occurring after episodes of forceful retching or vomiting, often following heavy alcohol consumption. The patient’s stable vitals and normal liver function tests (LFTs) make esophageal varices (Option A) less likely, as varices are usually associated with portal hypertension and cirrhosis. Gastric ulcers (Option B) can cause hematemesis but are not specifically linked to acute alcohol-related retching cycles. While alcoholic gastritis (Option D) can cause erosive bleeding, it typically results in slower blood loss rather than acute hematemesis following vomiting episodes. The classic presentation of hematemesis following initially non-bloody emesis in an alcoholic patient is highly characteristic of a Mallory-Weiss tear. Diagnosis is confirmed by endoscopy, which usually reveals a linear tear near the Z-line. Most cases are self-limiting and managed conservatively with acid suppression, though endoscopic therapy may be needed for active bleeding or visible vessels
questions.learning: A Mallory-Weiss tear is a longitudinal mucosal laceration at the gastroesophageal junction, typically occurring after episodes of forceful retching or vomiting, often following heavy alcohol consumption.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 2-month-old infant is brought to the OPD with a parietal swelling present since birth. The X-ray image is given below. What could be the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cephalhematoma

In the given clinical picture, the swelling over the infant's head is likely to be a cephalhematoma.

Cephalohematoma is a collection of blood in between the pericranium and the flat bone (subperiosteal) of the skull, usually unilateral and over a parietal bone. It is never present at birth but gradually develops after 12–24 h. The swelling is limited by the suture lines of the skull as the pericranium is fixed to the margins of the bone.

The arrow mark in the image represents cephalohematoma.

Note: Cephalhematoma is more likely to be identified soon after birth, and its presence as a defined area of swelling that does not cross suture lines is more consistent with this diagnosis.

Subgaleal hematoma occurs between the galea aponeurotica and the periosteum. It is commonly caused by birth trauma, particularly forceps or vacuum-assisted delivery. Subgaleal hematoma can cross suture lines and typically presents as a soft, fluctuant swelling on the scalp.

Caput succedaneum is an edema of the scalp that can cross suture lines. It is usually present at birth or develops shortly after due to pressure on the presenting part of the head during labor. It generally resolves within a few days.

Encephalocele is a neural tube defect that results in a sac-like protrusion of the brain and its meninges through an opening in the skull. It is a congenital condition and is typically diagnosed at birth or via prenatal ultrasound.
questions.learning: Cephalhematoma — In the given clinical picture, the swelling over the infant's head is likely to be a cephalhematoma. Cephalohematoma is a collection of blood in between the pericranium and the flat bone (subperiosteal) of the skull, usually unilateral and…

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the artery indicated by the arrow in the given image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Anterior Interventricular Artery

The anterior interventricular artery (left anterior descending artery, LAD) is a branch of the left coronary artery that descends in the anterior interventricular groove toward the apex of the heart. It supplies the anterior wall of the left ventricle, anterior two-thirds of the interventricular septum, and the apex, making it the most commonly occluded coronary artery in myocardial infarction.

FMGE/NEET PG Pearl

• LAD (Anterior interventricular artery) → Runs in the anterior interventricular sulcus with the great cardiac vein.
• Supplies the anterior LV, apex, and anterior 2/3 of the interventricular septum (including bundle branches).
• LAD occlusion causes an anterior wall MI and is often called the “widow-maker” lesion due to its high mortality.
• Left circumflex artery runs in the left atrioventricular (coronary) sulcus, while the right marginal artery courses along the acute margin of the heart.
questions.learning: Anterior Interventricular Artery — The anterior interventricular artery (left anterior descending artery, LAD) is a branch of the left coronary artery that descends in the anterior interventricular groove toward the apex of the heart.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A Mother of a breastfeeding child only eats vegetables. Which deficiency is common in this case?
questions.explanation: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) is uniquely synthesized by bacteria and is found almost exclusively in animal-based foods, such as meat, eggs, and dairy. A mother who follows a strict vegan diet (only eating vegetables) is at extremely high risk of Vitamin B12 deficiency. This is particularly critical during breastfeeding, as the infant’s B12 stores are primarily derived from maternal milk. Deficiency in the infant can lead to megaloblastic anemia, developmental delays, and permanent neurological damage. Vitamin A (Option B) is readily available in orange and green vegetables as beta-carotene. Vitamin D (Option C) is synthesized via sunlight, though supplementation is often required regardless of diet. Vitamin K (Option D) is found in green leafy vegetables and synthesized by gut flora. Therefore, strict vegetarianism without supplementation most predictably results in B12 depletion. Vegan mothers must be counseled on B12 supplementation to protect their own health and ensure their infant’s proper growth and brain development
questions.learning: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) is uniquely synthesized by bacteria and is found almost exclusively in animal-based foods, such as meat, eggs, and dairy. A mother who follows a strict vegan diet (only eating vegetables) is at extremely high risk of Vitamin B12…

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis?
questions.explanation: The synthesis of cholesterol occurs primarily in the liver. The rate-limiting and primary regulated step of this pathway is the conversion of 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA (HMG-CoA) to mevalonate. This reaction is catalyzed by the enzyme HMG-CoA reductase. This enzyme is highly regulated by feedback inhibition from cholesterol levels and hormonal control (stimulated by insulin, inhibited by glucagon). 7-alpha-hydroxylase (Option B) is the rate-limiting enzyme for the synthesis of bile acids from cholesterol. Carnitine acyltransferase 1 (Option C) and 2 (Option D) are involved in the transport of long-chain fatty acids into the mitochondria for beta-oxidation. HMG-CoA reductase is the pharmacological target of the statin class of drugs (e.g., atorvastatin), which competitively inhibit the enzyme to lower blood cholesterol levels. Because cholesterol synthesis is most active during fasting or sleep, these medications are often taken at night. Understanding this enzyme is fundamental for managing atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and hyperlipidemia
questions.learning: The synthesis of cholesterol occurs primarily in the liver. The rate-limiting and primary regulated step of this pathway is the conversion of 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA (HMG-CoA) to mevalonate.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: In which procedure is the incision showed in the image used?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Open rhinoplasty

The incision shown is used in open rhinoplasty.

This procedure involves a transcolumellar incision, an incision made across the columella to lift the nasal skin, allowing full access to the underlying nasal structures. This approach is used for cosmetic or reconstructive surgery. The open technique allows better visibility of the nasal framework compared to closed rhinoplasty.

Other options:

Option A: The Caldwell-Luc operation, also known as anterior antrostomy, involves opening the maxillary sinus via the canine fossa through a sublabial approach to address various pathologies within the sinus. It's indicated for conditions like chronic maxillary sinusitis, dental cysts, oroantral fistula, neoplasms, and certain fractures. Surgery is contraindicated for patients below 17 years of age.

Option B: The modified Denker's procedure is similar to the Caldwell-Luc procedure but involves more extensive exposure of the maxillary sinus and nasal cavity. It’s used for the removal of larger sinus tumors.

Option D: Midface degloving approach is a facial incision-less approach used for accessing the midface, including the nasal cavity and sinuses.
It’s commonly used in removing large nasal and sinus tumors, and it involves incisions within the oral cavity and nasal vestibule, avoiding external scars. No incision on the nose itself is involved.
questions.learning: Open rhinoplasty — The incision shown is used in open rhinoplasty. This procedure involves a transcolumellar incision, an incision made across the columella to lift the nasal skin, allowing full access to the underlying nasal structures.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following statements is false about non-invasive prenatal testing?
options: It uses cell-free circulating fetal DNA in the maternal serum
It is used for the diagnosis of trisomy 13, 18 and 21
It can be performed after 10 weeks of gestation
It is done after the routine first trimester ultrasound assessment
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. It is used for the diagnosis of trisomy 13, 18 and 21

Non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT) is used for the screening of trisomy 13, 18 and 21 and Turner's syndrome. It is not a diagnostic test.

It is a novel genetic test that uses cell-free circulating fetal DNA in the maternal serum for screening of chromosomal anomalies.

DNA from the fetus is found circulating in the maternal blood in two forms - either inside the intact fetal cells or as cell-free DNA from the breakdown of placental fetal cells. In NIPT, the cell-free chromosome fragments are measured and the quantitative differences from normal fetuses are noted.

NIPT can be performed after 10 weeks of gestation and is recommended after the routine first-trimester ultrasound assessment in high-risk pregnancies or if either 1st or 2nd-trimester screening becomes positive. Its disadvantage is that it is very expensive and it can be used for screening of only a few chromosomal anomalies such as trisomy 13, 18, and 21 and it doesn't analyse the entire karyotype.
questions.learning: It is used for the diagnosis of trisomy 13, 18 and 21 Non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT) is used for the screening of trisomy 13, 18 and 21 and Turner's syndrome.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following is correct with regard to Carey Coombs murmur?
options: Soft systolic murmur due to mitral regurgitation
Soft mid-diastolic murmur due to mitral valvulitis
Harsh early diastolic murmur due to aortic regurgitation
Blowing late systolic murmur due to aortic stenosis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Soft mid-diastolic murmur due to mitral valvulitis

The Carey Coombs murmur is a soft, short mid-diastolic murmur heard at the cardiac apex during the acute phase of rheumatic fever. It is caused by active inflammation (valvulitis) of the mitral valve, resulting in turbulent blood flow across the inflamed but non-stenotic mitral valve.

The murmur is:

• Mid-diastolic
• Soft and low-pitched
• Best heard at the apex with the bell of the stethoscope
• Caused by rheumatic mitral valvulitis, not true mitral stenosis

Why not the other options?

• A. Soft systolic murmur due to mitral regurgitation: Acute rheumatic fever may produce a pansystolic murmur due to mitral regurgitation, but this is not the Carey Coombs murmur.
• C. Harsh early diastolic murmur due to aortic regurgitation: Describes the murmur of aortic regurgitation, unrelated to Carey Coombs murmur.
• D. Blowing late systolic murmur due to aortic stenosis: Incorrect. Aortic stenosis produces an ejection systolic murmur, not a late systolic murmur.
questions.learning: Soft mid-diastolic murmur due to mitral valvulitis — The Carey Coombs murmur is a soft, short mid-diastolic murmur heard at the cardiac apex during the acute phase of rheumatic fever.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 6-year-old girl is admitted for evaluation for recurrent seizures. She has a large port-wine stain on the right side of her face as shown below. The MRI of the head shows a leptomeningeal angioma. What is the most common ocular manifestation of the underlying condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Glaucoma

The given clinical picture of a young child presenting with unilateral port wine stain in the region of trigeminal nerve supply and leptomeningeal angioma as seen on MRI is indicative of Sturge-Webber syndrome (SWS). Glaucoma is the most common ocular manifestation of SWS.

Sturge weber syndrome is a neurocutaneous disorder(phakomatoses) that is characterized by unilateral capillary malformation at the region of trigeminal supply known as port wine stain or nevus flammeus, ipsilateral diffuse cavernous hemangioma of the choroid and ipsilateral leptomeningeal hemangiomatosis, which causes seizures and mental retardation.

Ocular manifestation of SWS include:

• Glaucoma - most common ocular manifestation. It develops anywhere between infancy to adulthood. When developed in infancy it presents as buphthalmos.
• Diffuse choroidal hemangioma
• Serous retinal detachment
• Visual field defects- homonymous hemianopia due to the leptomeningeal hemangiomas affecting the optic tract or occipital lobe.
• Heterochromia of the iris
• Episcleral and conjunctival lesions

Option A: Uveitis is the inflammation of the uveal tissue of the eyes. It can be associated with a number of systemic conditions such as sarcoidosis, behcet's disease, ankylosing spondylitis, reiter's syndrome,Toxoplasmosis and Posner–Schlossman syndrome (PSS).

Option B: Retinitis pigmentosa is an inherited or acquired pigmentatory retinal dystrophy affecting the rods more. The earliest manifestation is worsening of night blindness which gradually progresses to tunnel vision and ultimately loss of central vision. The classic triad of findings in RP comprises bone-spicule retinal pigmentation, arteriolar attenuation and waxy disc pallor.

Systemic Associations of RP include:

• Laurence-Moon-Biedl syndrome
• Cockayne's syndrome
• Refsum's syndrome
• Usher's syndrome
• Bassen-Kornzweig syndrome

The below given image shows the classical triad findings of Retinitis pigmentosa.

Option C:Keratitis is the inflammation of cornea which is characterised by corneal edema, cellular infiltration and ciliary congestion. It can be either infectious or non-infectious in nature which includes allergic keratitis, neurotrophic keratitis, exposure keratitis and peripheral ulcerative keratopathies such as Rosacea keratitis and Mooren's ulcer.
questions.learning: Glaucoma — The given clinical picture of a young child presenting with unilateral port wine stain in the region of trigeminal nerve supply and leptomeningeal angioma as seen on MRI is indicative of Sturge-Webber syndrome (SWS).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is the most common type of renal stones?
questions.explanation: In the global population, calcium oxalate stones are the most frequently encountered type of renal calculi, accounting for approximately 75–80% of all cases . These stones are typically radiopaque on X-ray and can form in both acidic and alkaline urine. Triple phosphate stones (Option C), also called struvite or staghorn calculi, are associated with chronic urinary tract infections caused by urease-producing bacteria like Proteus. Uric acid stones (Option D) are unique because they are radiolucent and are often seen in patients with gout or high purine diets. Cystine stones (Option B) are rare and result from a specific genetic defect in amino acid transport. Identifying the chemical composition of the stone is vital for metabolic evaluation and preventing recurrence through dietary modifications and pharmacological therapy. Therefore, based on broad epidemiological data, calcium oxalate is the definitive "most common" type of stone. Patients are often advised to maintain high fluid intake to reduce the concentration of stone-forming salts
questions.learning: In the global population, calcium oxalate stones are the most frequently encountered type of renal calculi, accounting for approximately 75–80% of all cases .

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: The audiogram of a patient who presented with a gradually progressive hearing loss, tinnitus and vertigo is given below. Which among the following would be the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Ménière's disease

The given audiogram is seen in Ménière's disease in its early stages. It shows an upsloping/ascending curve suggesting that the lower frequencies are affected first.

Presbycusis, ototoxicity, and sound-induced hearing loss have downsloping audiograms since the higher frequencies are affected first in these conditions.

Points to remember in PTA audiogram:

* AC abnormal, BC normal, Air-bone gap present – conductive deafness

* Downsloping/descending audiogram- higher frequencies affected first like in presbycusis, ototoxicity, noise induced hearing loss.

* Upsloping/ascending audiogram - lower frequencies are affected first like in early stages of Meniere's disease.

* U shaped/trough shaped/cookie bite shaped audiogram suggests midfrequency hearing loss and is seen in congenital hearing loss and cochlear otosclerosis.

* Acoustic dip - characteristic dip in both AC and BC at 4000 Hz

* Carhartz notch - dip at 2000 Hz in BC curve
questions.learning: Ménière's disease — The given audiogram is seen in Ménière's disease in its early stages. It shows an upsloping/ascending curve suggesting that the lower frequencies are affected first.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following nerves is responsible for ear pain after a tonsillectomy surgery ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Glossopharyngeal nerve

The glossopharyngeal nerve (cranial nerve IX) is responsible for referred otalgia after a tonsillectomy.

The tonsils and tonsillar fossa are supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve. The glossopharyngeal nerve and the styloid process lie in relation to the lower part of the tonsillar fossa. Therefore, any irritation or pain can be referred to the ear along the tympanic branch of the glossopharyngeal (Jacobson's) nerve.

Image below shows the anatomic relations of tonsil and tonsillar bed.

The ear receives an extensive sensory innervation via four cranial nerves (V, VII, IX, and X) and two spinal segments (C2 and C3).

Jacobson's nerve, along with branches from the sympathetic plexus forms the tympanic plexus. This plexus provides sensation to the middle ear, upper eustachian tube, and medial surface of the tympanic membrane. Referred otalgia transmitted by the glossopharyngeal nerve may be secondary to lesions and/or inflammatory processes of the nasopharynx, palatine tonsil, soft palate, or posterior one-third of the tongue.

Causes of referred otalgia via glossopharyngeal nerve:

* Acute pharyngitis

* Tonsillitis

* Peritonsillitis

* Peritonsillar abscess

* Post-tonsillectomy

* Foreign bodies embedded in the base of the tongue or tonsillar area

* Elongated styloid process

Causes of referred otalgia
Nerve responsible
Site

Temporomandibular joint and dental conditions, parotid infections/tumor, and anterior 2/3rd of tongue
Auriculotemporal nerve
Tragal area, crus of the helix, and anterior wall and roof of the external auditory canal

Acute tonsillitis, peritonsillar abscess, carcinoma base of the tongue or tonsils (oropharynx)
The glossopharyngeal nerve (Jacobson's)
Medial surface of the tympanic membrane and middle ear

Carcinoma of the larynx (cough), hypopharynx, epiglottis, vallecula, esophagus, and thyroid
Auricular branch of the vagus nerve (Arnold's/Alderman's nerve)
Concha, posterior wall, and floor of the external auditory canal

Cervical spondylitis
Great auricular nerve (C2,3)
Lateral and medial surfaces of the pinna

Acoustic neuroma
Facial nerve (nervus intermedius/nerve of Wrisberg)
Concha, retroauricular groove, and posterosuperior part of the external auditory meatus. Numbness in the posterosuperior meatal wall, known as Hitzelberger's sign, is seen in acoustic neuroma.
questions.learning: Glossopharyngeal nerve — The glossopharyngeal nerve (cranial nerve IX) is responsible for referred otalgia after a tonsillectomy. The tonsils and tonsillar fossa are supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A female presents with 35 weeks and 3 days of gestation, AFI = 5 and there is no end-diastolic blood flow. What is the management?
options: Give surfactant and wait till 36 weeks
Do Doppler everyday to check for reversion
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Immediate termination

The given case scenario is suggestive of fetal compromise. The management in this patient is immediate termination of pregnancy. Since this pregnancy has crossed 34 weeks, it can be terminated by cesarean section.

Abnormal flow patterns in the umbilical artery:

• Reduced end-diastolic flow indicates uteroplacental insufficiency (S/D ratio increases)
• Absent end-diastolic flow suggests fetal compromise, hence the pregnancy is terminated by C-section if >34 weeks.
• Reverse end-diastolic flow suggests impending doom of death, hence the pregnancy is terminated by C-section if >32 weeks.
questions.learning: Immediate termination — The given case scenario is suggestive of fetal compromise. The management in this patient is immediate termination of pregnancy.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: JAK2 mutation is most commonly associated with _____
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Polycythemia vera

Polycythemia vera is strongly associated with activating point mutations in the tyrosine kinase JAK2.

A mutation in JAK2, a key member of the cytokine intracellular signaling pathway, can be found in 90–95% of patients with polycythemia vera.

It is characterized by :

• Increased marrow production of red cells, granulocytes, and platelets (panmyelosis)
• Low erythropoietin levels and elevated hematocrit
• Blood viscosity and sludging lead to both thrombosis and bleeding.
• Headache, dizziness, hypertension, dizziness, venous thrombosis (Budd Chiari syndrome due to hepatic vein thrombosis), bowel infarction, and stroke.
• Intense pruritus especially aquagenic pruritus
• Peptic ulceration, hyperuricemia
• 15% to 20% of patients after an average period of 10 years ->Myelofibrosis and extensive extramedullary hematopoiesis,
• PCV transforms into AML in 2% of patients.

Primary myelofibrosis

• Marrow fibrosis associated with extramedullary hemopoiesis in the spleen.
• Activating mutation in JAK2 (more commonly) or MPL.
• Presence of neoplastic megakaryocytes, which are responsible for the release of fibrogenic factors like PDGF (platelet-derived growth factor) and TGF-β.
• Bone marrow aspiration yields dry tap due to fibrosis of the bone marrow.
• So, bone marrow biopsy is the investigation of choice, which shows the presence of hypocellularity with increased deposition of reticulin inside the marrow, abnormal megakaryocytes and the characteristic finding of dilated marrow sinusoids.
• Blood shows mild leukocytosis, decreased Hb and hematocrit levels, and elevated LAP scores.
• Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) occurs in 5% to 20% of cases.

Essential thrombocytosis (ET) may also be associated with JAK2, MPL, or CALR mutations.

• Essential thrombocytosis (ET) is often associated with activating point mutations in JAK2 (50% of cases) or MPL (5% to 10% of cases), a receptor tyrosine kinase that is normally activated by thrombopoietin.
• In addition, recent DNA sequencing studies have revealed that most of the remaining cases have mutations in calreticulin (CALR), a protein with several functions in the endoplasmic reticulum and the cytoplasm. Since JAK2 and calreticulin mutations are mutually exclusive, it is hypothesized that the calreticulin mutations also increase JAK-STAT signaling through mechanisms that are currently unknown.

CML is the consequence of the balanced translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22 (t[9;22]).

PV, PMF, and ET are characterized by driver mutations that directly or indirectly constitutively activate JAK2, a tyrosine kinase essential for the function of the erythropoietin andthrombopoietin receptors and also utilized by granulocyte colony stimulating factor receptor.
questions.learning: Polycythemia vera Polycythemia vera is strongly associated with activating point mutations in the tyrosine kinase JAK2. A mutation in JAK2, a key member of the cytokine intracellular signaling pathway, can be found in 90–95% of patients with polycythemia vera.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 5-year-old girl is brought to the clinic with a fever, cough, red eyes, running nose, and rash. The appearance of the child is shown below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Measles

This child with a given clinical vignette and the rash has measles.

Measles is a common cause of fever with rash that spread via droplets. It is characterised by a prodrome of cough, conjunctivitis and coryza along with fever. Koplik spots are white grain lesions with surrounding erythema on the buccal mucosa opposite to the lower second molar. A reddish macular rash begins behind the ears on the 4th day, rapidly becomes maculopapular and spreads to the face, neck, chest, arms, trunk, thighs and legs.

Other options:

Option A: Mumps is caused by a paramyxovirus and spread by droplets and contact. It causes fever, malaise unilateral or bilateral parotitis. It also causes epididymo-orchitis in males.

Option C: Chickenpox is caused by varicella zoster and spreads by contact and airborne. It has a prodrome of fever, malaise, anorexia and headache which is followed by a rash in 1-2 days. It has pruritic erythematous macules that first appear on the trunk and spreads to face and extremities that evolve into papules, vesicles and pustules that become crusted. The presence of several crops of lesions that are in different stages of evolution is a characteristic of varicella.

Option D: Erythema infectiosum (fifth disease) is caused by parvovirus B19 transmitted by airborne route. The prodromal consists of low-grade fever, headache and mild upper respiratory tract infection. An erythematous slapped cheeked rash that first appears on the face is characteristic. A macular rash then spreads to the trunk and extremities that undergoes central clearing giving a lacy or reticulated pattern.

Pearl PF0095: Viral infections associated with rash

Viral infection
Rash characteristics

Chickenpox
Appears 1st day of fever, centripetal, pleomorphic, dewdrops on rose petal appearance

Measles
Appears on the 4th day over the face and retroauricular origin

Rubella
Rash on day 1 over the face

Erythema infectiosum

Rash on cheeks (slapped cheek appearance), moves to trunk and extremities

Exanthem subitum
Macules or maculopapular rash

Infectious mononucleosis
Associated with maculopapular rash
questions.learning: Measles — This child with a given clinical vignette and the rash has measles. Measles is a common cause of fever with rash that spread via droplets.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the marked nerve.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Medial pectoral nerve

The marked nerve pierces and supplies the pectoralis minor and then continues to supply the pectoralis major, a classic identifying feature of the medial pectoral nerve.

The lateral pectoral nerve supplies pectoralis major without piercing muscle, thoracodorsal nerve supplies latissimus dorsi, and long thoracic nerve supplies serratus anterior and runs on the chest wall.
questions.learning: Medial pectoral nerve — The marked nerve pierces and supplies the pectoralis minor and then continues to supply the pectoralis major, a classic identifying feature of the medial pectoral nerve.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Stages of the demographic cycle with the same birth rate but variable death rate are?
questions.explanation: The demographic cycle describes the stages of population growth based on birth and death rates. Stage 1 (High Stationary) is characterized by high birth and high death rates. Stage 2 (Early Expanding) features a continued high birth rate, but the death rate begins to decline rapidly due to improvements in sanitation and healthcare. Consequently, Stages 1 and 2 share a similar, high birth rate while the death rate varies significantly between them. Option B is incorrect because the birth rate begins to fall in Stage 3 (Late Expanding). Option C is incorrect as Stage 5 often sees birth rates fall below death rates (Declining phase). Option D is incorrect as Stage 4 (Low Stationary) has stabilized low birth and death rates. Identifying these stages is vital for predicting population trends; the gap between the high birth rate and falling death rate in Stage 2 is what causes the "population explosion" typical of developing nations
questions.learning: The demographic cycle describes the stages of population growth based on birth and death rates. Stage 1 (High Stationary) is characterized by high birth and high death rates.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is true about vaginal changes in a normal pregnancy?
options: Increased glycogen metabolism in the epithelium
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Increased glycogen metabolism in the epithelium

There is an increase in the metabolism of glycogen in the vaginal epithelium during normal pregnancy.

The changes in the vagina during pregnancy include:

• Increased vascularity and hyperemia resulting in a violet/purplish color characteristic of Chadwick's sign
• Vaginal epithelium undergoes marked proliferation (option D) with the extension of the squamocolumnar junction downwards
• Vaginal pH decreases and becomes more acidic (option C) and varies from 3.5-6.0.
• Increase in the number of Lactobacillus acidophilus (option A). It metabolizes the glycogen stores and causes an increased production of lactic acid. Therefore, the pH becomes acidic.
• Increased volume of cervical secretion during pregnancy results in the production of thick white vaginal discharge.
questions.learning: Increased glycogen metabolism in the epithelium — There is an increase in the metabolism of glycogen in the vaginal epithelium during normal pregnancy. The changes in the vagina during pregnancy include: • Increased vascularity and hyperemia resulting in a…

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which HPV strains are the most common cause of cervical cancer in India?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. HPV 16, 18

HPV types 16 and 18 are high-risk oncogenic strains responsible for the majority of cervical cancer cases in India, accounting for nearly 70% of cases. HPV 6 and 11 cause genital warts, while 31, 33, 52, and 58 are fewer common contributors.

Pathogenesis of HPV in Cervical Cancer- The virus infects squamous epithelial cells of the cervix, especially the transformation zone.

Oncogenic HPV strains produce viral proteins -E6 protein → inhibits p53 tumor suppressor & E7 protein → inhibits Rb protein. This leads to uncontrolled cell proliferation, cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) & eventually invasive cervical cancer.
questions.learning: HPV 16, 18 HPV types 16 and 18 are high-risk oncogenic strains responsible for the majority of cervical cancer cases in India, accounting for nearly 70% of cases.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The needle with the syringe is disposed of in which container?
questions.explanation: According to the Bio-Medical Waste Management Rules, sharps must be disposed of in specific containers to prevent needle-stick injuries and the transmission of blood-borne pathogens. A needle with a syringe (or any other metallic sharp) must be placed in the White container. This container is characteristically translucent, puncture-proof, and leak-proof to ensure safe handling and transport. The Yellow bin (Option A) is reserved for infectious non-plastic waste, such as anatomical parts, soiled dressings, and chemical waste. The Red bin (Option B) is used for recyclable plastic waste like IV sets, tubing, and syringes without needles. The Blue bin (Option C) is specifically for glassware, such as broken ampoules or vials. Adhering to these color-coded segregation standards is a fundamental requirement for healthcare workers to ensure occupational safety and environmental protection. Proper disposal in the white container typically leads to autoclaving and shredding or encapsulation of the metallic sharps to render them safe
questions.learning: According to the Bio-Medical Waste Management Rules, sharps must be disposed of in specific containers to prevent needle-stick injuries and the transmission of blood-borne pathogens.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A previously healthy 14-year-old boy comes to the physician because of a 5-day history of pain at the back of his left ankle. His mother had a myocardial infarction at 54 years. His BMI is 23 kg/m². A photomicrograph from a biopsy of the nodule is shown. Serum studies in this patient are most likely to show increased levels of which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Low-density lipoprotein

This patient likely has familial hypercholesterolemia (FH), suggested by tendon xanthomas at the Achilles, strong family history of premature myocardial infarction, and normal BMI. FH causes elevated LDL cholesterol, which deposits in tendons and skin as xanthomas, visible on biopsy. These nodules are cholesterol-rich, not urate crystals.

Why the others are incorrect:

B. Uric acid: Elevated in gout, but tophi in a 14-year-old without acute joint pain is unlikely; biopsy shows lipid, not urate crystals.

C. Triglycerides: Elevated triglycerides cause eruptive xanthomas, which are small papules, not tendon nodules.

D. Rheumatoid factor: Marker for rheumatoid arthritis, which presents with joint inflammation, not tendon xanthomas.
questions.learning: Low-density lipoprotein — This patient likely has familial hypercholesterolemia (FH), suggested by tendon xanthomas at the Achilles, strong family history of premature myocardial infarction, and normal BMI.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A 14-year-old girl was kidnapped by a male. The police arrested him, but he died in police custody. The inquest is conducted by
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Judicial Magistrate

BNSS 196 or section 176 Cr. P.C. deals with magistrate inquest in which the cause of death is not under natural circumstances. Magistrate inquest may be conducted by the District Magistrate, Sub-Divisional Magistrate, Tahsildar, or any other Executive Magistrate empowered by the State Government.

Indications for Magistrate Inquest:

* Death under police custody

* Death due to police firing

* Death in prison, reformatories, borstal schools

* Dowry death

* Death in a psychiatric hospital

* Exhumation

* Death or disappearance of any person, or rape of a woman who is under the custody of police or any other person authorized by the court.
questions.learning: Judicial Magistrate BNSS 196 or section 176 Cr. P.C. deals with magistrate inquest in which the cause of death is not under natural circumstances.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A newborn presents with conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, intrahepatic cholestasis, elevated alkaline phosphatase levels, and liver biopsy showing eosinophilic, PAS-positive cytoplasmic granules suggestive of alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency. What is the most common cause of jaundice in this condition?
questions.explanation: Neonatal hepatitis is a primary cause of liver dysfunction in newborns, presenting with jaundice, hepatomegaly, and conjugated hyperbilirubinemia. The specific biopsy finding of eosinophilic, PAS-positive cytoplasmic granules is highly suggestive of Alpha-1 Antitrypsin deficiency, which is a significant metabolic cause of neonatal hepatitis. Hypoplasia of the biliary tract (Option A) involves underdeveloped ducts and presents with cholestasis but is not the most common neonatal cause. A choledochal cyst (Option C) involves extrahepatic bile duct dilation and would typically be identified on imaging rather than by PAS-positive granules. Physiological jaundice (Option D) is a temporary condition that presents with unconjugated bilirubinemia, not the conjugated form seen here. Thus, the clinical constellation of cholestatic markers and specific histological inclusions confirms neonatal hepatitis
questions.learning: Neonatal hepatitis is a primary cause of liver dysfunction in newborns, presenting with jaundice, hepatomegaly, and conjugated hyperbilirubinemia. The specific biopsy finding of eosinophilic, PAS-positive cytoplasmic granules is highly suggestive of…

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A farmer presents with a warty cutaneous growth on his foot. Histopathological image of the growth is given below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Chromoblastomycosis

This patient is likely a case of chromoblastomycosis.

It is a subcutaneous infection caused by fungi belonging to the genera fonsecaea. It enters the skin by traumatic inoculation. Hence, seen in woodcutter and farmers. It appears as sclerotic bodies on histopathology examination and copper penny bodies on KOH mount. Treatment with antifungals are given.

Other options:

Mycetoma:

* It is caused by various types of Fungi (Eumycetoma) or filamentous bacteria (actinomycetes).

* It presents with a painless nodule but with time, papules and pustules may form which breaks down to form draining sinuses, with the discharge of granules.

Image: Mycetoma of Foot.

Sporotrichosis: Nodules generally develop along the draining lymphatics.

Phaeohyphomycosis : it is a chronic fungal infection involving the skin and subcutaneous tissue. The lesions maybe plaques which are verrucous, hypertkeratotis or ulcerated. The fungi implicated are usually of the class Phialophora or Cladophora or other demetacious fungi.
questions.learning: Chromoblastomycosis — This patient is likely a case of chromoblastomycosis. It is a subcutaneous infection caused by fungi belonging to the genera fonsecaea.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Asbestosis is a chronic lung condition resulting from prolonged inhalation of asbestos fibers. Which type of cancer is most commonly linked to this disease?
questions.explanation: Asbestosis is a form of pneumoconiosis caused by the chronic inhalation of asbestos fibers, typically in occupational settings like construction or shipbuilding. While asbestos exposure significantly increases the risk of bronchogenic carcinoma, it is most uniquely and strongly associated with malignant mesothelioma. Mesothelioma is a rare and aggressive cancer that develops in the thin layer of tissue covering the lungs (pleura) or abdomen (peritoneum). Option B (Anthracosis) is not a malignancy but a benign accumulation of carbon pigment in the lungs. Option C (Hepatocellular carcinoma) and Option D (Renal cell carcinoma) are malignancies related to viral hepatitis or genetic mutations and are not linked to asbestos inhalation. The latency period between asbestos exposure and the development of mesothelioma is often 20 to 40 years. Because of this strong link, any patient with a clinical history of asbestosis must be closely monitored for pleural changes or effusions indicative of malignancy
questions.learning: Asbestosis is a form of pneumoconiosis caused by the chronic inhalation of asbestos fibers, typically in occupational settings like construction or shipbuilding.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: What is the most appropriate next step in management for a 36-week pregnant woman with a prosthetic mitral valve, currently receiving warfarin therapy and having an INR of 3?
options: Stop warfarin, start LMWH and aspirin
questions.explanation: Warfarin is a highly effective anticoagulant for prosthetic heart valves but is associated with a high risk of maternal and fetal bleeding during delivery. To minimize this risk, clinical guidelines recommend stopping Warfarin at approximately 36 weeks of gestation and switching to a shorter-acting anticoagulant, typically Low Molecular Weight Heparin (LMWH) or unfrequented heparin. This allows for safer management of labor and easier reversal if needed. Continuing Warfarin (Option C) during delivery is contraindicated due to intracranial hemorrhage risks for the neonate and maternal hemorrhage. Aspirin alone (Option B) is insufficient to prevent valve thrombosis. While some protocols add aspirin to LMWH (Option D), the primary and most essential next step at 36 weeks is the transition from oral warfarin to injectable heparin. Therefore, starting LMWH is the standard obstetric management for this patient to ensure a safe delivery
questions.learning: Warfarin is a highly effective anticoagulant for prosthetic heart valves but is associated with a high risk of maternal and fetal bleeding during delivery.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs can cause secondary weight gain? I. Insulin II. Propranolol III. Orlistat IV. Thyroxine Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. I and II only

Several medications can cause secondary weight gain through mechanisms such as increased appetite, fluid retention, reduced metabolic rate, or improved anabolic state. Identifying drug-induced weight gain is important in the evaluation and management of obesity.

• I. Insulin ✅

• Insulin commonly causes weight gain due to improved glucose utilization, reduced glycosuria, increased fat storage, and occasional defensive overeating to prevent hypoglycemia.

• II. Propranolol ✅

• β-blockers (especially propranolol) may cause modest weight gain by reducing basal metabolic rate, decreasing exercise tolerance, and promoting fatigue.

• III. Orlistat ❌

• Orlistat promotes weight loss by inhibiting gastric and pancreatic lipases, reducing intestinal fat absorption by about 30%.

• IV. Thyroxine ❌

• Thyroxine increases basal metabolic rate and generally causes weight loss, especially when used to treat hypothyroidism.
questions.learning: I and II only Several medications can cause secondary weight gain through mechanisms such as increased appetite, fluid retention, reduced metabolic rate, or improved anabolic state.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text:
A COPD patient with a history of smoking presents with respiratory symptoms. High resolution CT showed panacinar emphysema. Which enzyme deficiency is associated with this condition?

Periodic Acid–Schiff = PAS

Alpha 1 anti trypsin = α1AT
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Alpha-1 antitrypsin

Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency is associated with panacinar emphysema.

Panacinar or panlobular emphysema is associated with α1 antitrypsin (α1AT) deficiency. It is exacerbated by smoking. Panacinar occurs more commonly in lower zones and the anterior margins of the lung. In this type, the acini from respiratory bronchiole to terminal blind alveoli are uniformly enlarged.

α1AT deficiency is an autosomal-recessive disorder of protein misfolding. Deficiency of α1AT protein results in excessive degradation of alveoli by neutrophil elastase causing panacinar emphysema. It also causes liver disease as a consequence of the abnormal accumulation of the misfolded protein within hepatocytes.  α1AT deficiency is characterized by the presence of round-to-oval cytoplasmic globular inclusions in hepatocytes. These hepatocytes are strongly Periodic acid–Schiff positive and diastase resistant.

Trypsin, chymotrypsin, and elastase are endopeptidases. They cleave the internal peptide bonds. Trypsin is specific for cleavage at the sites of basic amino acids, while chymotrypsin and elastase are specific for cleavage at neutral amino acids.

Other options:

Option B: Elastase is inhibited by alpha-1 antitrypsin. In the case of alpha 1 antitrypsin deficiency, there is the destruction of lung tissue (elastin) by the elastase released by macrophages.

Option C: Chymotrypsin degrades trypsin and protects the pancreas from trypsin-related injury.

Option D: Type 2 surfactant deficiency is associated with respiratory distress syndrome as type 2 pneumocytes produce the surfactant which decreases the surface tension.
questions.learning: Alpha-1 antitrypsin Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency is associated with panacinar emphysema. Panacinar or panlobular emphysema is associated with α1 antitrypsin (α1AT) deficiency.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Consider the following pairs. How many of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Only two pairs

Abnormal urine discoloration can provide an important clue to the drug or poison ingested. Recognizing characteristic urine colors helps in the early diagnosis of poisoning and guides appropriate management.

Why is the answer B (Only two pairs)?

• 1. Pink – Cephalosporin ✅

• Some cephalosporins (especially cefdinir, particularly with iron-containing preparations) may cause pink to reddish discoloration of urine.

• 2. Brown – Chloroquine ✅

• Chloroquine poisoning may produce dark brown urine, often due to hemoglobinuria or myoglobinuria in severe toxicity.

• 3. Greenish blue – Phenazopyridine ❌

• Phenazopyridine classically causes orange to red-orange urine, not greenish-blue.
• Greenish-blue urine is classically seen with methylene blue, amitriptyline, propofol, indomethacin, and triamterene.

• 4. Red-orange – Amitriptyline ❌

• Amitriptyline is associated with blue-green urine, whereas red-orange urine is characteristic of phenazopyridine or rifampicin.
questions.learning: Only two pairs Abnormal urine discoloration can provide an important clue to the drug or poison ingested. Recognizing characteristic urine colors helps in the early diagnosis of poisoning and guides appropriate management.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient not able to chew the food and food stuck between cheeks and teeth. Which muscle weakness is associated with this clinical condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Buccinator

The correct answer is Buccinator.

Buccinator compresses the cheek against the teeth, preventing food from accumulating in the vestibule during mastication.

Weakness leads to food getting trapped between cheek and teeth, a classic sign seen in facial nerve palsy.
questions.learning: Buccinator — The correct answer is Buccinator. Buccinator compresses the cheek against the teeth, preventing food from accumulating in the vestibule during mastication.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following organisms exhibits pathogenesis by cell-to-cell transfer, facilitated by actin filaments, eliminating the need for extracellular transport?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Listeria monocytogenes

Listeria monocytogenes exhibit pathogenesis by cell-to-cell transfer with the help of the host cell's actin filaments.

L. monocytogenes is a short, gram-positive, non-spore-forming bacteria. It enters the body through the GIT after ingestion of contaminated food such as cheese or vegetables. It has two cell-surface proteins, internalins A and B, which interact with the epithelial E-cadherin and promote its own phagocytosis into the gut epithelial cells, leading to the formation of the phagolysosome.

Low pH activates the bacterium to produce listeriolysin O, which lyses the phagolysosome and allows Listeria to escape into the cytoplasm of the epithelial cell. Here, the organisms proliferate and produce ActA, a listerial protein that induces host cell actin polymerization, which propels them to the host cell membrane.

While pushing against the host cell membrane, they produce elongated protrusions called filopods, which are ingested by adjacent epithelial cells, macrophages, and hepatocytes, resulting in the release of listeriae and the cycle starts again.

In this way, Listeria moves from cell-to-cell using the host's actin framework without being exposed to antibodies, complement systems, or neutrophils. Gram-negative bacteria like Shigella flexneri and rickettsiae also make use of the host cells’ actin and contractile system to spread their infections, just like Listeria.

Other options:

Option A: Enterohemorrhagic Ecoli (EHEC) is one of the six different types of diarrheagenic E.coli. They produce verocytotoxin (VT) or Shiga-like toxin (SLT), which can lead to a spectrum of illnesses, from mild diarrhea to more severe, life-threatening conditions such as hemorrhagic colitis (bleeding in the colon) and hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS), which can cause kidney failure.

Option B: Salmonella typhi is a non-spore-forming, facultative anaerobic, gram-negative bacilli. Following ingestion of contaminated foods or beverages, salmonellae enter the small intestine, where they pass through the epithelium via specialised M-cells overlying the Peyer's patches, and then enter the intestinal lymphatics, with subsequent invasion into the bloodstream. Unlike Listeria, it does not utilise the actin filament of the host cell.

Option D: H.pylori is a gram-negative, flagellated, helical bacterium. Virulence factors of H.pylori include:

• Flagella- which allows motility in viscous gastric mucous
• Urease production- urease generates ammonia and bicarbonate from endogenous urea, creating an alkaline microenvironment that protects it from gastric acidic pH.
• Adhesins- for bacterial attachment to surface foveolar cells
• Toxins- such as cytotoxin-associated gene A (CagA) and Vacuolization cytotoxin (VacA). CagA is translocated into the gastric epithelial cells where it interferes with the epithelial cells’ cytoskeletal structure and induces IL-8 production, leading to neutrophil attraction. VacA causes gastric mucosal injury by inhibiting T cells.
questions.learning: Listeria monocytogenes Listeria monocytogenes exhibit pathogenesis by cell-to-cell transfer with the help of the host cell's actin filaments. L. monocytogenes is a short, gram-positive, non-spore-forming bacteria.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A militant presents with rashes all over his body sparing the palms and soles. On examination, he was febrile and lice were noted. Which of the following is responsible for his condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Rickettsia prowazekii

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of epidemic or louse-borne typhus caused by Rickettsia prowazekii.

Pediculus corporis (human body louse) is the vector for the parasite, although the head louse may also transmit the disease. After the incubation period of 5 - 15 days, the disease typically starts with fever and chills. By around 4 - 5th day of fever, a characteristic rash appears, which starts on the trunk and spreads over the limbs but spares the face, palms, and soles.

The infection can be transmitted by

• Contaminated louse feces rubbed through abrasions caused by scratching
• Inhalation of aerosols of dried louse feces or directly through the conjunctiva

The disease is often severe with the fever lasting for over 2 weeks and is more fatal in patients older than 40 years of age.

Other options:

Option A: R. typhi causes murine (flea-borne) or endemic typhus. Rats are the reservoirs of infection and the parasite is transmitted by Xenopsylla cheopis (flea). The infection is transmitted when the flea feces is rubbed into the bite wound. The clinical features are similar to that of epidemic typhus but are milder and rarely fatal. Patients can present with fever, headache, myalgia, and rash.

Option C: R. akari causes rickettsial pox, which is a mild disease resembling varicella. The disease is transmitted by mites and the patients may present with fever, headache, and a vesicular rash.

Option D: R. conorii causes the Mediterranean spotted fever. The parasite is transmitted by ticks and the patients present with fever, headache, rash, and eschar (tache noire).
questions.learning: Rickettsia prowazekii — The given clinical scenario is suggestive of epidemic or louse-borne typhus caused by Rickettsia prowazekii. Pediculus corporis (human body louse) is the vector for the parasite, although the head louse may also transmit the disease.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: You are a medical officer at a PHC. Which of the following would you advise for mass prophylaxis/ treatment for anemia?
options: FeSO4 + Vit C + Folate + Vit B12
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. FeSO4 + Vit C + Folate + Vit B12

Among the given options, FeSO4 + vitamin C + Folate + vitamin B12 may be considered for mass prophylaxis against anemia.

Vit C enhances the absorption of iron from the stomach by acting as a reducing substance.

Subclinical folate deficiency is seen in up to 30% of North Indian pregnant women. Moreover, it may be masked by widespread iron deficiency. It is, for this reason, iron and folate supplementation is carried out in national programmes.

Clinical vitamin B12 deficiency is not commonly encountered, but subclinical cases might be seen in up to 30% of adults and children due to widespread restriction to consumption of vegetarian products only. Hence supplementing vitamin B12 is a good idea provided the cost factor is not an issue.

Option B: Iron (III) hydroxide polymaltose was marketed as being superior to iron sulfate in terms of efficacy, but it lacked any data to back up the evidence.

Option C: Ferrous fumarate may be considered for the treatment of iron deficiency anemia with similar efficacy as that of ferrous sulfate.

Option D: Injection iron sucrose or any parenteral form is not used as a first-line option. It is only indicated if the oral form is not tolerated.
questions.learning: FeSO4 + Vit C + Folate + Vit B12 Among the given options, FeSO4 + vitamin C + Folate + vitamin B12 may be considered for mass prophylaxis against anemia.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: What is the mechanism of action of alteplase a tissue plasminogen activator(tPA)?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Promotes fibrinolysis

The mechanism of action of alteplase, a recombinant tissue plasminogen activator is by promoting fibrinolysis.

Alteplase is a recombinant tissue plasminogen activator and activates plasminogen bound to fibrin, and catalyses the conversion of plasminogen to plasmin, resulting in increased formation of plasmin. This results in fibrinolysis of formed thrombus(thrombolysis). It is indicated in pulmonary embolism with hemodynamic instability, severe deep vein thrombosis, ascending thrombophlebitis, acute ischemic stroke, and acute myocardial infarction.

Alteplase has the advantage of only activating plasminogen bound to fibrin (clot specific) but not free plasminogen.

Contraindications of alteplase:

* Risk of bleeding - subarachnoid hemorrhage, intracranial hemorrhage (Option B) or any ongoing internal bleeding.

* Recent history of significant head trauma, intracranial or intraspinal surgery, within the past 3 months.

* Intracranial neoplasm

* Bleeding diathesis

* Arteriovenous malformation/ aneurysm

* Severe uncontrolled hypertension

Pearl PF0777: Plasminogen activators (classification of fibrinolytics)

Fibrin non-specific plasminogen activators

* Streptokinase - least fibrin specific and has the lowest incidence of intracranial hemorrhage

* Anistreplase

* Urokinase

Fibrin specific plasminogen activators

* Alteplase - has the shortest half-life

* Tenecteplase - most fibrin specific and given as a single bolus dose

* Reteplase

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Identify the pathology from the given flow-volume loop:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Fixed central airway obstruction

The given flow-volume curve shows flattening of both the inspiratory and expiratory limbs, which is seen in fixed obstruction of the central or upper airway.

The curve denotes airflow limitation during both inspiration and expiration.

Examples of fixed central airway obstruction include tracheal stenosis (caused by intubation) and circular tracheal tumors.

Other options:

Option A: The image given below shows a concave upward, pattern in the expiratory limb (scooped-out or coved) pattern seen in lower airway obstruction. Examples include asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, bronchiectasis, and bronchiolitis.

Option C: The image below shows airflow limitation and flattening in the expiratory limb of the loop. It is seen in variable, nonfixed intrathoracic obstruction.

Examples: intrathoracic airway, bronchogenic cysts, or tracheal lesions.

Option D: The image below shows airflow limitation and flattening in the inspiratory limb of the loop. It is seen in nonfixed variable extrathoracic obstruction.

Examples: vocal cord paralysis, extrathoracic tracheomalacia, polychondritis, etc.
questions.learning: Fixed central airway obstruction — The given flow-volume curve shows flattening of both the inspiratory and expiratory limbs, which is seen in fixed obstruction of the central or upper airway.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient with an acute subarachnoid hemorrhage is found to have associated vitreous/intraocular hemorrhage on ophthalmological examination. What is this association known as?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Terson syndrome

Terson syndrome refers to intraocular hemorrhage associated with acute intracranial hemorrhage, classically subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH).

The ocular hemorrhage may occur at different levels, including:

• Vitreous hemorrhage
• Subhyaloid/preretinal hemorrhage
• Intraretinal hemorrhage

It is classically described following aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage, although it may also occur with other causes of sudden severe intracranial hemorrhage or raised intracranial pressure.

Why not the other options?

• B. Duane syndrome: Congenital cranial dysinnervation disorder characterized by limitation of horizontal eye movements with globe retraction and narrowing of the palpebral fissure on adduction.
• C. Brown syndrome: Characterized by restriction of elevation of the eye in adduction due to dysfunction of the superior oblique tendon–trochlea complex.
• D. Tolosa–Hunt syndrome: Causes painful ophthalmoplegia due to granulomatous inflammation involving the cavernous sinus, superior orbital fissure, or orbital apex.

Educational Objective:

• Remember the classic association:

• Subarachnoid hemorrhage + intraocular/vitreous hemorrhage → Terson syndrome
questions.learning: Terson syndrome Terson syndrome refers to intraocular hemorrhage associated with acute intracranial hemorrhage, classically subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: In a child with bilateral sensorineural hearing loss who does not benefit from conventional hearing aids, what is the most appropriate next line of management?
questions.explanation: When a child has profound bilateral sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL) and derives insufficient benefit from conventional high-power hearing aids after a trial period, a cochlear implant is the gold standard of care. Unlike hearing aids that amplify sound, a cochlear implant bypasses damaged hair cells in the cochlea and directly stimulates the auditory nerve. Option A (BAHA) is used for conductive or mixed hearing loss where the inner ear is functional but sound cannot reach it. Option B (Tympanoplasty) is a surgical repair for a perforated eardrum or middle ear structures and does not treat sensorineural loss. Option C is what the patient has already failed. Early implantation (ideally before age 2) is critical for the development of normal speech and language skills due to the brain's neuroplasticity. The success of the procedure depends on an intact auditory nerve and dedicated post-operative auditory-verbal habilitation
questions.learning: When a child has profound bilateral sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL) and derives insufficient benefit from conventional high-power hearing aids after a trial period, a cochlear implant is the gold standard of care.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient was prescribed an antipsychotic drug following which he developed parkinsonism. Which of the following drugs can be given?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Trihexiphenidyl

Trihexyphenidyl is the drug of choice for drug-induced parkinsonism. It is a central anticholinergic.

Drug-induced parkinsonism is a condition caused by certain drugs having D2 antagonistic action (typical antipsychotics). The decrease in dopaminergic activity results in an unbalanced cholinergic activity. Anticholinergics act by restoring the balance.
questions.learning: Trihexiphenidyl Trihexyphenidyl is the drug of choice for drug-induced parkinsonism. Drug-induced parkinsonism is a condition caused by certain drugs having D2 antagonistic action (typical antipsychotics).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is the best treatment for the relapse of immune thrombocytopenic purpura?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Splenectomy

Splenectomy is the treatment of choice in a case of immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) relapse after first line therapy with glucocorticoids. The relapse usually occurs once they are tapered. Vaccination against encapsulated organisms (pneumococcus, meningococcus, H. influenzae) is advised before splenectomy is performed.

It is important to note that in some patients ITP resolves by itself, and observation along with intermittent IV immunoglobulins and anti - Rh(D) administration or administration of a thrombopoietin receptor agonist (eltrombopag, romiplostim) can be a viable option before splenectomy is considered.

The treatment of ITP is as follows:

Clinical features
Management

1.

Minor bleeding manifestations (and/or)

Platelet count > 5000/ μL

Prednisone (OR)

Anti-D immunoglobulin therapy - effective only in Rh-positive patients (OR)

Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG)

2.

Severe ITP (any of the following):

• Significant GI / intracranial bleeding
• Platelet count < 5000/μL
• Signs of impending bleeding (retinal or large oral mucosal bleeds)

Platelet transfusion (AND)

High-dose glucocorticoids (AND)

IVIG / Anti-D immunoglobulins + Rituximab

3.
Relapse after first-line therapy
Splenectomy

4.
Unresponsive to all other therapy or relapse after splenectomy
Thrombopoietin receptor agonists - romiplostim (subcutaneous), eltrombopag (oral)

ITP is an acquired disorder characterized by the immune-mediated destruction of platelets and possibly inhibition of platelet release from the megakaryocyte. Secondary causes of ITP include systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), HIV-AIDS, and Hepatitis C.

ITP usually presents with mucocutaneous bleeding, very low platelet count, and normal peripheral blood cells. Patients typically exhibit ecchymoses and petechiae or they may incidentally discover thrombocytopenia during a routine complete blood count. Rarely, life-threatening bleeding may occur. The presence of wet purpura (blood blisters in the mouth) and retinal hemorrhages can serve as warning signs of potentially life-threatening bleeding.
questions.learning: Splenectomy Splenectomy is the treatment of choice in a case of immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) relapse after first line therapy with glucocorticoids.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A 30-year-old patient presents with several weeks of persistent low mood, marked fatigue, reduced appetite, and loss of motivation. They also report a constant sense of hopelessness and a clear lack of interest or pleasure in activities they previously enjoyed. Based on this clinical picture, which core symptom is most characteristic and fundamental to a diagnosis of depression?
options: Loss of interest in pleasurable activity
questions.explanation: In the clinical diagnosis of Major Depressive Disorder (MDD), the fundamental and highly specific symptom is Loss of interest in pleasurable activities, also known as Anhedonia. While Low mood (Option B) is a core diagnostic criterion, anhedonia is often considered the most biological and pervasive marker of the depressive state. Suicidal ideation (Option A) and Loss of appetite (Option D) are common and significant symptoms included in the diagnostic criteria but are considered secondary to the primary core emotional deficits. According to the ICD-10 and DSM-5, a diagnosis of depression requires at least one of the two "core" symptoms: persistent low mood or anhedonia. Anhedonia represents a significant disruption in the brain's reward system and is often associated with more severe or melancholic subtypes of depression. Identifying this specific lack of "drive" and pleasure is essential for clinicians to distinguish clinical depression from ordinary sadness or grief
questions.learning: In the clinical diagnosis of Major Depressive Disorder (MDD), the fundamental and highly specific symptom is Loss of interest in pleasurable activities, also known as Anhedonia.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: In arterial blood gas (ABG) analysis, which of the following parameters is a derived or calculated value rather than one that is directly measured?
questions.explanation: In arterial blood gas (ABG) analysis, certain parameters are directly measured, while others are derived mathematically. pH is measured using a pH electrode pO₂ is directly measured using an oxygen electrode pCO₂ is directly measured using a carbon dioxide electrode In contrast, bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻) is not measured directly. It is a calculated value, obtained using the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation, which relates pH and pCO₂: Thus, the ABG analyzer computes bicarbonate based on measured values

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 25-year-old woman (P1L1) with one living child is planning to conceive again and has been newly diagnosed with Graves’ disease. Which antithyroid drug is preferred for use during early pregnancy?
questions.explanation: For women with hyperthyroidism planning a pregnancy, Propylthiouracil (PTU) is the drug of choice during the early gestation (first trimester) (Option A). PTU is preferred because it is more highly protein-bound and crosses the placenta less readily than other options, and most importantly, it is not associated with the specific "methimazole embryopathy". Methimazole (Option B) and its prodrug Carbimazole (Option C) are associated with rare but severe congenital defects such as aplasia cutis, choanal atresia, and esophageal atresia when used in early pregnancy. Many protocols involve switching the patient to PTU for the first trimester and then back to Methimazole for the remainder of the pregnancy to minimize PTU-related maternal hepatotoxicity. Therefore, to protect the fetus during organogenesis, PTU is the definitive standard recommendation for early pregnancy management of Graves' disease
questions.learning: For women with hyperthyroidism planning a pregnancy, Propylthiouracil (PTU) is the drug of choice during the early gestation (first trimester) (Option A).

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A man assaults his colleague and, when apprehended, states that he heard his boss’s voice instructing him that the colleague intended to kill him. He claims that he was not mentally stable and did not understand the nature or consequences of his actions. What is the next appropriate step in the management of this case?
options: Refer him to a psychiatrist for comprehensive evaluation of mental state
Do not proceed with the trial as he is not legally responsible for his actions
Punish him immediately as the act of violence is proven
Proceed with routine trial without psychiatric referral
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Refer him to a psychiatrist for comprehensive evaluation of mental state

In an accused person showing signs of mental illness (e.g., hallucinations, delusions), the first step is psychiatric evaluation to assess mental state and fitness for trial.

• The accused describes auditory hallucinations and paranoid delusions → suggestive of psychosis (e.g., schizophrenia)
•

Two important legal assessments:

• Fitness to stand trial: Can he understand proceedings and defend himself?
• Criminal responsibility (insanity defense): Mental state at the time of the act

•

Determines whether the accused is:

• Fit or unfit for trial
• Eligible for insanity defense (McNaughten rule)

• Guides further legal proceedings

Why not other options:

• B: Cannot declare not responsible without evaluation
• C: Immediate punishment ignores mental health assessment
• D: Trial should not proceed without assessing fitness

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which among the following is the least radiosensitive cell?
questions.explanation: Radiosensitivity depends on the rate of cell division and level of differentiation (Law of Bergonié and Tribondeau). Cells that divide rapidly are more radiosensitive, while non-dividing, mature cells are more radioresistant. Platelets are considered the least radiosensitive because they are non-dividing cell fragments derived from megakaryocytes and have minimal metabolic and genetic activity. Since they do not undergo mitosis, they are less affected by radiation compared to other blood cells. Why other options are incorrect: (A) Red blood cells: Although anucleate and resistant, they are not considered the least radiosensitive in standard exam context. (C) Lymphocytes: Among the most radiosensitive cells due to high turnover and metabolic activity. (D) Neutrophils: Derived from actively dividing precursors, making them more radiosensitive than platelets
questions.learning: Radiosensitivity depends on the rate of cell division and level of differentiation (Law of Bergonié and Tribondeau). Cells that divide rapidly are more radiosensitive, while non-dividing, mature cells are more radioresistant.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 17-year-old male with severe acne vulgaris is planned for treatment with oral isotretinoin. Which of the following baseline investigations should be performed before initiating therapy?
options: Renal function test + Complete blood count
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Liver function test + Lipid profile

Oral isotretinoin is the most effective treatment for severe nodulocystic or treatment-resistant acne vulgaris, but it is associated with hepatotoxicity and hypertriglyceridemia. Therefore, baseline liver function tests (LFTs) and a fasting lipid profile should be obtained before starting therapy and monitored periodically during treatment.

• LFT: Detects baseline liver dysfunction, as isotretinoin can cause elevated transaminases.
• Lipid profile: Detects hypertriglyceridemia, the most common laboratory abnormality during therapy.

Why not the other options?

• A. Complete blood count + Lipid profile: CBC is not routinely required before isotretinoin.
• C. Renal function test + Complete blood count: Neither is routinely indicated unless clinically warranted.
• D. Liver function test + Serum electrolytes: Electrolytes are not routinely monitored with isotretinoin.
questions.learning: Liver function test + Lipid profile Oral isotretinoin is the most effective treatment for severe nodulocystic or treatment-resistant acne vulgaris, but it is associated with hepatotoxicity and hypertriglyceridemia.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The components given below are part of ___ ? Fertility Marriage Mortality Migration Social Mobility
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Demographic process

Demographic processes include fertility, mortality, marriage, migration, and social mobility.

Demographic process:

* Fertility

* Mortality

* Marriage

* Migration

* Social Mobility

Demographic cycle:

Stage 1 : High stationary High birth rate and high death rate render the population stationary. Narrow demographic gap.

Stage 2 : Early expanding Death rate declines and birth rate remains unchanged. Demographic gap starts increasing and then becomes maximum.

Stage 3 : Late expandingDeath rate decline further and birth rate falls. India is in this stage, currently
Demographic gap starts declining.

Stage 4 : Low stationary Low birth rate and low death rate renders the population stationary. Narrow demographic gap.

Stage 5 : Declining Population begins to decline as birth rate is lower than death rate. Demographic gap is negative.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the diagnosis shown in the image below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Dichorionic Diamniotic twin pregnancy

A Dichorionic Diamniotic (DCDA) twin pregnancy is identified on ultrasound by the presence of two separate placentas (or a thick intertwin membrane) and the lambda (twin-peak) sign, indicating two chorions and two amniotic sacs. DCDA twins have the lowest risk of complications among twin pregnancies.

Why not the other options?

• B. Monochorionic Monoamniotic (MCMA): Single placenta, no dividing membrane, highest risk of cord entanglement.
• C. Monochorionic Diamniotic (MCDA): Single placenta with a thin intertwin membrane and T-sign.
• D. Dichorionic Monoamniotic: Does not occur because each chorion has its own amniotic sac.

| Twin Pregnancy | Chorion | Amnion | Ultrasound Sign

| -------------- | ------- | ------ | ---------------

| DCDA | 2 | 2 | Lambda (Twin-peak) sign

| MCDA | 1 | 2 | T-sign

| MCMA | 1 | 1 | No dividing membrane
